It is very satisfactory to them that such an eminent authority as Sir Andrew Clarke, the London Physician, corroborates opinion. Here is an extract front an interesting lecture, delivered by Sir Andrew the other day, to the Students of the London Hospital:

"Tea is a blessed beverage. Ido not know what I should do without it. But there is tea and tea, an one of the teas I haveln my mind is the representation of all that is physiologically wicked. Igo about town a good deal holding consulta- tions here and there, and about five o'clock. when I get into a place, the lady of the house, will say to me ; 'Sir Andrew, you look tirociodo let me give you a cup of tea.' I say • thank you very much. But the tea has stood for half-an-hour, and she remarks,' I know you do you not like it strong, Sir Andrew.' and she then pours about a tablespoonful of the tea into a cup and fills thecup up with water. Now I call it positivecruelty to give tea like that to anybody and I hope you, gentlemen, will always set your face against it. Tea. to be useful, should be first of an Black China Tea ; the Indian Tea which is being cultivated has become so powerful in its effects upon the nervous system that a cup of it taken early in the morning, as many do. so disorders the nervous system that those who take it actually get into a state of tea intoxication, and it produces a form of nervous disturbance, which is most painful to witness. If you want to have, either for yourselves or for your patients, tea which will not injure and which will refresh, get Black China Tea, putting in the right measure—the old fashioned teaspooultil for each person and one for the blessed Pot. Then pour on briskly boiling water, and within five minutes you nattst pour it off again., or it will become wicked instead of good." Such is Sir Andrew Clarke's opinion and advise. A few words of warning, however, are necessary to those who have for gotten what this.crid fashioned tea is like. The colour of the ,tea after it is nrewed will be found tobe much paler than that now in use, and the taste may not be acceptable at first oMtng to its apparent insipidness ; but if its use is persisted in, it will very soon be found to be much more suitable for the se-stem,. an,l if, in a week to two after its use, a trial is again made of the kind now in ordinary use, you will wonder howevernyou could have nem using it,and you will endorse Sir Andrew's statement.

div.head: "CAPITAL" CHAT.
div.p: "CAPITAL" CHAT.

Her Majesty has given Lord Salisbury a condi- tional promise that she will open Parliament in per- son' and it is to suit her Majesty's convenience that the date of that function had been deferred until so unusually late a day as Tuesday, February 9.

Lord lingh Cecil, the youngest'son of Lord Salis- bury, who was on Saturday nominated to a fellow- ship at Hertford College, Oxford, is likely to prove an acquisition to that society. He obtained a first in history, and showed consilerable ability as a speaker at the Union. He is no athlete, something of a cynic, and a clever man.

The troopship Malabar is taking out three live Kerry bulls on the order of the Indian Government. The idea of exporting "Irish bulls" opens up an entirely new source of wealth for the Emerald Isle, for we believe the supply is practically inexhaust- ible. But what will " Baboo English" become with this new element grafted upon it?

Dr. Mary Hall, who was the principal speakey at Monday night's temperance meeting at Exeter Ball, is not, as was generally supposed, an Ameri- can, but an English, lady. She spent eight years of her life in America ; and she came back partly be- cause British women need her to teach them the medical aspect of the drink question far more than her sisters of the United States.

Mr. Balfour talked on Wednesday to the Conser- vatives of Huddersfield, but his remarks were spoken over their heads to a much wider _audience. He directly addressed the wing of his own follow- ing which has gone astray. There was no sign of surrender in his speech. Strengthen the position of the one central Parliament and decentralise local affairs—that is the programme. This must be done, or there will be a Home Rule Parliament to perform the duty after its own fashion.

The Countess Russell, whose matrimonial suit has been heard this week is the second daughter of Lady Selina Scott, and well known to all boaters on the upper reaches of the Thames. She it was who so skilfully sculled her mother's guests in the little cherry-coloured dingy, "The Little Duck," to and fro to to her house-boat during the Henley and Marlow regattas. Lady Russell, who is only two- and-twenty, is a good horsewoman, and constantly to be seen driving tandem round Walton, where she resides at The Hurst, her mother's house. All the neighbouring poor have a smile for "the Lady Mabel." Among her intimate friends she is known by the pet name of "Babe."

Earl Russell is a young manof seven-and-twenty, above the average height, rather stout, and in- clined to stoop. Re has light brown hair, and a very wide forehead. The fact that he wears spec- tacles gives him a somewhat prematurely aged ap- pearance. Earl Russell is only the second holder of the title. His father, Lord Amberley, who gave great promise as a writer, died in 1876, predeceas- ing his grandfather, who survived till 1878. , Earl Russell, who was left fatherless and motherless at ten 'years of age, was brought up by his grand- mother, the Dowager Countess Russell, with whom he resides at Pembroke Lodge, in Richmond-park.

The House of Lords will, owing to the Bishop of Carlisle's death, receive an acquisition at the next meeting of Parliament in the person of the new Bishop of Bangor, Dr. Lewis Lloyd, who has had to wait a very short time for his turn to come, as he has not been a bishop for much more than a year. The new bishop will be generally congratulated through Wales on his elevation, as be is generally popular. As a schoolmaster at Friars School, Ban- gor, and at Brecon, he did much for Welsh educa- tion. He also takes an interest in the Eisteddfod, and presided this year at Festiniog, and even frater- nises 'with Welsh Liberals at the N.L.C. What is still better, he has recently written a letter to the "South Wales Star" on the latest job of Lord Hals- bury, and condemned the appointment of English judges in Welsh-speaking Wales. •

Professsor Skeat has put in a plea for writing verse on the unusual ground that it "leads the wayto writing prose." In soma respects prose is, ih his opinion, the harder of the two. In prose, (he says) you have to be more explicit, and to make clear to all men what is the sense intended; and I am not at all sure that all poets impose upon themselves such conditions. It is to be hoped that the Brovening eociety -will not take offenceat -thie. In Dr. Skeat's opinion one reason why many men cannot speak in public is that they only know English conversationally. A man who has to make a speech might, he considers. conceivably, think within himself—" Well, you know, it's rather rough on a fellow to get him on his legs ;" but he also feels that such a form of expressir,n is beneath the dignity of the occasion: and hence his confu- sion.

There is no such thing as a home in America, according to a friend of Mrs. Frances Courtenay Baylor, the American novelist. There is abundance of handsome lodging-hOuses, where people eat and sleep and dress very comfortably when not engaged or obliged to eat, sleep or dress elsewhere. But a home requires a wife in it. And where (asks this,. cynic) are our wives? /n the streets (he answers), at teas, luncheons, dinners, in the shops, travelling abroad, or away for an "outing," at Browning Cluhs, Faith-Cure Seances, Women's Rights Meet- ings, Ibsen Re-unions,Meredith Mornings, Blavatsky Circles, Indigent Female Rescues, Arriving Fmigr- ants' Shelters, Mothers' Meetings, Church Sociables, Jewish Refuges, Bulgarian Bazaars anywhere everywhere, except at home. America, he thinks will soon have to adopt the Zastepn " dodge " of locking up their shoes to keep them in the house.

The death of Mr. Richard Power,. M.P., removes from the Irish Parliamentaiy benches one of the most genial and popular of their occupants. No one ever had a harsh or unkind word of Dick Power,. as he was known amongst his colleagues; and no one ever heard him give expression to an ungenerous word of friend or foe. He voted for the retention of Isaac Butt's Ileadership years ago; he voted again for Shaw, as against the claims of Pltrnell, and last year, as he himself avowed, he voted in favour of his " chief " from an inherent hatred of change. But it is notorious that he dissociated' himself from the later stages of Parnellism. Mr. Power had been married only a few days before,and his death is therefore almost tragic. He had been engaged to Miss O'Donnell for many years past ; and,. although the young lovers were both in affluent eir- cumstances, various obstacles prevented the union.. Mr. Power was the only member of the Irish party who dined with the Prince of Wales.

There are some reminiscences of Madame Thg- lioni in "London Society" of this month which recall the glorious times of the ballet. The writer only knew the once famous dancer in her later days, when an evil turn of fortune's wheel com- pelled her for a while to earn her living by teach- ing. One day when her visitor called she found the poor old lady's heart rejoiced with a gleam of royal favour. Thee Queen had happened to call that morning at Kensington Palace just as her young cousin the Princess Victoria of Teck was starting for Connaught-square to receive her danc- ing lesson, and hearing where she was going, her Majesty charged her with the following message to the veteran artiste: "Tell Madame Taglioni from me," she said, "what great pleasure it gives me td know that you are receiving lessons from gush an instructress. Tell her, also, that it was her inimi- table grace—which I can never forget—that in- spired me with the passionate love of dancing . which 1 possessed in my youth."
WRECK OF A VESSFL.
LOSS OF OVER 220 LIVES.

NEW YORK, MONDAY.—According to advices from Mexico, a vessel which has arrived at Manzanilla reports traving passed the wreck of the brig Tahiti, which was floating bottom upwards. This news has excited a pain- ful interest here, for the Tahiti arrived at Drake's Bay, near San Francisco, in September last, in distress. She bad on board 220 natives-of the Gilbert Island, in the Pacific, who were under contract to work in Mexico at starvation wages. As the unfortunate people were practically slaves, there was much talk of seizing the vessel, but it was decided that the authorities had no right to do so, and the brig eventually sailed. It is believed that the officers and crew, together with the 220 Gilbert Islanders, have perished. The disaster must have occurred a month ago.

div.p: PLEASANT PARAGRAPHS.

GILT-EDGED men are produced by brass. IN this world a knowbody is a nobody. . ALL men are born equal. After that the fun begins. WHILE waiting for the ought-to-bees, the will- bees may sting you. A MAN has a right to his opinions as long as ho keeps them to himself. HOISTING too much sail has wrecked many characters on life's voyage. UNLESS you can raise the wind, do not expect to play tunes on the horn of plenty. " WiUTER Is this fish fresh 2" "Don't know, I've only been here a week, sir." A FRIEND in needeis a friend who generally strikes you.for a loan of five shillings. JEALOUS people love themselves more than they do those whom they torture with their jealousy. WE ain't got no confidence in the ha'f way man. Hot an' col' meat won't spile,.,but wa'rn meat will. JOSH BILLINGS says :—" The best medicin I know for the rumatiz is to thank the Lord it ain't the gout." DUNNER—" See here, I'm tired running here after that bill of mine." Servant—" An' why don't yer kape yer bill at home, thin 2"

_ A LADY once said she could always know when she had taken too much wine at dinner—her hus- band's jokes began to seem funny. "My son, why is it that you are always be- hindband with your studies. " "Because if I were not behindhand with them I could not pursue them."

A DOCTOR assuring an old swell that he would live to be a hundred, he promptly replied—" Then I suppose my coffin may be called a cent'ry box." "Air, Adolphus 1" she murmured, "I fear I am not worthy of you. You are so gocd." "Never mind, darling," he said, tenderly, "wait till we're married." TRAVELLER: "Porter, is there another station between this and the next one 2" Porter: "No, sir; the next station is the other." (And they seemed to understand eaeh other). No man ever has a correct idea of the estimation in which he is held by his fellow-creatures until he attempts to borrow a five-pound note. FASHION has been cleverly hit °off as an "arbit- rary disease which leads all geese to follow in single file the one goosethat sets the style."
A. SCIENTIFIC wonder has discovered that "in another thousand years we shall be bald." Well, in another thousand years we sha'nt care if we are.

WE were once told that money did everything fot I a man. This set us to thinking that money won't do as much for a man as some men will do for money. A MAN was heard to remark to a friend the other day—" Say, 'Arry, me boy, do you want to know how to raise some dust ?" "Yes, I do, lam very hard up." "Well, shake a carpet." "Did you know," said a cunning Gentile to a Jew, "that they hang Jews and jackasses together in Portland ? " " Indeed ? " retorted Solomon, "den it ish well dat you and I ish not dere." "FATHER, is a blind man always heavy ? " "Don't ask such foolish questions; you know very well he is not." "Well, pap, you know he is generally led." At this juncture the juvenile offender dodged a flying book. HOUSEMAID (to footman who is beating the dust out of his master's coat)—" What makes you put on such a merry face when beating master's coat, Johann ? " Johann (in a whisper)—" Whist I I'm thinking master's inside 1" UNCLE JAMES, who is a trifle near, has given his niece a silver watch for her new year's present. "I'd have made it a gold one, my dear, but then how much greater the loss if you had been so unfortunate as to have it stolen."

A MAN taxed a friend with having been "obfus- cated," to use a polite phrase, on the previous evening. "That could not be," the friend replied; "I am a teetotaller." "Ah, then," was the quick answer, "you were probably water-tight 1" STRANGER (to young man consulting his watch) —"I see that you are carrying your first gold watch." Young Man (somewhat surprised)—" Er-yes, sir; but how do you know that 2" Stranger—" Because you carry it in a chamois-skin case." AT a gathering at which Moore was present they talked of Sir Alexander M— and his son, on -whom the following conundrum was made:—" Why is Sir A. like a Lapland winter 1" "Because he is a long night (knight), and his sun (son) never shines,'

A FARMER and his wife went into a dentist's "How much do you charge for fillin' teeth 7" asked the farmer. "From 10s. to £l." "And for pull- ing 7" "2s. Gd." " Mariar," he said, turning to his wife, "you'd better get it pulled." BlDDY—There's a couple o' ladies called, Missus De Vere. Mrs. De Vere—Oh, dear, I can't see any- one now. Excuse me, Biddy. Tell them I'm asleep. Biddy—Missna De Vere presents her compliments, an' sez she't very sorry, but she's aslape. "I MUST have order," said the magistrate of Mulberry-street, looking round the court; "I must -and will have less noise and confusion here. I have already disposed of three important cases without being able to hear a single word of the evidence." HE--" I'm going to propose, Miss Edith "—. She (interrupting)—" 0 my, Mr. Jenkins, so sudden and in such a strange place 1 " He (desperately)— "I'm going to propose that we stay here when the rest go to suppgr, because—because—l've left my purse at home." ' INDIGNANT Mrs. Smith—" You are home very late. I wonder that you got here at all to-night." Plausi- ble Mr. Smith (blandly)—" I wonder too, my dear. ' The snow drifts are terrible. It was two hours - before I got out of one. Policeman kindly assisted me at last."

AT one of the Board Schools the master, in' a general kaercise, wrote the word "dozen" on the black board, and asked the pupils to each write a sentence Containing the word. He was somewhat taken back to find on one of the papers the follow ing unique sentence—" I dozen know my lesson."

THE late Bernal Osborne, having delighted the House of Commons by one of his brilliant speeches, soon after met an artist, one of whose pictures he warmly commended. The painter returned the compliment in kind, eulogising the orator's speech. "I'll tell you what," said Mr. Osborne, "I'll exchange my tongue for your palette!" IN the obituary notice of a lady an editor wrote: —"lt is feared that her husband will not be able to bear her demise," which the careless compositor, .with but a change of two letters, transformed to "it is feared that her husband will not be able to wear her chemise." The horror of the bereaved husband, and of the editor, and of the mourning relatives, may be imagined. "IT'S positively wonderful how much these child- ren learn at school, isn't it ?" "Oh, I don't know about that, when you come to consider the kind of teachers they have." "Well, I like that I would have you understand I am one of those same teachers." "Oh, then, I'll take it all back. It is, indeed, as you say, wonderful." "THEY tell me you've travelled, Mr. Crimson- beak," said Miss Fussanfeather, during a lull in the conversation the other night. "Yes, l've travelled considerable. I used to travel for a dry goods house. I wish I was travelling now." "I wish you were," innocently rejoined the young lady, noticing that both hands of the clock were pointing • upwards. SHE—" Oh, how do you do, dear Mr. Lyon? Have you forgiven me for cutting you at Mrs. Leo Hunter's last night? I was actually stupid enough to take you for that horrid bore, Mr. Tetterby Thompson, whom you're said to be so like. It's a horrid libel—you're not like him a bit." He—" A— a—l wasn't at Mrs. Leo Hunter's last night—a—a— and my name is Tetterby Thompson I" HE—" Miss Angelina, I love you." She—" But I haven't a penny in the world." He—" Excuse me; You did not allow me to finish. I love you not." She—" So; I only wanted to try you. You see I have a fortune of ten thousand pounds." He— " Yes ; but you interrupted me again. I love you not for your money's sake." She—" Well, I'm so -glad, for that was only a joke about the ten thousand -pounds." 'Ay—l say, ol' chappie, I've been wolling tenpins.—Ever twy it? Jolly good exercise; don't ye know? Algy—No, clear boy, but I've wolled cigawettes for exercise, fwequently ; yaw.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, DECEMBER 5, P9l.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, DECEMBER 5, P9l.
APPEALS AGAINST HUMAN INJUSTICE.

A great judicial crime was the condemnation and burning of Urban Grandier. The story of the possessed girls of Loudun, in France,in 1625, is well known. The nuns were poor; they hired a house and received boarders. Some of these boarders were of a frolicsome disposition, and frightened the nuns with strange noises and freaks that made them suppose the house was haunted. At this time there was at Loudun an eloquent young priest named Urban Grandier, who was an object of jeal- ousy to the canons of St. Croix, and they utilised the hauntings to effect his destruction. The nuns and girls became a prey to hysteria, and in convul- sions declared they were possessed by devils sent to them by Grandier. On this accusation the un- fortunate priest was condemned and burnt alive. Before his death he solemnly cited his persecutor, the instigator of the whole infamous plot, to meet him before the throne of the Judge of all in the course of a month from that day ; and exactly a month afterwards the man died.

Terence O'Brien was Bishop of Emly. When Limerick was beseiged, Ireton, Cromwell's com- mander in Ireland (1651) sent him word that he would give him £40,000 sterling, and permission to retire in safety, if he would exhort the people to surrender. This the Bishop refused, and Ireton ex- cepted the Bishop from amnesty ; he proposed to the beseiged to bring him the head of the prelate together with those of 20 men who had voted against surrender. If they would do this he would spare the town. This was refused by the citizens. At length the city surrendered, and the Bishop fell into the hands of Ireton. The stern Puritan at once ordered the prelate to death. Bishop O'Brien turned to the general and said," I summon Ireton, the arch-persecutor,to appear in eight days to stand before the heavenly tribune to answer for his deeds of cruelty." On the eighth day Ireton, stricken with the plague, was a corpse. In Gothland, a certain John Turson, whJ was in- nocent, was sentenced to death by a magistrate, off- hand, seated on his horse. Turson protested his innocence, and summoned the judge to attend with him before the highest Judge. As Turson's head was struck off the judge fell from his horse and broke his neck.

Meinwerk, Bishop of Paderborn, was abused by a certain monk with great violence and with many charges. The Bishop answered him : "Well, let us appear toger.ber before the Judge of both, and let Him decide between us." Singularly enough, the monk died on the same day (June 5, 1039), as did the Bishop. One of the most horrible of the many crimes com- mitted on both sides in the revolt of the Netherlands against Spanish rule was the execution of Nanning Koppezoon, by the Dutch governor of Holland. " He bore," says Mr. Motley, " with perfect forti- tude a series of incredible tortures ; after which, with his body singed from head to heel, and bis feet almost entirely flayed, he was left for six weeks to crawl about his dungeon on his knees. He was then brought back to the torture room and stretched on the rack." When finally led to execution, the Cal- vinist minister, "Julian Epeszoon, endeavoured by loud praying to drown his voice, that the people might not rise with indignation; and the dying prisoner with his last breath solemnly summoned this unworthy pastor to meet him within three days before the judgment seat of God. It is a remarkable and authentic fact," continues Mr. Motley, " that the clergyman thus summoned went home pensively from the place of execution, sickened immediately, and died upon the appointed day" (1575).—Chambers' Journal.

div.head: IN THE WILDEST WEST.
div.p: IN THE WILDEST WEST.
BY H. WHITHAIV.

Where next? It is really impossible to say where' we shall go to, or what we shall next be doing on this little globe of ours. I can lay no claim to be- ing a traveller, nor yet can I truthfully say I have any wish for travel, yet here I am on the very verge of civilisation. Away out on the Snohomish river,or, to be more precise, at the confluence of the Snohomish river with Paget Sound, dame nature in one of her kindest and most pleasing moods seems to have tried her bett at fashioning a new starting point for completing the civilisation of the West. As the white man advances, the red man disap- pears, and poor puny I am feeling drawn towards taking a part in the accomplishment of this object. Out on the Snohomish river, with the red man and his squaw to look on,in their blear-eyed fashion,the white man is wielding the hammer and driving the key that is to end in the

div.head: ERECTION OF A WIRE MILL
div.p: ERECTION OF A WIRE MILL

with a capacity of 1,000 kegs of wire nails per ten hours. At present the plans include the construc- tion of blast furnaces, steel plant, a rod mill, &c. The works for -which the buildings are now in course of construction, embrace a warehouse 200 ft. long by Soft.; a cleaning house 100 ft. by 100 ft. ; a wire mill 200 ft. by 80ft.; a machine shop 64ft. by 90ft.; boiler house 64ft. by 48ft.; and a nail factory 200 ft. by 80ft. All this to be done on the latest and most improved devices. With deep water at their I service, the constructors are preparing plans for docks that will enable rods and all other material to be shipped without need of cartage. Coal and iron I are abundant in the neighbourhood. • It is proposed to fix blocks with a turn-out capacity of 50 tons per ten hours, and all is to be under the immediate management of Messrs. A. R. Whiting and Co. of New York. There need be no fear of trade; the shipments last year of wire mails to the Pacific coast were 300,000 kegs, so there is a large market to be supplied.

div.head: DISTRICT OF SEATTLE
div.p: THE DISTRICT OF SEATTLE

which includes Facoma, Everett, Port Gardner, and Lowell, is remarkable fertile, neither mountainous, nor yet dreary plain, justifies me in saying that it is certainly the best for business and trade purposes out West. The states of Washington and Oregon in which the above new settlements are placed are within easy and convenient distances of California by way of Paget Sound. A very few miles places British Columbia also within easy reach of the new enterprise. I may not be an authority, and there- fore not justified in giving an opinion as to the relative merits of San Francisco and Port Gardner, as manufacturing and distributing centres, but, most. certainly, I think, after travelling near upon two weeks around and about the districts of Everett and other places in Paget Sound, that it is the coming business centre of the West. It has every- thing that San Francisco lacks. Railways and steam boats provide cheap carriage. In addition to the Rod and Wire Mills, ship building is also being started :—A Steel Barge Co. has already bought land and commenced the construction of large works 'which will find work for hundreds of men. More than this, it has a fine, hearty class of people who, as pioneers, are deservedly looked upon as the fathers of the new settlements, men who at once hold out the right hand of fellowship and think it no trouble to plod knee deep in mud to show a stranger all the points of interests. Especially was this the case with myself. My thanks are especially due to two gentlemen, Mr. McNamara and Mr. Sedgwick, of Seattle, who kindly took me in charge during this voyage of discovery. Mr. G. R. Sims, Managing Director of the Lombard Trust Co. (Limited) is now in this city. Mr. Sinis left London several weeks ago, and has since been making an inspection of Tacoma, Seattle, and Everett, on Paget Sound, for the purpose of invest- ing in real estate. He has also examined some sil- ver properties in the Monte Cristo district;in the Cascade mountains, north of Seattle, and has bounded twenty one claims there. An expert will come from London and examine them, and if satis- factory they will be parchased through Mr. Sims. A telegram from St. Paul recently quoted Mr. Sims as saying he had 5,000,000 dol. of English money to invest in real estate, mines,and different. enterprises in America. He says this is true only in a measure. The actual amount of cash now ready for invest.- ment is 2,500,000 do], but English capital is looking this way, and before fie gets through, he expects to put in several millions more. It is reported that this Co. will invest 1,000,000 dol. in this new town of Everett, and Mr. Hewitt, the Tacoma millionaire, is the manager of-the company. The Philadelphia Capes Company is also erecting a very large paper mill there, so that with the wire mills, the whale

back barge works, and lumber* mills, cutting 2,000,000 feet a day, it is calculated that not less than 5,000 labourers will be employed within a year or two. In fact the promoters say that 25,000 people will be settled here within three years. I should most certainly baveitayed here could I have made arrangements with Mr. Hewitt, with whom I had a pleasant ride,and that on the Snohomish river steam boat. I found him a genial, chatty gentleman, quite willing to give all information, either as to buying land, or locating as a workman. We may meet again. I hope so. To-morrow the 13th

div.head: CHRISTMAS CARDS.
div.p: CHRISTMAS CARDS.

One mode of testing the progress of art is in the Christmas cards and booklets which are issued year by year. A few seasons back the impression got abroad that Christmas cards would soon be out of fashion; they were getting, as the phrase goes, "so common ; " but there is no sign of a falling off to- day. Invention has been stimulated, some of the cleverest artists have been employed, and the result is, every year,. that designs in Christmas cards are prettier, brighter, and more original. This is espe- cially the case with the productions of Messrs.. Raphael Tuck and Sons who spare neither money, time, nor talent to meet the taste of the public. One of theft finest specimens this year is the repro- duction, on a large card, of Sir Joshua Reynolds's masterpiece "The Church Choir." It is a really beautiful picture, and well worthy of a frame. One of the calendars for 1892 is adorned for each month with figures—for the most part of children. Each scene is suitable to the month ; it is accompanied with an appropriate quotation, and finished as to colour in the highest style of art. The " Art Gem Calendar" is of a smaller kind and is as useful as it is pretty. The porcelain Christmas cards are adorned I with photographic reproductions, besides being ' brightened and framed with ffowers and- leaves. ' Some of the boxed cards are " emquisites" -in their way, and will form most suitable gifts to those who have a title to expe,it "something really nice. Many of the eards this year are ''shaped," and some may be described as booklets. Here is one which looks on the outside like a pug dog, the front shOw- ing the face, and the back the back of the head, while the interior is a series of pages cleverly illus- trated with dogs, cats, birds, and rabbits. One folding card resembles a vase, another a doll's bed, and a third a Japanese umbrella. They are all pretty, and, eonsidering the quality,they are remark- ably cheap. There are some admirable designs in private autograph cards, and, as they are boxed with envelopes of the right size, they are sure to be largely demanded. Speaking generally, Messrs. Raphael Tuck and Sons have shown themselves equal, as heretofore, in design, elegance, humour, and finish, to the most artistic and fastidious taste, . _ _ _

Some idea may be obtained of the vast business of the firm when it is stated,in round figures,that they disposed last year, of twenty-one million cards, to which must be added about half a million booklets, these being practically regarded as cards in another and somewhat more poetic guise, and utilised, in the same manner, as seasonable little gifts or reminders. The home,trade was responsible for about half the quantity named, the remaining half being exported to nearly every part of the world, the United States standing first on the foreign list, while the Colonies made a good second; the remainder being distri- buted on the Continent of turope, South America, the Dutch Possessions, China, Japan, &c., &c. Vile learn that the sale of cards this year promises to attain about the same figures, while the demand for booklets will not fall far short, if at all, of a million copies, a significant advance, this, of nearly 100 per , cent.

div.head: FREE GARDENERS' ANNUAL DINNER.
div.p: FREE GARDENERS' ANNUAL DINNER.

COUNCILLOR BEANIAN ON WARRINGTON TRADE AND SANITATION. The annual dinner of the Moss Rose Lodge, No. 1,099, of the National United Free Gardeners was I held at Bro. John White's, Ball Inn, Winwick-st., on Saturday evening: A most substantial and ex- cellent repast was portaken of, after which Bro. James Rudge, P.M., was voted to the chair,and Bro. Wm. Holloway, grand master of the lodge, to the vice chair. Among others present during the even- ing were Bros. John White, A. Davies (secretary of the lodge), Councillors J. Hill (district secretary), and S. Beaman, Dr. Jack,Joseph Cooper, D. M. of the Pride of Liverpool lodge, and Messrs. W. Paton, R. Mills, and 0. Yates (Ram's Head). The Secretary read a letter from the Grand Master of the Order, Bro. J. Venable:s, of Sandbaeh, and Bro. Win. Crosfield, hon. member, and from Bro. Councillor H. Roberts, honorary memberralso regretting their inability to attend, the first named through a continuous cold. A vote of regret for the absence and sympathy with the Grand Master was 'reseed. The Chairman proposed the toast of "The town and trade of Warrington," coupled with the name of Mr. Councillor Beaman. Councillor BIUMAN resprendel He said as regarded their town they all ought to feel proud of it. It was a good old town, not a town in a state of decay, but one of the most prosperous towns in the United Kingdom The future of Warrington was bright and hopeful. The trade was very good, much better than it was that time last year. Their town was well in the front in compari- son with other towns by which it was stirrounded. In I sanitation Warrington was not behind any town in the United Kingdom. Notwithstanding that its mode of dealing with its domestic and personal refuse had been so much carped and cavelled at, it was, though the sys- tem might be modified and improved, on the right track. Referring to the baths question Councillor Beaman said in a town like Warrington where the occupations were . not of the cleanlieet class, it was imperative upon the local authorities to provide proper and efficient baths for the populace ; and in connection with every plunge or swimming bath there ought to' be placed a shower or washing bath, where a man could get a good cleansing before entering tha' swimming bath. As regarded the trade of Warrington, first of all, he sup- posed, stood their wire. The wire made in Warrington went to all parts of the world. If you went down the crater of Vesuvius you would be pulled up by a wire rope manufactured in Warrington. A very great many of the electric and submarine telegraphs were manufac- tured here. The wire mattresses manufactured in Warrington wculd compare with any wire mattresses manufactured in any part of the world. Then they had leather. They had plenty of tanneries, which gave em- ployment to a lot of men. There were some people who said a nuisance arose from these, but he thought the nuisance was more than compensated by the employ- ment they gave to the toiling masses who worked in them. The cotton cloth manufactured at Cockhedge Mills would compare very favourably with cotton manu- factured in any other part of the world. There were all descriptions of iron work produced in Warrington. From the great big ponderous girder bridge down to the little round plates, 3-16ths of an inch in diameter, hoops, or sheets, all these were manufactured. The most useful classes of iron were manufactured there. There was not much better glass than was made in Warrington. The products of Warrington were distributed all over the world. Wherever the sun shone it could not shine on a single spot in the whole universe, but some product of Warrington was there. Warrington in its trade seemed to him (Council- lor Beaman) to be well to the frent, and when Warring- ton trade was bad it augured very badly for the trade of England. There was generally trade in Warrington if there was trade anywhere. (Applause.) Councillor Beaman then made some remarks on the improvement in the social condition of working-men, and said their future would surpass their present far more than the present surpassed the past. He- expressed the opinion that the Government would recognise the necessity of doing something for the working-man which would en- able him to look forward to something brighter and bettet, after 30 or 40 years' work, for the augmentation of the wealth of the country than the miserable work- house which now stared him in the face. (Loud ap- plause.) Councillor HILL proposed the-toast of "Success to the Order of United Free Gardeners." The Order he said some years ago was somewhat small but it now num- bered 52,000 members, an increase during the year of 2,600; although it had not done so well in Warrington as in some places. The funds of the Order had increased £2,700 during the past year.—The CHAIRMAN also m'ade some observations on the prospects of the Order. He said the last financial statement published was 12 months old, but the next report he believed would show 60,000 members. The Order, so far as the Warrington district was concerned was handicapped somewhat perhaps through want of energy, but it was now in a better posi- tion than it had been since he joined it. A juvenile society had been started in Warrington, and nothing had been lost by it. He urged parents to enter their children as members.—The SECRETABY made a statement as to the financial condition of the lodges, whichwas of a satisfac- tory character.—The toast of "Success to the Moss Rose Lodge," was proposed on the proposition of the Scene- TARY, and that of" honorary members and visitors," on the motion of Bro. JOHN RuDoc, and responded to by Bro. COOPER, of Liverpool, Messrs. MALKIN, and W. PATON, and Councillor BEAMAN, the last-named addressing some remarks to the brethren urging upon them the necessity of self-reliance.—The toast of "The host and hostess ,and the Press," responded to by the Examiner representative, were also drunk.—Songs were given by Bros. Cooper, Kempton, G. Perry, and others, and Mr. Thomas Miller, a Dailam forgeman, gave a recitation of his own compo- sition, for which he was much complimented. COAGITLINE.—Cement for Broken Articles, 6,1. and is.. ; postage, 2d. Sold everywhere, home and aobroad.—Advt. Mr. W. E. Field, the head of the firm of New York stockbrokers, who failed the other day,. has, been com- mitted to an asylum for the insane.

div.head: DARING IMPOSTORS
div.p: A DARING IMPOSTORS
THE STORY OF AN INNOCENT CONVICT.
BF ALFRED R. CALHOUN
CHAPTI3IR XXX. REYBOLD'S CONFEDEIUTES.

All men who commit crime are fools ; 'but they are doubly fools when they hire other criminals to assist them in carrying out their lawless designs. The very nature of these alliances forbids any- thing like respect between the confederates; and fidelity, when dependent on mere interest, without some prinsiple behind it, is simply masked treason. _ _

Mingo and Cash were held together by something like a bond of friendship. Each knew the misdeeds of the other, and both rather gloried in their ability to circumvent the law, and their daring at setting It at defiance.

But for Reybold they entertained no feeling of friendship or respect. They believed him, and rightly;to be worse than themselves in that his opportunitieq were greater; and they envied him that immunity from suspicion and prosecution that enabled him to dress and live like a gentleman, and to pass for one among the world's careless ox superficial observers. The only interest these wretches had in their employer was a pecuniary one. The instant he stopped paying them, they stood ready to sell him out, provided they could get anyone to buy their information without risk to themselves; and no one knew this better than Reybold. Cash, though believed to be a criminal, had, by the superior cunning of himself and his wife, suc- ceeded in keeping out of the clutches of the law. Mrs. Cash was a fitting companion for such a man. When a woman deliberately goes down, her descent is into a bottomless vortex, and she falls lower and lower—eternally lower. Mrs. Cash was a stout, dark woman, with fishy grey eyes, and a growth of hair on her lips and chin that gave her the appearance of a degraded man, disguised or trying to disguise himself as female.

Mingo kept in hiding, "for the good of his health," as the thieves' slang has it; and as he paid well for his shelter, and was withal a congenial spirit, Mrs. Cash did not seriously object to him as a boarder up to this time: She and her husband were sitting in their sitting. room, and they were sitting close together and talking in the low, confidential tones and with the interested manner that it is so lovely to see between a husband and wife. "I think it 'd be better for himself—l know it 'd be a great sight better for us—if Mingo, he was to take a tumble to himself an' go off to the country till things blow over. But 'taint him that troubles me so much," said Mrs. Cash.
, "No, I suppose not," said her husband, vaguely "No; it's that other one." "The other one 7" echoed Cash.

"Yes. What if the police was to waltz in hero all of a suddent, an' to find that feller strugglin' an' a roaring,' an' him strapped down, hand an fut, to the bed to keep him from gettin' out on the street an' a makin' a grand combination circus an' men- agerie of himself—what then, Larry Cash ? " And she slapped him on the knee and stared into his face.

"Ah what then, to be sure? Well, Molly, that'd be just about as bad as it well could be. But, then, shut one eye and take a peek at the other side of it," said Cash, with one eye shut and his head to one side, by way of setting her an example. "There aint no other side to it," she protested. "But take a peek, take a peek, Molly." " I have peeked, an peeked, an' I'm right." "And you didtf,t .0.f.1 the fifty dollars a week that Reybold should say Mr. Failey pays us for beardin' and tendin' to the most interestin' case "

"Yes, I've tuk in all that, an' I've weighed it," said Mrs. Cash, holding out both her red hands, and balancing them till one dropped down on her lap, as if pressed by a heavy weight. "But fifty thousand dollars wouldn't pay us if that man was for to die on our hands. You see," she added, after a pause, "there aint no ways of puttin' the body out of sight." "I guess yer right, Molly." • _ _
"I rcnow -I'm right. Now, I'd get rid of that howlin' maniac; but before you let him loose, or before you tell Farley that yer boarder has gone, bleed him again." "The boarder 1"

No; Farley." " You bet I will. He's makin' out of this job, nand over fist, though I'm free to confess I don't see what he 's drivin' after. But I 'ye got the grip on Farley, an' I II see him to-night and get another pull at him." The squeaking of the door leading into the hall caused this estimable couple to push back their chairs and to look behind them.

" Ah, that is a beautiful domestic sight," said Mingo, beaming on Cash and his wife with great admiration. "There is nothin' in the world more finer to see than a happy fireside, with husband an' wife sittin' beside it, an' a makin' love, just like they did when they was sparkin' years, an' years, an' years ago. If I'd only had a wife like yours, Cash, I'd a been an entirely different man." And Mingo sighed, closed the door, and came and sat down at the other side of the stove, where he con- tinued his looks of admiration.
"A man's wife," snapped Mrs. Cash, "is Fifty much generally what he makes her. If he interests her in his work, why, it follers to reason she'll, be interested in him." _ _

"Well, not allus," said Mingo, "for I've noticed that there's a sight more difference in women than there is in men. Now there was my last wife. I tried, an' I tried, an' / tried, till tryin' made me weary, to interest that woman in my business. But the more I Let her tnto my secrets an' wanted her to help, the more she kicked. Nothin' but a right down preacher would ever suit that woman for a husband. Oh, she was too good for this sinful an wicked world." An, so you sent her to a better one," broke in Mrs. Cash, with a laugh that made Mingo tremble, as if a mine had exploded under his feet. " oilers treated her well," gasped Mingo. "Mingo, there's some folks don't think so," con- tinued Mrs. Cash, "but that ain't here nor there. Now do you know what I've just been a sayin' to Larry? " -

Mingo declared that he had not the gift of second sight, and so could not well know *hat she said to Larry, or any one else, when he was not within hearing. "I was a saying that New York's got to be right down unhealthy for a man of your build just 'bout this time." "It never was a very healthy place for men like Cash an' me," said Mingo, adding: "You see, some trades is much more sickly than other trades." "Well," persisted Mrs. Cash, without showing the least anger at Mingo's allusion to her husband's "if Larry was threatened with throat dis- ease so bad as you are, I'd send him off till the air got purer. Why I've knowed good strong men to be strangled with that disease, right when they was in the prime of life, an' I'm slue, Mingo, you don't want to die.". " Mebbe yer right," said Mingo, rising heavily and stroking his forehead in a dazed sort of way. "But afore I leave, I'm agoin' to collect some due- bills. The best friend a man has when he is travel- lin', or at any other time for the matter of that, is a little ready money. But, it appears, I broke in on a family confab.' "Wife's right," said Cash, when Mingo had taken two steps towards the door, "the fact is, Mingo, the cops are after you again, and there's talk of a reward—" "What for?" "For burnin' down the house; and then it's believed that you was in with Lee in the Edgefield and Phipps's jewellery business." "It's one thing to make a charge," said Mingos with a defiant manner which he did not feel, "but it's another thing to prove it. I aint no green band at the business. I've got my tracks covered I guess," and with this he left the kitchen and went to the dirty little den in which he slept. He lit a tallow candle, for it was night, and again he put on the disguise that had served him so well before.
About his person, he concealed as much of the more valuable plunder as he could well carry and which he had brought with him in the carpet bag, and then he stole quietly out of the house.
By flu) light of the few lainps in the narrow streets e could see here and there a figure moving, andhe took care before advancing that the figure was not that of an officer. -

Now and then, when he did catch sight of a blue uniform, he darted into some alley-way, or hid in the shadows of some recessed door till the danger was passed. A bolder course would not have been half so hazardous, but conscious crime is ever cowardly. At length he reached Broadway, with its electric lights, its surging throngs coming from the theatres and the roar of its glittering equipages. Here he felt bolder. and. falling in with the

human current; he was swept across Ma ison Square, and thrown up on the doorstep of iteybold's lodgings. He crept upstairs, and was admitted by the ser- vant, who had seen him before, with and without his disguise, into the little reception room. Here he waited, but not in patste for fully two hours.
He could heart he clinkingof glasses,the tipsytorists and the boisterous laughter of the men in the next room as they rejoiced at their winnings, or swore over their bad luck at cards.

" Ah, if I was only rich an' a gent like Farley, then I might do just as I please without danger," thought Mingo, as he squirmed uneasily in his seat. The clock in a neighbouring church struck one; then, after an interminable time, it struck two, and Mingo could hear "the guests" going down stairs. At length two doors opened at the same . stant. Reybold appeared in one and Cash, with a frightened face, stood in the other, while he cried out:
"Mr. Farley, the man has gone I Frank Lefferts has broke away and is lost I"
CHAPTER XXXI.

div.head: SEAECII.
div.p: THE SEAECII.
"Frank Lefferts has broke away and is lost 1" shouted Reybold. "Broke away and lost 1" echoed Mingo.

And both men stared at Cash, whose ashy face and trembling limbs showed conclusively that he was neither acting nor lying. " Yes ; hope I may be struck dead • this minute If I ain't a givin' you the straight truth," said Cash. Hissing out an oath, Reybold sprang forward, caught Cash by the throat, and jerking him into the room, he closed the door and drew a pistol from his belt.

"Oh, don't shoot! It wasn't my fault!" cried Cash, as he retreated from the furious Reybold. "Don't be skeert, Cash. If Farley wants to try that sort of thing, I'll shoot with him for keeps, said Mingo, who had risen to his feet, and stood, pistol in hand, before his employer. Reybold did not need a second glance at his ruffianly henchman's eyes to convince him that he meant just what he said, and that another move- ment against Cash would result in his own death. If his pluck had been as great as his tact, a bloody fight must have followed; but anger does not always mean courage. Reybold, on the spur of the moment, could not even assume a quality which was so foreign to his nature. Returning the pistol to his hip pocket, he became suddenly calm, if not complacent, and dropping into a chair with an air of exhaustion, he said, apologetically: "Excuse me, boys, but that news so upset me that I didn't know what I was doing." "Well," said Mingo, as he concealed his revolver, "if there's any one time more than another when a man had orter have all his senses about him, it's when he pulls out a gun in a crowd where other folks may have t'cmns an' know how to use 'em. No 1 one should ever drawr a pistol onless he means to , shoot; an' he shouldn't never shoot unless he means to trill, leastwise, that's how I allus felt about it." ; By this time Cash had sufficiently recovered from his fright and the exhaustion of his run hither to make an explanation. "Yesterday our boarder took on so that we had either to strap him down or else get out of the house and lot him tear round till he'd smashed everything to pieces; so we strapped him. Soon after dark, he kinder calmed down and went to sleep. wife—she's the most tender-heartedest woman I ever saw—she seed that he was restin' quiet. So, just afore she went to bed, she took off the straps and made him comfortable, sproadin' her Own plaid shawl—" "Never mind the details, Cash," said Reybold, his impatience increasing with the other's prolixity. "You are sure Lefferts is gone ? " "There aint no two ways about that. Soon after twelve o'clock, I thought I'd tike another look over the place, for my wife she's awft2l geared of burg- Jars; so I lit a candle and left goinJ later Leffert's room for last. But when I got there, lo and be- hold what did I see? Nothin' but the L'ed 01-qv and the winder up." "He'd vamoosed through the winder," said Mingtl, evidently thinking an explanation necessary at this point. " Yes ; that was it, Mingo. Well, I 'larmed my wife and she got up quick, I tell you, for • she liked that young man; and then she lit another candle, and we two s'arched, and we s'arched, and we s'arched."

"And didn't find na,wthin'," prompted Mingo, for Cash looked as if he were going to repeat "and we s'arched." indefinitely. "Yes, we found tracks outside the winder. I follered them tracks around and around the yard, and at last I saw marks that showed he must have clum over the board fence, and dropped into an alley way, at the back, that runs up to Third Avenue, and comes out near Roper's pawn shop. Well, I quick dressed, and started off, like a Wild West Injun on the trail; and I follered, and fol- lered, and follered-T"

"An' didn't find nawthin'," prompted Mingo again. "No, I didn't see a hide nor a hair of him; so, sez I to myself, 'the only thing for me to do is to see Mr. Farley at wanst, and tell him the straight atom' So off I ran. and here I am."

Cash drew a long breath and looked around as if expecting prompt approval of his conduct. "Cash, what did I pay you for ?" asked Reyhold, with a severity of tons that an honest employer might have assumed IL his explicit orders were dis- obeyed. "For many things," said Cash, guardedly "But the last agreement?" "That was to watch and keer for Lefferts, in the first place, and, in the second, to keep my Inouth shut, and I've been as mute as a clam—"
"But you have not cared for this man, and until you find him, and take him back, you get not one cent from me."

"See here, Farley, do you mean that 2" asked Mingo. "Yes, I do." • "You are in dead earnest, eh 7" "I am." "I guess you'll change yer mind!' "Why should I " " Bekase / say so," said Mingo, with a command- ing manner that once startled and stung Reybold. "Because you say so 7" "Yes, that's it." .

"Pray, whert did you become my master?" asked Reybold, his anger again threatening to burst out. "Why," grinned Mingo, "I became your master when you first hired me to do dirty work for you, years and years ago Just as soon as one feller gives himself away to another, as you've give yersel' away to me, then the other feller aint the hired man, but the boss." "We shall see about that." _

"No, we know all about it now. You'll pay Cash All the money you 'greed to, even if he couldn't hold onter that lunatic; an' that reminds me that I'm thinkin' of startin' to the country to-night for the good of my health, an' I want a little money." "I paid you all I agreed to," said Reybold, scorn- fully.

"-So you did; bnt I didn't agree not to take no mere, nor not to ax no more. In business like ours, where a man takes pay to buck against the law. he's a fool if he ever signs a receipt in full to the man that hires him. Now, I want five hundred dollars to-night, and I'll promise not to call on you again for a month of Sundays ; " and Mingo reached out his grimy hand; as if expecting the mony to be dropped at once into his palm. "Five hundred dollars I " repeated Reybold, and he told the truth in what he added: "I haven't got five hundred cents about me to-night. The play has run against me for a week and I'm broke; but I can give you a eheque." "A cheque I 'chuckled Mingo.
"You'll give me

a cheque 1- Na if I knows my-self. You're-a great hand at gettin' up cheques, Mr. Farley. Oh, there aint no better man in the country for that lay, but I aint on it. No, give me the cash, or the collateral that I can hock." "Collateral that you can hock!" repeated Rey. bold.

"Yes, diments an' things of that kind that I kin spout, kin pawn; don't you understand that jabber 2" "Yes, I understand that jabber, and I'll replj, in jabber that you can understand, too, and that is, I haven't got the money, and—" "See here, Mingo,' said Cash, "Mr. Farley he 's a gent, and I 'm most sure he 's tellin' the down- right truth. Now, let us give him some time; the game 'II change after a bit, and when he gets flush he 'll divvy square; won't you, Mr. Farley 2" • Reybold bit his lips and nodded. "I aint fool enough to try an' get blood out of a turnip; but I kin get Money out of Mr. Farley, and I'll wait for a tew days till he makes a strike. New York has as good hidin' places as the country, if it comes down to that," said Mingo, rising, for the _ _ _ . _ _ _

clock in the neighbouring steeple struck three, and as the season of the year was mid-May, it would be daylight in an hour. "Find Frank Lefferts, get him put in jail, if you can,. and trust roe to pay you.. Get laipa put in_jail

and neia, ana tnere will be a barrel of money in it for us all," said Reybold, when his visitors stood up to go. Promising to report if he heard anything about the escaped man, Cash went out, followed by &lingo. "Cash," said Mingo, as they hurrifxl along the deserted streets, if it hadn't been for me that cuss would have shot you to-night." "It looked that way for a bit," said Cash. "An' your wife, she wants me to git oue, an' I'll agree she's 'bout right. But, you kin see, I tried uo mosey to-night, but I didn't make the riffle. I've got to have more money afore I start, so, under them sarcumstances, you'll see that I'm 'bleeged to go back to your shanty an' lie low a bit." "All right, Mingo, but the old woman's so nervous it won't do to let her know nawthin' about it; so I'll smuggle you in and hide you away in the garret, and I'll see that you have blankets and lots of grub and stuff to drink till yer ready to get out. But you must be awful still after dark, for Molly, she has a holy horror of ghosts in the night time." _ . _ _

With such confidential and -amicable converse as this, they hurried in the direction of Ninth street. They were within a few hundred yards of their destination, when they were brought to a standstill by the clanging of an ambulance bell, and the flashing of bull's-eye lanterns a short distance ahead.
Concealing themselves in a convenient doorway, they watched a number of police officers lifting from the gutter to the ambulance the body of a man.

"I'm to bet ten to one," said Mingo, feeling in his pocket as if he expected his bet would be promptly taKen, "that that helpless cove is Frank Lefferts" ; and for once vodka° was right. To be continued.
WHAT TARRING AND FEATHERING MEANS.

People who read of tarring and feathering by White Caps and others know that the punishment is a very unpleasant one, but few imagine how ter- ribly painful and dangerous it is. In Wyoming I once saw a man who had been tarred and leathered, and, although he fully deserved the discipline, I could not help pitying him. Hardened tar is very hard to remove from. the skin, and when feathers are added it forms a kind of cement that sticks closer than a brother. As soon as the tar sets the victim's suffering begins. It contracts as it cools, and every one of the little veins on the body are pulled, causing the most exquisite agony. The per- spiration is entirely stopped, and unless the tar is removed death is certain to ensue. But the removal is no easy task, and requires several days. The tar cannot be softened by the application of heat, and must be peeled off bit by bit, sweet oil being used to make the process less painful. The irritation to the skin is very great, as the hairs cannot be disen- gaged, but must be pulled out or cut off. No man can be cleaned of tar in a single day, as the pain of the operation would be too excruciating for endur- ance, and until this is done he has to suffer from a pain like that of 10,000 pin pricks. Numbers of men have died from the torture, and none who have gone through it regard tarring and feathering as any- thing but a most fearful infliction.

div.head: WRECKED ON THE GOODWINS.
div.p: WRECKED ON THE GOODWINS.

Erasmus Darwin, grandfather of .the famous Charles Darwin, the naturalist, inscribed upon his seal the significant words, " Ontnia ex eonchis "—all things arise from oysters. But from what do oysters arise? What is the origin of matter? Ah ! nobody knows. Yet one thing is getting plainer every day. Let this man's story show.

He goes on to say : On the 17th of December, 1872, whilst acting as ship's carpenter on board the steamship Sorrento, I wag wreeked on the Goodwin Sands. The Shock to'mVstem was so great as to produce an effect I never felt before. I fell into a low, weak state, and was seized with giddiness And a sinking, fainting feeling. I had a bad taste in the mouth, weight at the chest, and great pain after eating, and my face would burn likd fire. I had difficulty in breathing and palpitation, and often a pain seemed to run from the heart through to my shoulder. I had a kind of rumbling all over me, and a choking sensation at the throat, with a rush of blood to the head.

"I slept very badly, an d after a time I got so ner- vous and weak I was afraid to go about, and would sit in a chair quite powerless. I saw a doctor who treated me for a time, and then sent me to a hospital in Rattle- bone-place, London, where I was under treatment for three months, but got no better. I then put myself un- der a local doctor, who said I was suffering from ner- vous debiiity. He patched me up for a little while, but said to my wife, Your husband is in a critical condi- tion, and may die at any time.' "However, I got to work for a short time, and then was as bad as ever. I lingered on in this way for years—now a little better, now worse, but never well. 6' AboutlBBo, whilst working at Messrs. Westwood and Bailey's, Millwall, a mate who saw my sufferings told me of a medicine called Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup, and he brought me a bottle, After taking the first bottle I found my food agreed with me, and I began to im- prove. All nervous feeling gradually left me, and by persevering with the medicine, I was soon cured. From that time to this I have been a strong man, and done harder work than ever in my life before. I have since kept Mother Seigel's Syrup in the house, and my wife, who was a great sufferer from rheumatism and dropsy, has found more relief from it than from anything else. If any of my family ever an anything, a few doses soon sets them right."
The statement from which the foregoing is an extract was made by Mr. William Rill, ship's carpenter, 108, St. Anne's Road, London, E.

Now, what is the thing which we said is getting plainer every day? Why this : that almost an infinite number of different results arise frpm a single cause. Like the majority of people in all ranks of life, Mr. Hill had in his digestive organs the seeds—or what women, when they buy dress goods, call "the makings "—of dyspepsia. Ilk to the winter of 1872 it may not have troubled him much, but the excitement and exposure of the shipwreck was more than the system could bear. We must remember, too, that all shocks to the mind or. body, or to both, act directly on the stomach. Who can eat when under the influence of a great worry or a Igreat sorrow? And if this worry or sorrow continues long, it always upsets the digestion,permanently impairs or destroys the appetite, and thus brings on an appar- ently incurable dyspepsia and nervous debility. Why, gracious goodness r there are millions of women, and lots of men, crawling about under this thing in England every day in the year. And it is to them we are talk- ing. They are half dead, and :we want them to come to life, and get some good out of their existence. What- ever the ailment is called, you may be sure indigestion and dyspepsia is at the bcttom of it, as in Mr. Hill's case, and what cured him will cure you.

Alderman WEIGHT said that in thesematters thesehad Ito be guided by the borough surveyor. 'The minutes were then confirmed. SANITARY COMMITTEE.—THE DEATH RATE. 'Alderman SUTTON moved the confirmation af the minutes of this Committee the important parts of which we published last week. He also referred to ,the 'report by the Medical Officer of Health for the third 'quarter of the year 1891. The first part of Dr. Gornars report reads : The Registrar's returns for the third 'quarter of the year give a total of 290 deaths within the borough, equal to an annual death rate of 2032. per 1,600. 'Of these SO deaths were in the Warrington ; sub-district, equal to an annual rate of 2016 per 1,000; and :30 deaths were in the Latchford sub-district, equal ' to an annual rate of 20.39 per 1,000. Of the total deaths' 171 were males and 119 females. Compared with the annual rate of mortalty in the 28 great English tewna, the aggregate populatiod of which is estimated by the, Registrar-General to be nearly nine-and-a-half millions, the Warrington rate•was 2.22 per 1,000 higher. It was also 4.52. 'higher than that of the United Kingdom, and 2.92 higher than London. The lowest rates were 142 in Brighton and in Bristol, 14.3 in Portsmouth, 14.5 in Halifaa., and 149 in Derby; while the highest were 22.4 in Liverpool, 24.1 in Sunderland, and 26.7 in Preston. In registration London, the rate was 17.4. The birth returns give a total of `Ol5, equal to a birth-rate of 44.44 per 1,000. It is therefore 12.94 per 1,000 higher in Warrington than the 28 great towns, and 14-94 per 1,000 , above the rate in the whole country. The lowest rates ' were 24.1 in Huddersfield, 24.5 in 'Halifax, 25.6 in Brighten, and 25•Ø in Bradford; while the rate in thel other large towns ranged upwards to 34.8 in Sheffield and Cardiff, 35.0 in Preston, 35.2 in Newcastle-on-Tyne, and 35.4 in Sunderland. In fifty other large towns districts the birth-rate was 33.0 per 1,000, or 11.44 lawer than the Warrington rate. Estimated population to middle of 1891, 58,000 inclusive of Warrington 47,187, and Latchford 5,813." The doctor reported that the total number of admissions to the hospital during the year were eight, including one case of scarlet fever from Earlestown, as against 17 in the last year, and 35 in the corresponding quarter of 1890. Only one death was recorded.—The Inspector reported that the number of nuisances registered was 609, abated 600, number of houses, premises, Stc., inspected 2,749, orders issued for sanitary amendments of houses, 'fee., 30. Number of patients removed to hospital, 7; number of patients supervised at home, 4; number of houses disinfected after infectious diseases 41 ; sets of infected bedding and clothing disinfected, 6. Number of visits during the day to lodging-houses, 245; number of visits during the night, 75; miscellaneous visits in regard to infectious diseases, 4 ; legal proceedings—summonses, 37. Alderman Surro!esaid some alarm had been caused

_ with reference to the death rate being 29 per thousand, and he should not, therefore, be out of place if he re- ferred to one or two fads. The Registrar General's return for tke last quarter gave 290 deaths, which was equal to an annual death rate of 2032. per thousand. He explained that this quarter there were 14 weeks, so that the death rate would be 22 per 1,000, against 30.31 per 1,000 at the end of the previous quarter. Compared with the annual rate of mortality in twenty-eight large towns the death rate in Warrington was stated to be 2.22 per 1,000 inhabitants higher than the highest on the list, and 2.92 higher than London. On the other hand it would be seen that the birth rate was 44.44 per 1,000 inhabit- ants in Warrington, this figure being 12.94 higher than that of the 28 English towns. The unusually high birth Tata to some extent accounted for the high death rate, It

often occurred that a high death rate ensued on an abnor- mal birth rate, the reason being that a, number of chil- dren between the ages of one and five years succumbed. For the year ending November 21st, there were 1,1.87 deaths, and of these 522 were of children under the age of five years. The gross death rate for the year ended Saturday, November 21st, was 24.7. The high death rate was attributed by the Medical Officer of Health as due to lung diseases following on influenza, during the early part of the year, and the bad weather which prevailed caused a number of deaths from tuber- cular diseases. Ignorance in the feeding of children was also the cause of a number of deaths. A largenumber of deaths was also caused by persons exposing them- selves to the inclement weather when only in the first stages of convalescence. He thought that although they occasionally had a high death rate—the rate amounting to 28.00 in one case—one could not form an exact idea of the actual death rate by the result of one week's statistycs. It was necessary to take the figures for the year. It could not, of course, be denied, that the health of the town vas not as satisfactory as 'he would like it to be. He did not think that they need despair, inasmuch as the condition of the town was much better during the past year than it had been daring the past ten years. Councillor SHAW-GREEN said he regretted very fnuch the absence of the Chairman of the Committee, because he should have liked him to have the opportunity of explaining something which be wanted to refer to. •He attended in that chamber on Wednesday last to support the application before the Commissioners for the privi- lege of borrowing a certain sum in order to erect new baths, but the way in which the 'enquiry was opened turned his support into :unmistakable opposition. Councillor BROWN said thEr Committee expressed the opinion that the time had,arrived for abolishing the holding of the fairs in the public streets. Now the Mayor told them the Committee were already consider- ing as to the advisability of 'purchasing a site for street fairs. He thought this seemed like trying to bind the touncil to a particular scheme. Councillor SHAW GEtunii 'said the Committee had con- sidered the inconvenience caused in the streets by these fairs, and the opinion expressed by the Government Inspector that the fairs should be removed altogether, and that suitable premises should be erected for them, and passed their resolution. Since then other circum- stances had arisen. A valuable and important plot of land had passed under their notice. Councillor ,HurcsitNsonJagreed with Councillor Browne that the Council should have a full scheme brought be- fore them,'rather than have the matter put before them in the manner it was. What they ought to do was to look after their general markets and spend their money there. At present everybody was satisfied to have the fairs where they were, and that they were no nuisance to the town ; and the home dealers were satisfied. It was a very good horse market, and he did not think they ought to chamgeit and go to an extravagant expenditure of from £5,000 to £l.OOOO ;which would be necessary; and by contracting it in a small area drive away a fair which had been held for :300 or 400 years past in the same place. div.head: CONCERT AT THE GYMNASIUM.
div.p: CONCERT AT THE GYMNASIUM.

On Saturday evening a successful musical :End gymnastic entertainment wae.given at the Waring- ton Gymnasium. There was E, large audience. Mr. T. Morris presided. The musical portion ref the programme was opened with a quartette "Of.ti: the airts," by Messrs. Kirkham,l;. Edwards, j. Begin- botham, and N. P'. Burt, who were very successful. Another quartettfe, which v.as given later on by four gentlemen who went•tnder the name 'of the Liverpool quartette, entitled "A FranCynne's Dogge also gave much satisfaction to the amdience, who demanded an encore end "Johnny Seim oker " was rendered. Mr. N. FJBurt contributedrthe solos "The storm fiend" and" To-morrow will be Fri- day' in a credEtable manner. The "11 Eaccio" of Miss Fanny Boeffieur wave fine performance and won a deserved encore. Miss Foullieur also contributed the song" EsmeraZda" in an acceptable style. Mr. Begin- botham tgave "The Sailor's Grave," and -Master Fred Sharp's song," Comrades in Arms" was so well rendered as to win a hearty encore. Among the other items of a varied progrimme were duets " Maying-" by Miss F. Bouffieur and Mr. E. tEdwards, and '"'Excelsior " by Messrs. Sam Kirkham nrid N. F. 'Burt.; concertina solo by Mr. T.R. Ford; ballad, Mr. E. Edwerds. Master W. Steele, who has had the honour of singing before Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone at flawarden sang in a capital manner the song" Sailing Homewards." Tire accompaniments were played by Mr. Z. L. Waltern Bernet, musical lec- turer to the Liverpool Corporation. The other items en the programme included exercises by members of the gymnasium in dumb-bells, rings., dumb-bell race, barbells, horizontaPbar, and vaulting 'horse. The musid for these exercises was supplied hy Mr. Ford. In the ,dumb-bell race thewinner was awarded a silver medal. he race was divided into four heats and a find. W. Whittle, with a start ofEseven yards, won the first heat.; S. Wright, seven yards, the second heat; A. J. Mottram, scratch; the third heat; E. Osborne, scratch, fourth heat ; S. V'right winning the final and the medal. A display with barbells, by the members of the gymnas- ium, was followed by a strength competition on the horizontal bar, in which Mr. W. Podmore won the prize, a'silvermedai. lAn exhibition of Skill on the voutting 'horse was also given as the closing item in the gymnas- tic part of' the entertainment.
CII.I,RITY '.CONCERT IN THE WARRING- TON CO-OPERATIVE HALL

'On Monday evening a concert was held in the Co-operative Hall, Sankey-st., in aid of the poor and invalid widow and the daughter of the late Colour-Sergeant Hare, who died 19 years since. Mr. Thomas Morris presided, and the hall was crowded, among those present being the Rev. Fathers Feeny, Turner, Cody, and Sumner. The Chairman said there never was an occasion on which he thought the words of Scripture "Bear ye one an- other's burdens "seemed more applicable. He was not going to preach a sermon, but that text seemed very apprepriate to an occasion like that. He then read a •circular which had been issued appeal- ing for -support for the concert, and remarked that he had never heard a more melancholy ,account concerning one family ; it, was really heartrending. He expressed his satis- faction ,at seeing such a magnificent audience, and his thanks to those who were going to cater for their enjoyment. He believed that anything that was.given in charity was never needvd.: those who_gave to such objects as the present never suf- fered by it.

The •oci- ncert was then proceeded with as follows, Mr. 0. Riley, acting as accompanist:—Selection, ,band;.eang; " Old Comrades," Pinstai, Mr. William Wallington. Song, "Death of Nelson," 13 trahant ; encore, "' Let me like a Soldier fall," Mr. .Jos. Bate. Selection,.'3and.•Song, " Old Ireland shall blossom again," E. R. P. Whitehead; encore, ",Cush-la- litarhree:," Mr. A. Cavanagh. Song, ." Angus MacDonald," (with band accompaniments),,,noecke/; .encore;."" Rory o' More," Miss Bessie Fanshaw. Miss Fanshaw obtained the unusual distinction of being recalled three times after her encore song, though she did not sing again, but merely bowed on each occasion. . Part'ilnd was as follows :—Selection by the band. Song,." My Pretty Jane," Xr. Uoseph Bate. Zang, " Thacly 0' Flynn," encore,." Going to Market," Miss Cavanagh. Song, "The Skipper," Mr. A.Tavanagh. Song, "Killarney," encore,-" The Shamrock," Miss Bessie Fanshaw. Song,-". Off to Philadelphia;" encore, " The three beggars," Mr. William Wallington. Finale, selection, band. Mr. Kierman proposed a vote of thanks to the chairman, remarking that everybody who knew hitn,,knew that he was always foremost in doing good work. Father Teeny -seconded, observing that they all knew Mr. Morris to be agood hearty fellow in every respect.---The •.vote was carried with cheers, and Mr. Morris thanked the audience. Brooks; and the proceedings concluded with the national anthem.
