div.head: TERRIFIC GAS EXPLOSION.
div.p: TERRIFIC GAS EXPLOSION.

FIVE LIVES LOST. On Moniay afternoon a tremendous exTaosion oc- curred in It block of buildings at the bottom of Market- place, Blackburn. It was soon found by those drawn to the scene from all quarters by the violence of the re- port, that the Crown Hotel had been blown up, together with ashop next door used as a cheap bazaar. The ex- plosion is believed to have been due VI an escape of gas, a new meter having been placed on Monday in the cel- lar af the shop destroyed. The ruins of the two build- ings took fire, and the fire brigade were called out. Several of the occupants of the premises were buried in I the ruins, and up to nine o'clock at night eight persons ibad been extricated from the Zebris—one of these, Mr. Houghton, landlord of the Crown Hotel, after fefur r and a half hours' intprisonmett—and one dead body re- covered. On Tuesday four more bodies of persons killed in Monday's explosion were recovered. The first of these , were found by a rescue pc,rty at 1 am, on Tuesday. It was the body of an old man, and it is believed to be that of John Casey, who is missing from 17, Canning-st. Deceased's legs had been burnt off. At alxmt 11 o'clock, on Tuesday morning ancther body was brought out, and was identified as that of William Fielding, aged 60, a tailor, of Simmons-st. Soon after eleven the body of another man was extricated. A few minutes later another corpse was rec\lvered,that of James Patterson, a draper, of Langham-st. This makes the fifth death from the explosion. All the deceased recovered since Mon- day night were in the bar of the Crown Hotel at the tune of the disaster. Mr. Houghton and Mrs. Wilkinson who are at the Infirmary, are, notwithstanding their severe injuries, reported to be progressing favourably. POLICE PROCEEDINGS. Marrk Robinson, fruiterer, Old James-street, gave him- self zip to the police, on Tuesday stating that he had been concerned with the gas meter, the explosion of wbiehoaused the disaster. He was remandea on bail, himself in £lOO and two sureties of £5O each. So far as the circumstances of the disaster transpired, they were as follows :—Robinson had bought a large gas meter at the Crown Hotel, and went to disconnect it, but neg- lected to take with him a qualified gasfitter. On detaching the meter, he became alarmed at the rush of , gas from the large connecting pipe, and ran from the premises, shouting incoherently. The gas rushed out in such volume as to quickly fill the basement, and an explosion followed before the people in the hotel knew what was the matter. The statement that the Corpora- tion workmen had anything to do with removing the meter is erroneous. The victims are Mrs. Buckley. John Casey, William Fielding, James Patterson. and Henry Smithson. The bodies were fearfully•crushed and burnt and the features scarcely recognisable. The Crown Hotel belongs to Mr. Rutherford, brewer, alderman, and ex-MayoK, who has exnressei a desire to bear the entire expense of the funerals of the victims. The wrecked premises are insured, and the destruction will form the subject of heavy claims against the insurance companies. The clearing away of the ruins of the Crown Hotel and adjoining shops went on all Tuesday night with the aid of a number of flare lights. Several room are still choked ,up with rubbish, and two men are still reported missing. The wreckage will not be quite &eared away for a couple of days.

div.head: OPENING OF TETE TNQUEST.
div.p: OPENING OF TETE TNQUEST.

The inquest on the bodies of the five victims was opened on Wednesday, in the Town Hall, by Coroner Robinson. The bodies were laid out in the second court, 'there being no mortuary, and presented a sickening sight when their linen coverings were removed. Mr. Withers represented the police, and the man Mark Robinson in custody on the charge of causing the explosion was re- presented by Mr. Crossley. Alderman Rutherford,owner of the Crown Hotel, was represented by Mr. Costeker. Mr. Riley appeared for Mrs. Patterson and Mr. Buckley. The Coroner said the inquiry would necessarily take a great deal of time and patience, and he proposed to ad- journ after taking available evidence. The bodies having been viewed,
Joseph Buckley, husband of the deceased woman, said his wife went into the town on Monday afternoon, to call at the sixpenny bazaar. He never saw her alive again.

-Thomas Casey said his father frequented the Crown Hotel, and he told him he should call at the hotel after delivering his work on Monday. Amos Fielding recognised the body of his father by the watch and clothes. He was a master tailor.

Thomas Smithson, fireman,identified his father's body. He was a cloth dearer, and left his shop in company of the deceased Fielding. Jessie Patterson said her husband was in the habit of frequenting the Crown Hotel. She last saw him at half- past ten on Monday morning. John Wilkinson, one of the partners in the bazaar, said ho saw Mrs. Buckley enter the shop shortly before four on Monday afternoon. He was leaving the shop when the explosion occurred, and his premises were instantly demolished. He noticed the smell of gas five minutes before he left the shop Police-inspector Bryne said he saw Mrs. Buckley's body recovered from the ruins of the "Sixpenny Bazaar." A number of fibre mats were lying over her body, and no doubt suffocated her. The body of Casey was recovered at midnight from the basement of the Crown, immedi- ately under the vaults, the feet of the body being badly burnt. Fielding's,Patterson's,a,nd Smithson's bodies were recovered about eleven o'clock on Tuesday morning from the cellar beneath the public bar, where the meter was situated. He thought they had all been drinking in the vaults. They were terribly disfigured by the fire, but he thought they were all dead before the fire reached them. The Coroner's officer, Walmsley, detailed the ghastly injuries the deceased I:ad received, which caused sensa- tion in court.
At this point the inquest was adjourned for a week.

div.head: TERRIBLE RAILWAY COLLISION.
div.p: TERRIBLE RAILWAY COLLISION.
SUICIDAL ACT OF REVENGE BY AN ENGINE-
DRIVER.

BERNR, TIIESDAY.—A fatal collision occurred to-day on the riilway between Klingnan, in Aargau, and Waldshut in Badan, between a light engine and a passenger train. The accident is believed to have been due to a deliberate act of revenge on the part Af the driver of the light engine, who had received notice of dismissal at the end of the year, and was only trusted with a supplementary service to Waldshut. At the station of Doettinge, the signals were against him. but, taking no notice either of these or of the station officials, who also signalled him to stop by whistling, the driver dashed through the station, and continued at full speed down the line towards the passenger train, which was approaching from the oppo- site direction. The crash of the collision was terrible, and the two engines were reduced to a confused mass of wreckage. Both the driver and stoker of the light engine were killed, and three persons in the passenger train re- ceived severe injuries.

The accounts furnished under the failure of the English Bank of the River Plate show liabilities amounting to nearly £4,500,000, and assets exceeding £5,500,000. The committee of the Labour Commission decided on Wednesday that it was desirable two women sub-com- missioners should be appointed to inquire into problems ,connected with female labour. • Cooks are often called upon to provide sweet dishes of cus- tards and blanc-manges at short notice, and at times when it is not convenient to obtain eggs. SUICIDE AT ItAINHILL.
A SAD CASE.

Henri HOWL, 64 years of age, tailor, of Ellaby- road, Rainhill, committed suicide by hanging him- self in his bedroom-on Sunday afternoon. Deceased had been in 41 depressed state of mind for some weeks past, and had latterly been unwell. Shortly after noon on Sunday he told his wife he did not know what was to become of them. He went up- stairs to lie in bed, and on his wife asking him to change some of his clothes he said he did not think he should ever want them again. A few hours later his wife, who is blind, called her husband to come to his tea, but she received no answer, and en going upstairs she felt her husband hanging behind the bedroom door. She called for assistance, and on several pereons entering the room the unfortunate man was found to be dead. A rope had been fastened to the top of the door, and deceased who was in a kneeling position, had succeeded in hanging himself. On Tuesday evening, Mr. S. Brighouse, coroner, held an inquest on the body of the deceased, at the Railway Hotel, Rainhill—Sarah Halsall, deceased's widow, said that her husband had been low-spirited lately, as he was getting short of work. He went to the relieving officer's house on Saturday morning, with the view of getting an order for admission to the workhouse. He could not see the relieving officer, however, as he was away from home. Her husband told her that if he went into the workhouse he should never come out again.— The Coroner said the case was an extremely painful one, and it was for the jury to say in what state of mind the deceased was when he took away his own life.—The jury after a short consultation, returned a verdict of "Suicide whilst in a state of temporary insanity."

THE SHIP CANAL.

MANCHESTER CORPORATION AND THE CANAL. The members of the Manchester City Council held an unusually long sitting on Wednesday. Three hours were devoted to a discussion of the report of the Special Committee on the Manchester Ship Canal. The Mayor, in moving the adoption of thc report, said it did seem strange that after the lapse of eight months it should be discovered that the estimates had to be increased by £863,595. At the same time he declared that nothing had occurred which, in his judgment, at all affected the commercial prospects of the undertaking. Mr. Alder- man Walton Smith said the Committee had no doubt that when the canal was made it would be a successful con- cern, but what they wanted was that it be completed early and at the smallest possible expense. Mr. Alder- man Chesters Thompson, Sir John Harwood, Mr. Alder- man Marks and Mr. J. W. Southern (representatives of the Council on the canal directorate) also addressed the meeting. They urged the importance of retrenchment and a reform in some of the modes of procedure. Some remarkable statements were made with regard to the expenditure on salaries, the want of supervision, and other important matters. Mr. Andrews said that the Corporation, as representative of the ratepayers, should have a domininant voice in the expenditure of money in future, and that some at least of the old directors should be called upon to resign. The discussion was adjourned for a week.

div.head: SALT CARGO AT WEAVER POOL.
div.p: SALT CARGO AT WEAVER POOL.

The barque Deodata commenced loading a cargo of salt on Monday, in the finished portion of the Manches- ter Ship Canal at Weaver Pool. The vessel was visited during the day by Mr. Thomas Ward, the manager, and other representatives of the Salt Union ; by representa- tives of Messrs. Verdin Bros., who are loading the vessel and Mr. Klembies, of Braumuller, Klembies and Co., the charterers, who are large shippers of salt to the Baltic and North American ports. This trial shipment is con- sidered so satisfactory that the Ship Canal will probably be largely used during the next season,which commences in the spring, by vessels which are too large to navigate the river to Weston Point and Runcorn, where salt can be loaded considerably cheaper than at Liverpool or Birkenhead. The Manchester Ship Canal Company have presented to the owners of the Deodata, to be carried on that vessel, a handsome clock and barometer, bearing an inscription that she was the first vessel to discharge a cargo of timber and also the first vessel to load a cargo of salt in the Manchester Ship Canal.

THE MANCHESTER-RD. RELIFYING OFFICES.

Mr. DIGGLE called attention to the want of-a-Ccommo- dation for people applying for their out-relief money at the Manchester-rd. relieving offices, and he suggested that a more commodious relieving office might be obtained at the schools in Smith-st.—Mr. W. Hounwrox said Mr. Garnett, the relieving officer, had complained to him that there was not accommodation for the people. He (Mr. Houghton) thought an improvement might be made by a re-arrangement of the registrars and relieving officers rooms which were under the same roof.—Mr. GARNETT, the relieving officer, having been called into the room, said a good deal of the inconvenience arose from the fact that people came for their relief half-an-hour or an hour before the appointed time, and they had, therefore, to wait about.—lt was ultimately agreed to appoint acom- mittee, consisting of Messrs. W. Houghton,Jolley, Diggle, and Heaton to take the matter into consideration. "Tait BADGE OF PAUPERISM."

Mr. Hood Wright said that, oii-Sunday last, a sermon was preached in St. Peter's Church, Newton, on behalf of the Waifs and Strays Society, by a gentleman who he believed was a deleaate of the Society. He had great sympathy with the movement himself, but he was very much annoyed by a remark made to the effect, that they had saved certain children from the" number," and the "badge of pauperism," and from having to wear uniforms. The preacher held forth a considerable time on the subject, but, being a guardian, he (Mr. Wright) knew it was altogether different in this Union. He should like it to be known that, in the Warrington Union, at any rate, the children did not wear uniforms, and did not have numbers. The statements were not true in regard to this Union, and, ho believed, were net true in regard to most Unions. (Hear hear.)—The Clerk said the preacher had been giving them some ancient history. In the reign cf William the Third a statute was passed that any person in the receipt of relief, whether an adult or a youth, should wear what was cane! the "badge of pauperism." The badge required by the statute was a conspicuous letter " p upon the shoulder, in order that the people might be distinctly distinguished as paupers in moving about the towns and villages. In the 40th year of George the Third that statute was repealed, and he had no personal knowledge of the" badge of Pauperism "having been at, all used in the nearly 50 years that he had been acquainted with the poor-law system. He kad not met with it in any of the workhouses and other institutions of a poor-law character in England, Ireland or Scotland. ,1 With regard to the uniform, it might, to some extent,still prevail, but it would naean that the children are dressed in one kind of clothing. But in that Union they decided some time ago that even uniform dress should not ,be worn at their schools, but 1 that the dress should be varied in order that the boys land girls might seem like the boys ard girls of people who were better off in life. There was no doubt this movement was more in accordance with the enlightened times in which we happened to live.—Mr. Hood Wright added that there were no pauper adults connected with the schools. There were no paupers to wait upon the children, and they were not brought in contact with them at all.—The Clerk said the purpose of the Guar- dians in starting Padgate Schools was to wholly separate the children from Workhouse influences. For a little while they had pauper help, but for some time past they had wholly excluded that help, and the schools were now under the charge of officers who were paid for their ser- vices.

div.head: TRE RUSSELL DIVORCE SUIT.
div.p: TRE RUSSELL DIVORCE SUIT.

The suit of the Countess Russell for a judicial separa- tion from her husband, Earl Russell,on the ground of his cruelty, was commenced in the Divorce Court, on Tues- day, before Sir Charles Butt and a special jury. Sir Edward Clarke opened the case for the petitioner, who married the respondent on February 6, 1890. She alleged that from that period to the time she left her husband he had habitually treated her with harshness and cruelty, and had been violent in his condnct, terrifying her, and injuring her health. He had called her a useless, un- educated woman, and had taunted her with sterility. It was said that respondent insisted upon a man named Roberts, said to be a mathematical master at a college at Bath, remaining in the house three or four days and nights, respondent going up to Roberts's bedroom un- dressed, and stopping for several hours. Petitioner gave evidence, and in cross-examination by Sir C. Russell, who appeared for the respondent, said that after her final separation from respondent she heard news from the Dowager Countess Russell, Lord Carlisle, and others, which made her feel sure there had been impropriety in her husbancl'e, relations with Roberts.

On Wednesday Lady Russell, in further cross-exam- ination, said it was matters communicated to her by Earl Russell's family, respecting his past life, which led her to place an unfavourable construction on the Roberts incident. She admitted having written affec- tionately from Brighton. Questions being asked as to the dishonouring of a cheque, his Lordship said that was a small matter, but Sir Charles Russell replied that this was the whole ground of the present proceedings. Dr. Clement Godson, who had attended Lady Russell since childhood, stated that on the occasion specified he advised that a separation was desirable, Lady Russell being weak and worried. Mrs. Lena Russell, sister of Lady Russell, gave details as to the Albemarle Hotel incident, and Snell Youatt, Lady Russell's maid, spoke to seeing her ladyship's wrists red as if from violence. Eliza Ann Vale, an old nurse in the Scott family,narrated the bedroom incident, and stated that Lady Russell was entirely without clothes. His lordship threw a bath towel over her. Sir Charles Russell opened the case for the respondent, contending that the Countess could have no object in these proceed- ings but to better her monetary position, and but for the dishonouring of her two cheques she would have con- sented to return to her husband. With regard to the Roberts incident, if it were seriously relied on, why wh,s it not put in the petition ? Lady Russell's story was entirely untrue. Earl Russell was never in Roberts's bedroom, though he joined him in the smoking room. The hearing of the case was adjourned.

div.head: EXAAAIINER.
div.p: THE EXAAAIINER.

difference on the division of the surplus left after the production of commodities between employer and workman, between capital and labour." • There can be no doubt that as workmen grow in intelligence' and strengthen their organisations they will imrtwe their position ; labour will be on something like a footing of equality with Capital, and it will not be a case on either side of dictating terms, but of determining as equals the bases of an agreement for dividing the fruits of industry.. Meantime; and before this stage is reached, there are signs of harsh conflict—not so apparent in this. country as in the United States of America:. Capitalists have combinedto an extent absolutely' startling, and, by forming what are known as) Trusts or Syndicates, they are dominating the labour market, and exacting large profits at the expense of the labouring classes. The workers see. this ; they feel, that-they are being ground between the upper and nether millstone; and in the large cities in particular they are ex- asperated and-growing reckless:- Mr- GLADEMONE, referring more particularly to England,,saysthat workmen by the possession of political power have the means of self-defence in theirown hands ;•• and so they,have, hat-neither in this country nor in Ameriea•have they learned as yet- how to, make the best-use of it.. It still .happens • that, capital, and the representatives of capita 4 crowd' Parlia- ment and :Congress,while labour,like " Unregarded ',age, is into corners thrown." What a reflection .\on the fears that were expressed of being swemptid by an extension of the, franchise is the fact-that, after the lapse of over:twenty years,,less than-a, dozen working-men have seats in the House, of Commons r; Still, the. voice of the people :;s1 be- ginning te be heard above the Babel---of class, in- terests; and if, they do but cohere and ' persist they will not only. be -heard but heeded: The de- mand for shorter hours amongst miners and railway men has come to be regarded by politicians of all classes as one that must, ere long, be- conoeded; and, that secured, it is zt... matter of course to say/it will be followed by a shortening of hours=all round, to something approximating to the eight-hours.• day. But before this casibe accomplished there is-, much to do in the way., of bringing continental. workers into a line with British workers. It, is cf little use trying to get an eight-hours day-in- Eng-, land so !mg as ten or twelve hours are-being worked on the other • side •of the ChanneL - It is - something gained that Trades Unionists perceive- this, and,,are working, therefore, to international ends. They are on the right track, and if • they keep to it they will eventually succeed, and, that success wilt be a blessing to,humanity. Labour is well in its way; but employers. as well as employed , may have brio much of it. Let master and-man strive then to secure—
Ease and alternate labouTruseful life, Progresswe virtue, and approving Heavaxr!

div.p: SATURDAY. DECEU3EL 54 18.91.
THE manyrpidedrwss of Mr. Gla.d., In Praise of stone's mind.had its latest illustra-

Labotm tion in the two, speeches which he made on Saturtlay—one at. Spital. Station, on, cur- ent politics,. and the other, in opening the new. hall at Port Sunlight, on the variousaspects of Lthoun and the labour question. Politics, like thep9or,, are always with us, and it is pleasant therefore,: by way of a..change, to learn :what a great statesman. thinks about work andixorkers. Mr. Gladstone has always, been a busy man ;: he doesn't seem to, have any idea of what zome people regard .as,the luxury ,of having nothing, to do;. for, froim all, one. hears cflim,, his mode of relaxation is to goirom., one pl.:mot work to anotherof an entirely differ.- ent kindi—from cuttingidowa trees,for instance„.to. cutting: up Lord Salisbury.. We need nothe sur- prised:then at his saying,. whilst admitting„ that labour i.S, the burden ,of man, that "there are in the world worse things than& labour, worse things than heavy labour, andone of those is idle wealth. In vain the man escapesfrom the destiny of bard wonk—even hard work with some degrse of pov,erty —teattain wealtb,if that wealth is to bring with it the curse, the unmitigated curse, oZidlene.ss and self-indulgence." This a hard saying or the tens oi thousands whoJoil zot neither de the!. spin . and it is to be hoped it will have the effect of 'stimu'ating some..of them to lead lives worth living. iWe have not yet got to putting in. force the moral :law which says:if:any man will not work neither :shall he eat ; audit is because we; are so far from enforcing it that the extremes of poverty and wealth are urra: glaring to-day, than. ever they were beforeini\the history of the .world. It is as Byron has. it—
"The many still must labour for the one

And it is.becnne there seems to be no way of get- ting out. of this ever-deepening rut that Labour's cry is. growing loud and somewhat bitter.. Thoreau,. the American essayist,, has a pretty pic- ture of his, meeting a townsman at work in the early morning; of his reflections on the beauty and dignity of the scene ;• and how his pleasant thoughts were instantly succeeded by a feeling of revulsion upon lea-ning that ethe labourer was at work not on some really useful or necessary thing, but to gratify the latest whim of a, vulgar millionaire. The millionaire is a monstrosity; and it is because he exists and multiplies that he has at his beck and call so many of Adam's sons who are one remove, and one remove only, from the verge of starvation.

"Many faint with toil That few may know the ease and woe of sloth." Bdt what of , the future ? It is refreshing to observe that the toiling octogenarian takes a cheerful view of it. He says :—" I dismiss as being needless, as being, therefore, perhaps mischievous, those fears that greed on one side and greed on the other will lead to permanent and irreconcilable

div.head: "TOUCH AND GO."
div.p: "TOUCH AND GO."

Lord Monkswell presided over a meeting in London, on Monday, at which " a resolution was adopted that, in the interests of secondary educa- tion, the Greek language should be removed from the list of compulsory subjects in the examinations for degrees at the Universities." Let there be Greek by all means—for those who want it ; but not for those to whom learning it will be a waste ni time.

Emerson was a scholar as well as a thinker, and this is what he had to say on the subject many years ago : " Some thousands of young men are graduated at our colleges in this country every year, and the persons who, at forty years, still read Greek can be counted on your hand. I never met with ten." From this it will be seen that the boys who waste time over the Greek particle scarcely, as men, know a particle of Greek.

From a letter which appears on our second page, it will be seen that Mr. Whitham is not let- ting the grass grow under his feet, although he has been thrown out of work at San Francisco. He is now on his way to Worcester, Massachusetts, .He has, we understand, been in communication with Mr. Joseph Ellison, who is at Worcester,and, as there aro several wire and iron works in the district, Mr. Whitham has a fair prospect of get- ting a berth to his liking. It is to be hoped he will be suenssful.

Instead of taking a week to consider his.reply to the invitation to become the Conservative can- didate for Warrington, Mr. Robert Pierpoint is allowing himself a fortnight. The Tories as a party have not been accustomed to subscribe in these matters • for have they not always looked to the brewer of Walton Hall as their special Provid- ence? And what if there should be an intimation that for the future the financial tap will be stopped, or, at thebest, issue in driblets I It would make things awkward; and necessitate full use of the Considering Cap.

An ambassador has been described as a person who lies abroad for the benefit of his countrymen at home. Straightforwardness in negotiations is not expected, and when it is used there is risk of its being dealt with by "reading between the lines." The following excellent story is told of our relations with the Afghans :—" The only time they were ever puzzled at Cabal was when Lord Law- rence wrote a perfectly simple and lucid despatch, which meant exactly what it said. The Ameer and his advisers turned it inside out, read it back- wards and forwards, discussed it for hours, and then decided it to be utterly unintelligible."

This incident is suggestive of the story of the experienced tippler who boasted that he could, while blindfolded, name, after tasting, any intoxi- cant offered to him. A bet was made on the mat- ter, and he was put to the test. He got on swim- mingly, naming liquor after liquor as soon as it had passed his lips. The proceedings were just beginning to be monotonous when the wine- bibber paused after tasting; then he tasted and paused again, and again. At last he had to admit that he was beaten. "I cannot," he said, "name that liquor." Poor fellow ; it was quite new to him; it was water.

Another hunt, and another accident. A fox was killed, on Monday, after a chase through Appleton Dingle; and one gentleman was so hurt that he had to be taken home in a gig. Several 1 adies joined in the chase, for it is still considered con- sonant with the gentler feelings of the gentle sex to harry and agonise a poor brute for hours and be, if possible, "in at the death." "It is all in the way of sport, you know," as the Spanish ladies say who go to a bull fight. There is a difference; but it is one of degree not of kind. To kill anything merely for sport is barbarous—it is brutalising.

The appointment of a clergyman for Burton- wood in place of the curate-in-charge is causing no little dissatisfaction amongst the parishioners, who find that they don't count in such a matter. But they cannot eat their cake and have it. If they will have Church and State they must have it "for better or worse "—even When, as the darkey com- plained after marriage, it is "all worse and no better." The incident will have one good effect; it will set some Churchmen a-thinking ; and they .may perhaps be led to see that the way out by the door of disestablishment will not be a bad thing, after all.

The eight hours question is becoming a thorn in the side of Parliamentary candidates. It is pricking Mr. Henry Broadhurst, who sits for West Notting- ham. He declines to commit himself to the bill, and some of his constituents are dissatisfied. But will it better them if they cause a split and allow a Tory to ran in? The labouring-class must "learn to labour and to wait" in this as in other matters. Mr. Broadhurst is of more value to them than a hundred Tory M.P.s. Happily, the Liberals as a whole in West Nottingham recognise this; and a vote of confidence in him was carried on Monday by a large majority.

Lord Ribblesdale narrates a conversation he once had with the late Mr. Parnell in which reference was made to the late Lord Carnarvon's views as Lord Salisbury's lord-lieutenant of Ireland. "Lord Carnarvon7 said Mr. Parnell, "had a very com- plete scheme of Home Rule worked out in all its details, but the scheme was only to come into operation gradually—that is, Home Rule was to be a measure granted to Ireland on her prefer- ment." This is strong confirmation of much that has been heard before; and it is quite sufficient to explain why Lord Carnarvon resigned when he found that his "message of peace" was to be followed by Coercion.

There is some reason to fear that as the resnit of the syndicate on the Alkali trade there will be a reduction, in the number of employed both at Widnes and at St. Helens. Lessening the cost of - production may be good for business; but it is— immediately at any rate—a bad thing for workmen, who are left to shift for themselves. There is such a thing as removing to another town ; and that is what should be done when there is a certainty of employment. The outlook is by no means bright; and,when winter sets in, the unemployed will most likely stand in need of a helping hand which, it is to be hoped, will be extended to them.

The latest crisis—would it were the last ! in connection with the Ship Canal makes it pretty clear that more time and more money will be re- quired before the undertaking can be completed. It is very disheartening, and has caused share- holders to use "a big big D" who are albeit unused to .that mode of expression. It is now plain as a pikestaff why the Canal Company want to put off the making of Warrington Docks; but why should Warrington be sacrificed more than any other place on the Canal? The Cor- poration must be firm in this matter; .it is not good even for the Company that the making of Warrington Docks should be delayed beyond the three years specified, for that means, in all proba- bility, five years from the present time.

div.head: SHOCKING FATALITY ON A RAILWAY.
div.p: SHOCKING FATALITY ON A RAILWAY.

As a married woman named Webster and her child, residing at Byrom Bridge, Lowton, were walking along the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lin- colnshire Railway to catch a train at St. Mary's Station, for Liverpool, they were taught by a pas- eenger train and killed on the spot. The husband, who was with them, escaped uninjured. The police were informed, and had the bodies removed to await an inquest.
Umuitar..x.es- REcovERED.—.T. aud W. DUTTON, Sankey-st., Warrington.—Advt.

SCALDING FATALITY NEAR ST. HELENS. Annie Bridge, two years of age, daughter of Win. Bridge, labourer, of 34, Fiddler-st., Thatto Heath, died on Wednesday night from the effects of scalds received on Tuesday night. A pan of broth was boiling on the fire/ and the child was left in a rock- ing chair, while Mrs. Bridge wav working in the back kitcben. The child screamed, and Mrs. Bridge found that by some means the chair had upset, and the child was lying against the fender. The pot of broth had been pulled from the fire, and the little girl was badly scalded about the legs and body. Dr. Jackson was sent for, but notwithstanding every attention the child died.

div.head: PRESENTATION ALMANAC.
div.p: PRESENTATION ALMANAC.

***Our Annual Sheet Alrcanac will be presented on Saturday, December 19th, It will be adorned with a beautiful view of Abbeystead, and portrait of the Earl of Sefton, LG., and will contain a large quantity of local and other information. This issue of the "Examiner," being on the Satur- day before Christmas,will be furnished with tales, sketches, Szc., uuder the title of "Our Christmas Corner." Advertisers will do well to avail them- selves of the extra circulation on Almanac day. News agents are requested to order early.
"EVENINGS FOR 'FRE PEOPLE?'
On Thursday evening Mr. W. P. Copeland delivered a lecture, illustrated by lime-light views,at Waterloo-road Schools, Widnes, on" Martin Luther,his life and times."
NARROW ESCAPE PRODI DROWNING AT RUNCORN.
About noon on Wednesday, a girl about 11 years of age, named Maud Kirkham,fell into the canal'at Savage Bridge. Hercries attracted the attention of two men who promptly rescued her.

div.p: THE SEAMEN'S INSTITUTE AT RLTNCORN.

This Institute will be opened on Thursday afternoon nexts by the Bishop of Chester. Afterwards there will be tea provided, and in the evening a public meeting will be held. Particulars in our advertising columns.

div.head: BENEFIT FOOTBALL MATCH AT WIDNES
div.p: BENEFIT FOOTBALL MATCH AT WIDNES

On Thursday afternoon a football match between Craig's Widnes team and dross's St: Helens team was played on the Widnes Football ground, the proceeds to be -devoted to the fur& of the Widnes Tradesmen's Foot-- ball Club. The final result was—Craig's team, 2 tries, and Cross's team 1 try.

div.head: TEMPERANCE SUNDAY.
div.p: TEMPERANCE SUNDAY.

Last Sunday was "Temperance Sunday "and sermons on the evil effects of intemperance were preached in the whole of the Nonconformist Churches in Runcorn and district. A juvenile temperance meeting was held in Brunswick School, on Sunday afternoon, Mr. T. Simister presiding. Addresses were delivered by Messrs: W. Millington, E. Marshall, and D. Bisbrown.

A RAILWAY TRESPASSER SERIOUSV INJURED AT WIDNES. • 1, About eleven o'clock on Saturday night', Thos. Coghley, of Midwoed-et., was found lying on the railway be- tween Appleton and Farnworth, with a wound in his forehead large enough to admit three fingers. Dr. McLennan and Dr. Hudson dressed the wound, and he was conveyed home. The injured mln said he was walking on the line to Farnworth, but could not account for his injuries. • PETROLEUM OIL.—J. S. Garland, Ironmonger, Bridge-st., Warrlngton.—Advt. ASSAULT ON A WIDNES GROCER.

At the Widnes Petty Sessions on Thursday, Thomas Noon, caretaker at West Bank Board School, was sum- moned for assaulting Mr.T.Smith, grocer, Mersey-rd. De- fendant was vexed about being put in the County Court, had, it was stated, struggled with and struck Mr. Smith. He kicked Mr. Smith on the shin, causing it to bleed considerably, and also causing him to be lame. He was bound over in his own surety and two other sureties to be of good behaviour for six inonths,or go to goal for one month.

div.head: ATTEMPTED SUICIDE.
div.p: ATTEMPTED SUICIDE.

The Widnes magistrates,on Saturday, committed John Helsby, of Milton-st., to the Workhouse for 14 days. On the previous day the prisoner had threatened to murder his mother,and had then attempted to hang himself, but was prevented by his sister. P.C. Fisher went to the house to take him in charge, when the prisoner seized a knife from the table, and attempted to cut his throat, and it was only after a severe struggle that the officer wrested the knife from him. He will be placed under medical care at the Workhouse. UMBRELLAS RECOVERED.—J. and W.PUTTON, Sankey-st., Warrington.—Advt. • FOUND DEAD AT RfINCORN. •

On Tuesday the naked body of a man, one leg being missing was found in the reservoir at the top 4. Dukes Field, Runcorn. The body was terribly battered and was in an advanced state of decomposition. It is sup- posed that the body had come through the culvert from the Bridgewater Canal. The body was identified by P.S. Gosling as that of Joseph Hopley, carter, of Bridge- water-st., who had been missing for about three months. Mr. .1. E. Worsley held the inquest on Wednes- day and a verdict of" Found Dead" was returned. WESLEYAN FOREIGN MISSIONS AT RUNCORN. _ _ _ _ _ _ _

The annual gatherings in aid of the Wesleyan Foreign Missions were held at Widnes last week end. On Satur- day night the Rev. W. R. Winston, a Missionary from Burmab, delivered a lecture in Lacey-st., School. on " Burmah and its People," his remarks being illustrated by lime light views. The chair was occupied by Mr. E. Woodward, of Liverpool. In Victoria-road Chapel on Sunday Mr. Winston delivered two eloquent sermons to large congregations. On Monday, evening the annual meeting was held in the chapel, and addresses on Foreign missionary work were delivered by the Revs. W. R. Winston, W. Pritchard, G. S. Meek, and others, The col- lecitons were very satisfactory. UMBRELLAS ILECOVESED.—S. and W. DUTTON, Sankey-st., Warrington.—.Adv.

div.head: LICENSE VERY PROPERLY REFUSED. – – -- – – –
div.p: A LICENSE VERY PROPERLY REFUSED. - - -- - - -

Before Mr. H. Reynolds and Mr. James Handley, at Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, William . Holt applied for a 14 days' license under the Public Health (Amendment) Act, to enable him to keep a public danc- ing room in Alexandra Buildings, Waterloo Bridge. He said he intended to keep the room as private as possible. There was no harm in young people enjoying themselves and this was the only place in town where they could keep away from the public-house. Young people had told him that they had spent less money than ever they did before through keeping away from the evil of drink. —By Superintendent Large: He had kept this as a dancing room for five years.—Superintendent Large said he opposed this application, and he would call evidence to prove that a great deal of immorality took place and rude conduct generally on the part of the young women and young men who assembled in the room. The appli- cant was fined two weeks ago for keeping the dancing room without a license.—P.S. Woolley said he had had this building under his observation ever since it was opened, and whenever he visited the place he found a lot of rowdyism, and men and women were drunk. Many of the women came from Widnes,and they created all sorts of disturbances, and had to be followed to the Bridge. On. the 24th Dec., last year; Holt called witness and P.C. Hamersley there to quell a disturbance. The conduct of the frequenters of this place the witness des- cribed as horrible.—Mr. Reynolds: We refuse this appli- cation altogether. GAS FITTINGS.—:r. S. Garland, Gas Fitter, Bridge-st., Warrington.—Advt.

div.head: FUNERAL OF MR. BERT NORMAN, WIDNES.
div.p: FUNERAL OF MR. BERT NORMAN, WIDNES.

Mr. Herbert T. Norman, of Stanley Villas, Runcorn, earthenware manufacturer, died on Monday morning after a long and painful illness at the early age of 27 years. He was a young man full of promise, and with good prospects in life, and his early death plunged his relations into the deepest grief, and caused widespread grief amongst his numerous friends and acquaintances. His remains were interred in the family grave at the cemetery on Thursday at noon, amid a eoncourse of spectators. The coffin, which was hidden beneath a large number of beautiful wreaths, was conveyed in a hearse, and following were five coaches, the occupants being Rev. T. Wilkes, Rev. W. Arrowsmith, and Rev. H. Hanby, and Dr. McDougall; Messrs. William Fred, Alfred, and Charles E. Norman (brothers), Robert and John Norman (uncles), and John and Thomas Nornian (nephews), W. Deakin (Liverpool). Frank Timmins, R. Fryer, Andrew Matthews, Aldtrman McKechnie (St. Helens) ; B. Leach, S. Looker Williams, and Dr. Hewitt. Preceding the hearse were a number of townspeople, of whom were noticed Rev. Jno, Simpson, Rev. J. P. Wil- liams, Messrs. J. Pbsnett, J. J. Potter, J. Bridgewater, J F. Moulton, S. Coventry, J. Woodland, R. Morris, W. Dutton,l. Hadfield, P. Jones, and B. Kniveton. The coffin was carried from the cemetery chapel to the grave on the shoulders of eight of the deceased gentleman's friends. The burial service was conducted by the Revs. T. Wilkes, W. Arrowsmith, and H. Hanby. Mr. R. Morris had charge of the arrangements and Messrs. Yar- wood supplied the conveyances,

div.head: FRODSIIAM INQUIRY OF LORD SALISBURY.
div.p: A FRODSIIAM INQUIRY OF LORD SALISBURY.

Writing to a Frodsham correspondent, Lord Salis- bury's secretary, referring to the remarkable story recently published to the effect that a lady had dis- covered in his lordship's major-domo an Italian Jesuit priest in disguise, wno disappeared on his identity being discovered, states that he is desired by Lord Salisbury to say that the story is a silly invention, and absolutely devoid of any foundation. KITCHEN KANGERS.—GarIand Builders Ironmonger, War rington.— Advt. 1:1.07,Y TRINITY CHURCH BAZAAR.

On Thursday afternoon a two days' bazaar as commenced in Trinity Schools with the object of liquidating a debt incurred in connection with the day schools and repairing the buildings, and also of raising funds to renovate and beautify the church. There were four stalls charmingly set out, and the appearance of the room was bright. There was also an admirably arranged retreshment room. There was a large attendance at the opening cere- mony, which was performed by Lady Brooke, of Norton Priory. The proceeds of the first day amounted to £l4O. Yesterday the bazaar was opened by Mr. A Hornby Lewis,of Marbury Hall,Northwich. .7 UMBRELLAS RECOVERED.-J. and W. DUTTON. Sankey-t., Warrington.--Advt.

div.head: FAILURE OF ST. HELENS BUILDERS.
div.p: FAILURE OF ST. HELENS BUILDERS.

A meeting of the creditors of Messrs. Crake and Marsh, builders and contractors, was held On Mon- day afternoon, at the Fleece Hotel, when Mr. Cook, (Messrs. Barrow and Cook, solicitors) submitted a statement of accounts, from which it appeared that the liabilities amounted to £1,871, and the assets to £1,216. The statement as supplied by the debtors differed considerably from the claims of the various creditors. It also transpired that the Manchester and Salford Banking Co., who were down as credi- tors to the amount of £583, were in possession of security byXl37 over that sum, as the debtors had assigned to them portions of certain contracts, principally those for property being built fot Colonel Gamble and Lord Gerard.. The debtors made an offer of 7s. fith in the X but this was refused outright, and the debtors were asked to advance the amount to 103. and to find security for the last half-crown instalment. This was finally done and Mr. Bate (Bates and Co.) and Mr. W. Mills (J. T. and W. Mills), were appointed trustees. The first portion of the estate of Mr. Thomas Roberts, was brought under the hammer by Mr. Joseph B. Leach, of St. Helens and Liverpool, acting under in- structigns from the Board of 'trade, on Wednesday. There as a large attendance of the general public, and for the horses, carts, waggons, &c., offered, fair prices were realised. _

isseuLTiNp • :17rrNass.—Catherine Hynes, Marsh-st.. ,was charged with committing an aggravated assault on Mary Tracy. A DESERTER.—Private George McVicar, from Alder- shot; was _charged with being a deserter.—The prisoner stated that he had not returned to Alcjershot because he aad no money to ptty his fare.—Ele was remanded until Monday for the authorities to be made acquainted with the case.

div.head: WIDNES CONSERVATIVE CLUIt.
div.p: WIDNES CONSERVATIVE CLUIt.

The annual meeting of members was held in the Club Assembly Room on Monday evening. Mr. R. Lewis presided and amongst those present were Messrs. W. T. Husband (hon. Sec.), S. Upward (treas.) W. S. Callender J. C. Crawford, W. Treaey, T. H. Thomas, A. E. Jervis, C. H. Wats3n, J. P. Kershaw, I W. E. Oakden, H. White, J. Treacy, G. E. Sam, and C. F. Yates.—The Chairman read the report of the I Committee, which stated there were 217 members and the subscriptions paid amounted to £llB 4s. It was evident that the club was appreciated owing to the man- ner in which its various advantages had been made use of by the members of the club. The possition of the Committee as regarded interest in the building and in the Club: Buildings Committee had been strengthened by the late Sir Thomas Moss, bart., and Sir. J. C. Ed- wards Moss, Viscount Cross, and Mr. E. Whitley, present- ing their shares in the Company to the Club Committee. The Committee hoped that the members would rally round and bring fresh strength to the club in the year. just entered upon, because in all prabability during the year the organisation would be put to the test, by a se- verely contested election .—The report was unanimously adopted,—The treasurer's report showed total: receipts £352 17s. 9d.; and expenditure £305 2s. 2id., leaving a balance in hand of £47 15s. W.—Viscount Cross was unanimously re-elected president, and the list of vice- presidents was also adopted. The Chairman remarked that 11(fr. Husband found it was impossible for him to once r bald the position of secretary, which he had filled with much ability. He therefore proposed that Mr. J. Treacy be appointed at a salary of £s.—Mr. W. E. Oak- den seconded, and Mr. Husband supported the proposi- tion, which was carried unanimously.—Mr. Upward was re-appointed treasurer.—ln concluding the proceed- ings the Chairman said they were on the eve of a general eloctim, and he hoped that all the members would work hard.

div.head: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.

The monthly meeting was held at the Town Hall, on Tuesday night. Mr. J. Pritchard presided, and there were present the Rev. Canon Maitland Wood, Messrs. T. Handley, A. Salkeld, S. Taylor, and G. Moss (clerk.)
SCHOOL ATTINDANCH.

The minutes of the Sch4ol Attendance Committee showed that 78 parents had been summoned before the Committee for not sending their children regularly to school ; 70 appeared, and proceedings were ordered to be taken against 11 parents. The Clerk submitted statistics he had prepared for the Education Department showing the attendance at elementary schools in Run- corn, for the 12 weeks since the Assisted Education Act came into operatien as compared with the correspond- ing period last year. As regarded infants there was an increase of 89 on the rolls, and 116 in the average atten- dance. Of the older children there was an increise of 49 on the rolls, and 113 in average attendance. It was recommended that the salary of G. Howard be advanced to £B5 per annum, commencing January Ist, 1892, and that it be intimated to him that this is a maximum salary for his position as second visitor.—Mr. Salkeld moved and Mr. Taylor seconded the adoption of the minutes, and the motion was carried.

div.head: SCHOOL MANAGEMENT.
div.p: SCHOOL MANAGEMENT.

The School Mani-e-in-en't-a-,-;;;;-2-i-t-t-had considered a scale of salaries for assistant teachers,but it was deemed advisable not to fix a scale at present. It was recom- mended that a sum not exceeding 30s. be allowed for biro of ,slides for the magic lantern to illustrate the teaching of geography at the evening school during the current session.—The minutes were approved.

div.head: COST 07 VICTORIA-ROAD.
div.p: THE COST 07 VICTORIA-ROAD.

The Clerk said in-, -September the Board received notice from the Improvement Commissioners that they sere about to make and sewer Victoria-road, and the work was now nearly finished. He was informed that the School Board would have to contribute £2oo.—The Chairman said this ought to be regarded as capital ex- penditure and the amount spread over a term of about 20 years. Mr. Taylor said the Commissioners were in want of the money and the sooner they had it the better.—Mr. Handley : Are not the Commissioners borrowing the money ,and spreading the cost over a term of years ?—The Chairman : No,they have not got to that perfection yet.—On the motion of Mr. -Taylor it was unanimously resolved that.the Clerk apply to the Public Works Loan Commissioners for a loan of £2OO for a term not exceeding 20 years ; the same to be applied

div.head: TECHNICAL INSTRUCTION
div.p: TECHNICAL INSTRUCTION

The Clerk said he had received a letter front Mr. E. Marshall, Clerk to the Runcorn Board ot Commissioners, intimating that the Board had voted to the School Board the sum of £1,90 for the purpose of purchasing apparatus for teaching science and art, on the under- standing that the School Board, on the establishment of a Technical Institute, transfer the apparatus to the Com- missioners or the Committee having control or manage- ment of the Institute, whenever called upon to do so.— The Chairman isnoved,and Mr. Taylor seconded, a motion accepting the money on terms cited.—Carried.
RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMISSEONERS.

The monthly meeting was held at the Town Hall, on Thursday. Mr. H. J. Grice presided, and there were present Messrs. P. Speakman, C.C., W. Fisher, W. Timmins, J. W. Lightburn, B. Bisbrown, S. Tay- lor, F. Wiswall, R. Abel, W. Hankinson W. R. Was, P. Smith. J. Pritchard, E. W. Humphreys, H. Co- ward, J. Meadowcroft, H. White, F. A. Lake (law clerk), E. Marshall (secretary), and M. Barker (sur- veyor).

div.head: CONGRATULATIONS TO MR. SMITH.
div.p: CONGRATULATIONS TO MR. SMITH.

Upon Mr. Smith entering the mons, Mr. Lightburn congratulated him upon his marriage, and wished him much happiness.—The Chairman also said he had also great pleasure in congratulating Mr. Smith, who did not fail to recognise the Board through the Chairman, and the bridescake he sent was partaken of by the members. —Mr. Smith thanked the members for their kind ex- pressions.

div.head: HEALTH OF THE TOWN.
div.p: HEALTH OF THE TOWN.

The medical officer (Dr. McDougall) reported that the number of deaths registered during the past Month amounted to 39. One of these was an inquest case. The average death-rate was 234 and exclusive of the inquest cas* of 22.8.

div.head: HIGHWAYS AND BUILDINGS COMMITTEN.
div.p: HIGHWAYS AND BUILDINGS COMMITTEN.

This Committee recommended that the tender of Messrs. Henry Heys and Co. for the supply of 1,000 yards of edgings at is. 9d. per lin. yard and 1,000 yards of Channels at is. Bd. pe liii. yard or of such other quantity as may be required, delivered at Run- corn, less 2i per cent. discount, be accepted. That the plan of Mr. Joseph Pritchard for erection of a cottage in Jackson's-lane and of three sculleries at the rear of pre- sent cottages at the same place be improved.—Carried.

div.head: BETTHR LIGHTING
div.p: BETTHR LIGHTING

The General Purposes Committee recommended that a lamp be fixed in Irwell-lane, and at the end of Old Quay road, and that two of Bray's lamps be purchased for the pillars on Waterloo Bridge. THE SITE OF THE TECHNICAL INSTITUTE. ,

div.head: LIVELY DISCUSSION.
div.p: LIVELY DISCUSSION.

Mr. Pritchard moved the following recommendation of the Parliamentary Committee : That Messrs. Grice, Prichard, Lightburn and Wassail, be appointed a sub-Committee to draw up a schedule of requirements in respect of the proposed Technical Institute and that they be empowered to consult Mr. J. Bowden, C.E., Manchester. with a view to the nreparation of a draft plan and an estimate, and that such sub-committee re- port to the Commissioners.—Mr. W. R. Wass sbconded. Mr. Smith asked how much it was :ikely to cost to consult the engineer The Law Clerk replied about five guineas. Mr. Smith thought their Surveyor ought to be able to do work of this kind. Mr. Speakman said it was absolutely neces- sary that an expert should be employed, otherwise they might drift into something they.knew not of. The Com- mittee were unanimous in this opinion. The Chairman said they had a deputation from London, who distinctly told them they should have the question of the erection of a building and the arrangement thereof submitted to to a capable man and an expert; and this was the reason the Committee had decided to do so. Mr. Lightburn said the plans would have to be approved by the authori- ties at South Kensington before they could get a grant, and they had better pa Y a guinea or two more now than have to send several times down to London at more expense. Mr. Smith said he did not wish to cast any reflection on Mr. Barker, but he thought be had had sufficient experience to deal with this matter. Mr. Wiswall spoke of Mr. Bowden's qualifications to deal with this subject, and said the Committee had done the right thing. Mr. Barker was well employed now. Mr. Smith moved an amendment that the Surveyor do the work. Mr. Speakman: He cannot do it. Mr. Smith: It is for the Board to say and not you. Mr. Taylor: I hope it won't be seccnded. The amendment was not seconded and the original motion was passed, only Mr. Smith voting against. Mr. Lightburn moved the follow- ing minute of the Parliamentary Committee: "That the open space at the Town Hall be appropriated for the erection of a Technical Institute provided such a Site meets the requirements of the case, and in the event of the site being found to be eligible that the Local Government Board be asked to sanction its appro- priation." The Chairman of the Committee (Mr. Pritchard) was not in favour of this minute and therefore did not move it, but Mr. Lightburn argued that he was loyally bound to obey the dictates of the Committee and to have proposed it. The raison d'etre of that proposition was that the majority of the Com- mittee thought it a suitable site fora technical institute and they were fortified in that opinion by General Pest- lug, one of the highest authorities in the country, who considered this a very eligible site and it was to this gentleman the plans would have to be submitted. Be- sides they had got this land doing nothing ;, therefore why should they go to some spot they knew nothing of and further burden the ratepayers, who were already sufficiently burdened. Of course if the erection of the institute on that site would be prejudicial to the Town Hall, they could then fix on some other site for the in- stitution.—Mr. R. Abel seconded.—Mr. Pritchard said it was arranged that he should move the first minute and Mr. Lightburn the, second (Mr. Lightburn: I said if you refused to move both) and now he found Mr. Light- burn blamed him for taking a course which he him- self recommended. (Mr. Wiswall : No, no). He ob- jected to this minute because the Committee had not made a single inquiry aS to any other eligible site for this institute. He did not say this was not a suitable place and that eventually they might not have to erect the institute there, but when dealing with a question of this sort it was the duty of the Committee to make some preliminary inquiries be- fore they decided upon this sibe. Greenway-road Board Schools was an imposing structure which was an orna- ment to the town, and of which the ratepayers were justly proud. In his opinion a Technical Institute and a SchOol of Art should be a building of some architectu- ral pretensions, and he should be sorry if their institute should coriapare unfavourably and be eclipsed by an elementary school. For this reason he wished the Com- mittee to make inquiries as to the other sites.—Mr. Humphreys said as it WaS he who first moved a resolu- tion on this question, it was not likely that he should do anything to act prejedicially on technical education, and sympathising with Mr. Pritchard's views, he moved this amendment :—" That Mr. Bowden be asked to in- spect the building land adjoining the Tows Hall,and any other site considered by the Parliamentary Committee to be eligible,and in the event of such committee,after con- sultation with Mr. Bowden, being of opinion that the site adjoining the rown Hall is the most eligible, having regard to all the requirements of the case, that the Local Government Board be requested to sanction the appropriation of such land for the purpose of a Techni- cal Institute and Science and Art Schools."—Mr. Prit- chard seconded the motion. After an animated discus- sion a vote was taken. For the amendment there voted Messrs. Pritchard, Humphreys, and Smith, and the rest against. The original motion was carried with only one dissentient. WATERLOO BRIDGE AND DIRTY RpApsl._.

Mr. Spe;1;;;;;.-id-1;;;ICodd-like to ask the Chairman of the Waterloo Bridge Committee when they were likely to have the improvements finished and when the present dreadful state of things was going to come to an end,and the the people an the vicinity would have some satisfac- tion. The Board was made an object of ridicule in letters to the newspapers and it was time that something was done not only with regard to Waterloo Bridge but to the roads generally. Mr. Speakman also complained of the roads, parapets, and crossings of the town. They were in a dreadful condition and might be kept more clean.—Mr. Pritchard said two months ago he endeav- oured to come to an arrangement with the Surveyor, by which the road and footpaths of the Bridge might be put in good condition for the winter. With what success that had been achieved the Surveyor would state. With regard to the completion of the work, that' entirely depended upon some satisfactory arrangement being made with' Messrs. Greenall, Whitley and Co., with regard to setting back Waterloo Hotel. Why that arrangement was not in a more forward state the Law Clerk would be able to speak. With regard to the streets aud crossings, he had not during the wholeof the time he had sat on the Board, received so many complaints of the condition of the streets and thoroughfares as he had during the past three months.—Mr. Taylor as chairman of the Highway and Buildings Committee, said the pre- sent crossings had been there for years and had not been altered. He hoped Mr. Barker would take notice of the remarks made and have the crossings swept.—The Surveyor said he had a special man on crossing sweep- ing. As to Waterloo Bridge he was doing that periodi- cally in a temporary manner. He was having something done at it each week.—The Law Clerk said the negotiations with Greenalls as to Waterloo Hotel had no% yet come to a termination.—The Chairman said the subject would be dealt with by the Committee.

The Alersev Docks and Flarbour Board have resolved to maintain a lifeboat at Formby in place of that with- drawn some time ago. After the recent gales public at- tention was drawn to the want which the present action of the Dock Board will supply. The ship Lord Beaconsfield, from Grangemouth for I.4nclon with pig-iron, and now long overdue, is believed to have gone down with all hands in the recent gales. The barque Bertha Assmann, of Hartlepool, is supposed ,to have foundered during the great gale of the 11th ult. She sailed from Hartlepool for Portsmouth on the 13th ult., and had a crew of eleven all told.

div.head: RUNCORN VOLUNTEER CORPS.
div.p: RUNCORN VOLUNTEER CORPS.
PRIZE DISTRIBUTION.

The annual concert and distribution of prizes in connection with the Runcorn corps of the 2nd Earl of Chester's V.B. Regiment was held in Runcorn Public Hall, on Monday evening. There was a large audience, amongst those present being Sir Richard and Lady Brooke, Colonel AstVn, Captain Ashton, Rev. Dr. Preston, Quartermaster-Sergt. Hankinson. The proceedings opened with a selection by the Volunteer band, entitled" La Gazza Ladra," which was admirably performed. Mr. H. Pilgrim sang " Marguerita,' in a pleasing manner, and Misses Simkin and Heatherington rendered the duet "Over the hawthorn hedge," in a manner that earned them the hearty plaudits of the company. "The bugler," was next contributed by Mr. J. Nickson, who sang with much power, and Miss Ward ably sang "Sissie.' For the quartette "On the banks of Allan Water," Misses Jones and Birkett and Messrs. R. Morris an J. Birkett received a deserved encore,and responded with "All among the barley." Later they gave the charming madrigal" Brightly dawns our wedding day 'S (Mikado), with much effect. Miss Joynson was ap- plauded for her song " Nothing else to do." as was also Mr. R. Morris for a capital reading of "Trial by jury." Sergeant James Woods, bandmaster, performed a cornet solo in his customary skilful and tuneful style. Other items were "Trusty as steel," by Mr. Fred Wilkinson, duet" Sol fa," Miss Simkin and Mr. R. Morris ; song "In old Madrid," Mr. A. Kennion (Widnes.) Mr. A. G. Davies carried out the humourons part of the programme admirably, and his efforts were much appreciated. The accompaniments during the evening were played by Mrs. W. B. Bay, Messrs. W. H. Woodward (Roby), Clifford Le Couteur, and R. Musgrove. During an interval in the programme Col. Ashton introduced Lady Brooke to dis- tribute the prizes, and gave her a hearty welcome. Her kindness and interest in them was evidenced by her pre- sence that night, and by the fact that she had presented them with a challenge cup which had been won .by Sergeant Harvey. (Applause.) Lady _Brooke thee handed the lucky competitors their prizes, and Colonel Ashton proposed a cordial vote of thanks to her ladyship. He referred to the long connec- tion of the Brooke family with the detachment, and he hoped they would long take an interest in it. (Applause.) He was sorry their strength was below what it was three or four years ago, but he hoped that cext year they would get a goodly number of recruits to fill up the ranks. Perhaps it would be an inducement to some to know that instead of going into brigade camp next pair they were going into regimental camp, and for the first time they were going across the water, to the Isle of Man, so that although they were enrolled for the defence of England, they had the privilege of going out of the country for the purpose of drill. He hoped that would induce a good many to join, and thus obtain both train- ing and pleasure whilst in camp. The Rev. Dr. Preston seconded the motion, and said they were deeply indebted to Lady Brook for the interest She:took in philanthropic, patriotic, and religious matters. (Applause.) The motion was tarried with acclamation. Sir Richard Brooke responded, expressing the pleasure he and Lady Brooke had derived, in being present, and in seeing the efficient state in which the volunteers were at the pre- sent time. lie hoped the efficiency of the regiment would be maintained, for it always had his and Lady Brcoke's best wishes. Captain Ashton then proposed a Vote of thanks to the donors. With regard to the encempment it had been suggested, but had not yet been brought before Colonel Ashton, that every man who put in ten drills should have a day's leave whilst in the Isle of Man. Dr. Preston seconded the motion, which was carried unanimously. The following is a list of the prize winners :

div.head: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of the Prescot Board of Guar dians was held at Whiston Workhouse, on Thursday afterhoon, Mr. James Burchall presiding. There were. also present Rev. S. A. K. Sylvester; 'Messrs. Tyror, Ranson, Middlehurst, Marsh, Wareing, Hallas, J. Whal- ley, Peover, Davies, Mercer, J. Birchall, Kenwright, Gravee, Dame, Lowe, P. Longton, and A. F. Mann (clerk). THE RECENT FIRE AT A PRESCOTCHAPEL.—The minutes of the Visiting Committee stated that it had been re- ported to them that the Union Fire Brigade was called to a fire at the Methodist Chapel, Prescot, but owing to the hydrants not fitting the stand pipes they were unable to render any assistance. The Committee decided that the Local Board should be informed that until the hydrants and the stand pipes had been assimilated the fire brigade would not be available for the Local board's district.— The minutes were passed. TEA AND MARGARINE.—Tne Visiting COnntlittenreCOnl- niended that tenders be invited for margarine instead of butter for the use of the iumates, and that the quantity of tea allowed to make ten pints of tea be increased from loz. to 2oz. On the suggestion of Mr. Middlehurst the recommepdation with regard to the tea was referred back for reconsideration and that in reference to the margarine was adopted. In answer to Mr. Marsh the Clerk stated that the supply of margarine during the last six months had been very satisfactory.—Mr. Marsh con- sidered the adoption olf good margarine instead of cheap butter was a step in the right direction. The inmates liked it better, and there waS a considerable saving to the union.—Mr. Middlehurst said that during the last twelve months £ll4 had been saved by the adoption of margarine as a trial. - - .
RELIEF.—The Workhouse Master reported that there were 590 inmates this week,and 500 last week. Outdoor
relief had been granted to 2,917 persOns at a cost of £247 15s. 10d., against 2,913 persons at a cost of £209 Us. id. last week.
A RESIGNATION.:--MISS B. Priestley wrote resigning her position as nurse in No. 2 division of the Workhouse, which was accepted.

- - THE UNION FINANCES.—The Clerk submitted a state- ment of the claims for repayments to the Union under the Local Government Act, 1888, by the Lancashire County Council and the St. Helens County-Borough Council during the year ending 31st March, 1892. The total was £6,577 18s., £3,941 12s. Bd. being due from the County Council and £2,636 ss. 4d. from the St Helens Council. On the Rural Sanitary Authority Account £l2O was due from the County Council. CHRISTMAS FESTIVITIES.—On the proposition of Mr. Daine, seconded by Mr. Middlehurst, it was decided to give the inmates their annual treat on Christmas Day. This was the principal business.
