div.head: WIDNES GENTLEMEN CHARGED WITH
div.p: WIDNES GENTLEMEN CHARGED WITH
POACHING.

At Widnes Petty Sessions on Thursday, before Mr. T. S. Timmis, and Mr. J. Birchall, Robert Roth- erham, Sankey : G. E, Sayee, builder, Deacon-road, Widnes ; and Joseph Pownall, farmer, Bold, were summoned, the first named with trespassing in pursuit of game on the Bold Hall estate, and the two latter for aiding and abetting. Mr. Knowles prosecuted on behalf of 1%1 r. W. Jones, who has the shooting over the land, and Mr. T. Swift, barrister, instructed by Mr. W. T. Husband, defended.— Evidence having been given, Mr. Swift for the defence, said the defendants had not trespassed on Mr. Jones's land, but had kept to Mr. Pownall's land. Even i they had been on Mr. Jones's land, it was not for the purpose of securing game. He called Mr. Fraser and Mr. Haddock, who wire with the shooting party. The Chairman said the evi- dence was very conflicting, but they had the evidence of two respectable witnesses. The case would therefore be dismissed.

div.head: FRODSHAM.
div.p: FRODSHAM.
TRINITY MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT CLASS. —At the weekly meeting of this class, held on Friday, Mr. T. Fairhurst gave a descriptive lecture on Venice, illustrated by magic lantern views.

FREE CHURCH MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT CLASS.—OD Fri- day, Mr. Henry Lewis gave an essay, entitled Lessons on fruits," to the members of this class. The Rev. R. Trotter presided. UNION CHURCII.—The reading room at this church, which has been so generously provided by the managers for week evening gatherings,continues to be well patron- ized by those for whom it was intended. PLEASANT EVENINGS.—A miscellaneous entertainment was again given on Saturday evening, in the Sunday school, Chapel-lane, and comprised vocal and instrumen- tal music, recitations, and readings. Instead of holding these only fortnightly, it is the intention of tile Commit. tee to arrange for them to be held in future every Satur- day. ALLEGED CRUELTY TO A HORSE AT KINGSLEY.—At Oakrnere Petty Sessions, on Monday, John Spruce, of Bingsley,hucister,fwac summoned for ill-treating a horse by working it whilst in an unfit state, on the 29th of October; and Ann Littler was charged with causing the same to be ill-treated.—P.S. Doyle and Inspector Dowty, of the R.S.P.C.A. having given evidence, James Lancely, veterinary surgeon, said the animal was quite fit for work, and it was a most absurd case to bring before the magistrates.—The case was dismisged.

THE VOLUNTEER INN.—At Oakmere Petty Sessions, on Monday, an application was made for the temporary transfer of the license of the Volunteer Inn, Frodsham. from James Corker to Thomas Morris.—Superintendent Meredith said the late tenant, James Corker, left on the. sth of November. The applicant had taken the house and had resided there with his wife and family since the sth. The rouse had accordingly been open, although the police had ordered it to be closed. The house had no accommodation for man or beast, and was merely a drinking place.—The transfer of license was granted after some further evidence had been given. SUICIDE.—On Saturday forenoon a young man named James Eyes, in the employ of Mr. J. W. Rothwell, iron- monger, Church-st., Frodsham, hanged himself from a beam in the latter's stable. When discovered several hours later, by Mr. J. Frank Wright, Mr. Rothwell's nephew, life was quite extinct. The inquest was held by Mr. Churton, county coroner, at the Golden Lion Hotel, Frodsham; on Monday morning. Mrs. Clementina Eyes, said that her husband was subject to epileptic fits which made him very depressed at times. He had pre- viously threatened suicide, partly on account of his de- pressed mental condition, and also on account of domes-, tic differences with his mother who lived with him. The jury returned a verdict of "Suicide whilst temporarily insane." The deceased was 33 years of age, and leaves 'a widow and four children. CHURCH PARADE.—The officers and men of the I Com- pany of the 2nd Earl of Chester's Volunteer Battalion, Cheshire Regiment, under the command of Captain Harry Harrison, attended Divine service in the Parish Church, Frodsham, on Sunday afternoon, when the Bishop of • Chester preached, from the words " Every- man's work shall he made manifest:" He was very glad to speak to members of the Volunteer force, and he felt he mu,st thank OM r9r handing themselves together' for ii)e defence of their counteV. lie hoped they Would con- sider it as.a calling from God, and he trusted that others would give themselves in increased numbers to the cause. It was gratifying to know that there were such a ilarge body of men who gave up their time to train themselves for this great national work. The two bands of the company were in attendance also, and some portions accompanied the several hymns of praise in the church. There was a large congregation of -nen present.

div.head: MUSICAL SOCIETY'S CONCERT. "
div.p: MUSICAL SOCIETY'S CONCERT. "

The first 'concert for the present season of the Warrington Musical Society was held in the Public Hall, on Tuesday evening, when there was, as is customary at these gatherings, a large and fashion- able attendance. The programme was a most varied one, and it proved a most attractive one. The voca- lists who had been specially engaged Were Madame Adelaide Mullen (soprano), Miss Sarah Ferry (con- tralto), Mr. Gordon Fletcher (tenor), and Mr. Bantock Pierpoint (bass). The hon. organist was Mr. J. B. Caldwell, the hon. accompanist, Mr. Frank W. Reynolds, the conductor being Mr. Frank 11. Crossley. The chorus and orchestra, it may be stated, numbered 200 performers. Rossini's , "Stahat Mater" occupied the first portion of the evening, and was given, on the ' whole, with capital effect. The principal airs and choruses were admirably sung. It was evident that the band and chorus were responsive at every turn to the baton of the conductor, who is especially to be congratulated upon the results of his arduous labours. Mr. Pierpoint was notably successful with the recitative " Eia, Mater," which was unaccompanied, and too much praise cannot be given to the chorus for the precision and delicacy which they displayed. Mr. Gordon Fletcher's great success was in'. Cujus animam," Miss Perry was loudly applauded for her fine ren- dering of the " Cavatina,' and Madame Mullen sang the " Inflammatus," with fervour. Altogether it was evident that the Society had made, a distinct advance upon its previous efforts, and had achieved distinction with the " Stabat Mater." The second part opened with Men- delssohn's "Hear my prayer," Madame Mullen taking the solo somewhat nervously, but on the whole with feeling and effect, especially in her rendering of "Oh, for the wings of a dove." Mr. Gordon Fletcher made a "a palpable hit" in Pin- suti's song "The last watch," and being enthusias- tically encored he substituted "I will sing thee songs of Araby." The music for the part song "In a hammock," is by Mr. Crossley. It is a graceful composition and was well sung and well received, the composer being called upon to bow his ack- nowledgments. Miss Berry gave "The enchant- ress" in a powerful and artistic style. She has a beautiful voice of no small range and flexibi- lity, and promises to become a great singer. As an encore song she gave "Caller herring" to the great delight of the audience. "Moonlight" is a charming part song by Eaton Faning, and it was well presented. Mr. Pierpoint acquitted himself in grand style in the recitative and air, "Oh, ruddier than the cherry," and followed, on being vociferously recalled,- with Friar Tuck's song in "Ivanhoe," which brought down the house. The programme concluded with "Lord Ullin's daughter," interpreted by the chorus and orchestra in a manner that left little to be desired. The minor passages were especially good. Great praise is due to Mr. Reynolds, who throughout showed himself per- fect as an accompanist. The concert gave the, greatest satisfaction, and it is not too much to say' that it is the beat which has been given by the , Society.
On Thursday a woman named Matthewman was burned to death in a -fire at Cross Church-st., Hudders- field.

On Thursday Sir George Reid, president of the Royal Scottish Academy, and -Sir Francis Leighton had an audience of the Queen at Windsor. Letters have been received in Berlin .okom Emin Pasha's expedition, which show bhat he has been fPr a considerable time established on Albert Nyanza, that he has a large and well-armed force under his orders, and that hi the opinion of the writer of the letters, the posi- tion of the British in Uganda was very critical,.
TWO CHILDREN BURNED. TO DEATIL

• Lilly Fillingham, five years of age, daughter of Police-constable Pißingham, residing in flelsby-st., Sutton, died late on Friday night from the effects of burns received early in the day. The child was near the fire, and by some means her clothing got ignited. Before the flames were extiuzuished the girl was so badly burned about the body that she died as stated. At the time of the burning Mr. and Mrs. Fillingham were upstairs, and in hurrying to assist both fell downstairs and received injuries necessitating medi- cal attendance.—An inquest on the body of the deceased was held before Mr. Brighouse, coroner, on Monday, and the jury returned a verdict of "Accidental Death.' Samuel Kirkman, two years of age, son of Samuel Kirkman, bricksetter, of Burtonhead-road, Sutton, died on Saturday afternoon from burns received on Friday. The boy was left alone in the house for a few minutes, and was heard scaeaming. His clothes were found to be on fire, and he was burned about the jegs and body. Dr. Casey attended, but his services were of no avail. Mr. S. Brighouse, coroner, held an inquest on the body of the deceased at the Griffin Hotel, Peasley Cross, on Monday. A verdict of "Accidental Death" was returned.

div.head: PRESCOT.
div.p: PRESCOT.

CHURCH Or ENGLAND TEMPERANCE SOCIETY, PRESCOT BRANCH.—The third entertainment of the season in con- nection with the above branch, was held in the Hough- ton-st. schoolroom. An excellent programme of music was rendered. In the absence of Mr. Clarke Aspinall who was unable to attend, Mr Procter of Liverpool gave a very interesting address. There was a large attendance. A RAID ON DISTRICT FARMERS.—At the Prescot Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, John Huntington, farmer, Roby, was summoned for having unjust weights in his posses- sion. The case was proved by Inspector Kilpatrick, who stated that he found 15 light weights on the defen- dant's premises. A fine of 20s. and costs was imposed.— Ottiwell Ward, farmer, Whiston, was summoned for hav- ing five unjust weights on his premises. The defendant pleaded thatthe weights were not in use for trade purposes and that they were only left lying about the place. They were not used for weighing produce. The case was dis- missed.—Thos. Wigglesworth, a farmer at Tarbock, was fined 20s. and costs for having light weights in his pos- session.

PREscar HIGHWAY BOARD.—The monthly meeting of this authority was held on •Tuegday,Mr. H. R. WA. Willis, J.P., presiding. It was reported that a communication had been forwarded to the county authorities expressing the opinion of the board that it was desirable the Legis- lature should confer upon local authorities the power of compelling owners of houses and buildings abutting upon main roads and highways to make and keep-in repair footpaths of a sufficient width lacing their hold- ings. The receipt of the letter had been acknowledged, but nothing further had been beard. The Board decided to draw the attention ot Mr. Wood, the district county council representative, to the matter.—The question of the erection of finger-posts along the roads in the Board's district was discussed, and the surveyor was asked to report upon the subject at the next meeting. PRESCOT CATHOLIC TEMPERANCE SOCIETY.-011 Thurs- day evening the first anniversary of the newly formed society in Prescot promoted by the Rev. Father Jones, which now numbers no less than 260 members, was held lin the Yew Tree Schools. There was a crcwded attend- lance, the schoolroom being filled to its utmost limits. IThe society has only teen in existance for a period of 12 months, but its progress has been of a most pronounced character under the generalship of Father Jones. The two attractions of the evening were an address by Father Nugent, followed by a cantata entitled "Flowers of the Forest," which was rendered in a most creditable manner. The chair was occupied by Father Brindle and he was supported on the platform by Father Nugent and Father Jcnes, and among those prescnt were Mr., Mrs. and Miss Roskell, Mr. Mrs. and Miss Sanders, Miss Haydon, Miss Rogers, Reyes and others. Father Nugent's addresss on temperance wasan exceedingly able and effective one, and he was accorded a vote of thanks by acclamation. In the entertainment the children did their parts with their usual skill, which reflected great credit on Miss Scully and her assitstant teachers. Miss Arden was the accompanist.

div.head: APPLETON HUNT.
div.p: THE APPLETON HUNT.

Monday was the day fixed for the hunt. The day was very unfavourable, being very foggy during the early morning, but about 10-30 a.m., the sun cleared away the fog, and the ground, which was hard with frost, softened a little. The hunters had a good chase through the Dingle, where they killed a fox, to the Rose Wood, Daresbury Firs, and Newton Gorse, They saw four foxes, but only one was killed. In spite of the bad weather, there was a large number of huntsmen. Several ladies also joined in the chase. One gentleman was hurt, and had to be taken home in a gig, and another rider had his horse injured, but escaped himself. Foxes are more plentiful now than in former years, and 'should, therefore, make some good sport for the Cheshire bounds. TEMPERANCE MEETING AT LA.TCHFORD.

A. public temperance meeting in connection With the Latchford Good Templars was held in the Tem- perance Hall on Monday evening, Mr. Holloday, a Ship Canal missionary, being in the chair. Ad- lresses were given by Mr. Price, of Warrington; , and Mr. Luke Ellison. The remainder of the even- ing was then devoted to a programme of songs, &c. The first item was a comic song by Mr. David Elli- son, entitled "There goes Johnny." A recitation, "A starveling," was given by Miss Cooke, followed by" Children'sToices," by Miss Lucy Hough. Miss Jones then sang " The V acant Chair.' A recitation, "Brave Jack Chiddy," was read by Mr. J. Adams in very good style. A song was contributed by the audience, entitled " Love at home." "The Cuckoo Clock," a comic song, was tastefully rendered by Mr. B. Few. Another song was contributed by Mr. D. Ellison. The evening closed with the pronounc- ing of the Benediction. A collection was taken in aid of the Good Templar funds. ENTERTAINMENT AT STOCKTON HEATH. The members of St. Thomas's young men's class gave an interesting entertainment in the school- room, which was crowded. The first part consisted of a lime-light exhibition of local and other views, including the stories of the life boat and the signal box, the connective readings being well rendered by Mr. James. two connective songs, "The little Church round the corner" and " Childhood's Scenes." given by Mr. Timperley,were well rEceived, and an encore was demanded. The lantern was successfully manipulated by Messrs. Edward and Leonard Davies. The second part of the programme, consisting of songs, recitations, and instrumental music, was well sustained by the following :—Mr. J. Shaw, Mr. W. Hankey, Mr. E. Baldwin, Mr. Hughes, Mr. H. Hughes, and Mr. C. Smith. The performers are to be congratulated upon the man- ner in which they went through their respective parts. The entertainment was concluded by a humorous 'dialogue, entitled "The Bachelor's Wants," by Mr. E. Baldwin, Mr. F. Berry, Mr. F. Rathbane, and Mr. F. Langley, which was given in a very pleasing style, and was received with roars of laughter. The Rev. C. J. Rolf, after a few re- marks, proposed a vote of thanks to all who had taken part in the entertainment. This was seconded by Mr. A. Down, and carried. After paying all ex- penses, the members were enabled to hand over to the churchwardens the sum of four guineas towards relayilg the church walks. HEALTH AND WEATHER OF WARRINGTON. Forweek ending Saturday, 28th Nov., 1891, which was the 48th of the cuirent year, the following births and deaths were registered :—Birtbs : War- rington, 25; Latchford, 6; total 31. Deaths: War- rington. 23; Latchford, 4; total 27. The excess of births ovt,r deaths was 4. The death-rate from all causes was equal to 26.5 per 1,000 against 2769, the average of the previous fouitveeks, and agaiiist 15'6 the corresponding week of last year. The death rate from the seven chief zymotic diseases was equal to 7.8 per I,ooo,against 4.37,the average rate of the four previous weeks, alid against 2.08 the corresponding week of 1890. The ages of mortality, were- 0 to 1, 5 ; 1 to 5,8; 5 to 15,1 ; 15 to 25, 1; 25 to 60, 7; 60 upwards, 5; total 27. The deaths included-1 from diarrheea, I from enteric fever, 2 from measles, 1 from croup, 2 from diphtheria, 1 from whooping cough, 1 from acute rheuma- tism, 2 from phthisis, 9 from lung disease 3 from heart disease, 1 from brain disease. The following cases of infectious disease have been reported during the week :—Diphtheria 2 cases, scarlatina 4 cases, typhoid fever 1 case. Meteorology—The mean tem- perature was 35 Fah., and therefore 11 degs. colder than the preceding week. The maximum tempera- ture 46 F., was recorded on the 22nd ult., and the minim= temperature 22 F., on the 26th ult. The rainfall measured 48 inch. The general direction of the wind was N.E., the reading of the Anemometer denoting 730 miles.—JoHN H. GORNALL, Medical Officer of Health.

div.head: BEFORE THE MA.GISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MA.GISTRATES.

ANOTHER CELEBRANT OF THE New MAYOR'S ACCESSION. At the Borough Magistrates' Court, on Monday morn- ing, Robert Dakin was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Rose and Crown-st., on the 21st Of Novem- ber.—Alderman Francomb asked the defendant how it happened that he was a week late this time, remarking that he got drunk every year when the new mayor was elected, and came to see him at the Court. He only got drunk once a year.—Major Pickmere : So overjoyed.— Alderman Francomb : I should treat him as I have done for yesrs—let him off.—The defendant, who had no- thing to say for himself, was dismissed.

THEFT OF LEAD. Patrick Lynch. residing in Gee-st., Was charged at the Borough Police Court, on Tuesday, with stealing, some time between Thursday afternoon and Monday last, 33Ibs. of lead, the property of Messrsr Gibson and Sons, or receiving the same knowing it to have been stolen.— The Chief Constable said about half-past three o'clock on Monday afternoon, Detective-Sergeant Monaghan found the defendant with a quaatity of lead in his pos- session in Bewsey-st. The prisoner had the lead wrapped up, and he told Monaghan he was carrying tools, but on lead being discovered, he said his wife had picked it up in the country. He also said he was taking it to Gib- son's yard. It appeared that on the previous Thursday Messrs. Gibson and Sons, who were making some altera- tions at Lawless's fish skop, had carted away some lead piping, and the lead found on the prisoner was identified as this,—After evidence had been given in confirmation of thq Qhief Constable's statement, the prisoner was "teminitted for 14 days' hard labour._

ANOTHER THEFT OF BOOTS. At the Borough Police Court, on Mond ty,James Ennis, employed at Bewsey forge, was charged with stealing, on Saturday night, a pair of boots value 35. 11. d., from the shop of Stead Simpson and Nephews,9,Horsemarket- tr. He went into the shop with his wife and bought two pairs of boots for himself and her,and paid for them, but put another pair under his coat, without paying for these. A boy in the shop informed the manager, and information was given to the police, and the prisoner was apprehended by P.C. Corbett in Peter-st., with the boots under his coat. He was under the influence tof liquor.—The defendant said he picked them up thinking they were a pair he had bought.—The Constable having given evidence, Mr. Kent, the manager of the shop stated the facts, and said he was going away without paving for one of the pairs that he bought, when the asfistant reminded him. He was under the influence of liquor and might have taken the third pair in his con- fusion but did not seem so drunk as not to know what he was about. The defendant was fined 105. and costs, 30s. in all. A bUSPICIOUS CHARACTER AT A SALL At the Warrington Borough Police Court, on Wednes- day, William Lee,a stranger to Warrington,was charged with frequenting Knutsford-road, the previous afternoon, with intent to commit a felony.—Margaret Higham, wife of a tanner, residing at Latchford, said she attended a sale on Tuesday afternoon, at 143, Knutsford-road, when she saw the prisoner hanging about with a topcoat on his arm. She felt him pushing about her dress, and she ;pissed her purse containing a sovereign, two half-crowns, -and some halfpence. She saw the prisoner then in com- pany with another man. They walked very fast, and she followed them, and informed P.C. Woods, who caught the prisoner near the Norton Arms.—P.C. Woods said ' when the complainant informed him, she was so excited that she hardly knew what she was saying.—The prisoner told him he had come to the fair, and was going to Crewe. He had 10d. on him and a lot of papers as to horse racing and fairs, and railway rates.—Inspector Bowen deposed that he found on the man a watch, 10d. and a pair of spectacles, and he said he came from Beverley.—The prisoner said when he saw the crowd at the sale, he thought it was a row instead of a sale. •He denied the charge.—Asked what he did for aliving, he said "Some- times I do a bit backing a few horses."—He was com- mitted to prison for a month's hard labour. CHARGE OF STEALING A NEIGHBOUR'S CARPET. Elizabeth Allen, wife of Joseph Allen, forgeman, of 27, Gladstone-street, was charged with stealing on the 28th November, a tapestry carpet the property of James Rimrner, 21, Walker-street. Mr. P Davies defended. Mrs. Rimmer said that about 8.30 on the date mentioned she put the carpet in the back yard for her husband to shake, and on their coming there about 9 o'clock, she found it had disappeared. She had put the blind up that she might watch the carpet, as she had missed so many things. She was much surprised that the defend- and whom she had long known to be a respectable woman should have done this.—P.S. Monaghan said he and Inspector Spinks,about 3 o'clock on Sunday morning, found the carpet in the prisoner's house rolled up and placed in a corner. The Inspector shortly after brought her to the house and she stated that she had found the carpet in Gladstone-street, just opposite to Winstanley's shop on the other side, and had been to the shop to see whether it was his, but afterwards said that was not true.—Mr. P. Davies submitted that the evidence did not prove the case, she had tumbled over the carpet in the street, and took the carpet into her own house. She had never been in the court before and both she and her husband were respectable people. She would never dream of taking anything from such a friend as Mrs. Rimmer had been to her. She had been sufficiently punished in being locked up all Sunday, instead of being summoned as she might have been.—The Mayor said the prisoner would have the benefit of the doubt and be dismissed.

WARRINGTONIANS AND THEIR COUNTRY SPORTS. John Rabbit and John Cunningham were charged with causing an obstruction of Sandy-lane, Orford, on the 21st ult., by foot racing. James Whitfield was charged with obstructing it on the same occasion by standing thereon, and also with firing a pistol off in the lane. John Burns was charged with obstructing the lane on the same date by allowing a horse and cab to stand an un- reasonable time.—Thomas Drinkwater and Robert Grace were charged with obstructing it,the former with a waggonette and the latter with a cab. Mr. Browne appeared for the prosecution.—P.C. Pope gave evidence in support of the charges. Rabbit and Cunningham, he said, were running a race in the road,having nothing on but their shoes and a covering about their loins. There* were about 3000 people in the road and the lane was blocked for about a quarter of a mile. It was about three o'clock in the afternoon. He told the men they must not run the race. All the defendants came from W arrington.—Mr. Browne submitted that the cabmen must be dismissed, as they were bound to wait for their return fare. Burns, he asserted, did not fire the pistol wantonly and to the danger of passengers or the injury of the highway, because he fired carefully and to start the race, and used ' only poiyder. The men who ran the race did not advertise it and did ' not run it for the purpose of causing the crowd. Mere i running on the highway was not illegal. The whole lane would not hold 2,000 or 3,000 people. The people would only stand a few moments till the race was over. No passenger came either way, therefore there was no obstruction. There was no recreation ground in Warring- ton for such men to go to.—Major Pickmere : I am very sorry we haven't.—J. Carey, Winwick-st.' Warrington, gave evidence confirming Mr. Browne's statement as to the circumstances. The bystanders he said stood in the gutter.—Thos. Wrench, 43, Oliver-st.' Warrington, gave similar evidence. The cases against the cabmen were dismissed. The other defendants were fined the costs, Whitfield having in addition to pay is.

div.head: THEFfOF A LOAF.
div.p: THEFfOF A LOAF.

-At the borough p9lice- court, yesterday, William Holliwell, a little boy, aged 10, son of a widow named Elizabeth Holliwell, Litton's-road, with stealing, the previous night, from the shop of John Barnes. Butter- market-street, a loaf of bread. He was discharged on account of his youth, on his mother promising to look after him:in future.

GOING A FAIRING AND FARING BADLY. At the Warrington Magistrates' Court,on Thursday, be- fore Alderman Sutton (chairman), and Councillor James Fairclough, Thomas Brown, who described himself as a ' mechanic on board a ship and a native of Liverpool. was charged, that he being a suspicious character was found frequenting the fair ground with intent to commit a felony about eight o'clook the previous night.—The pri- son : I plead guilty to being drunk,but nothing else. —Francis Percival deposed to seeing the prisoner put his hand in a woman's pocket. He said to him" Take your hand out of the woman's pocket." He took his hand out and went away without taking notice. He saw him with his hand in several other women's pockets. He asked two of the women if they had missed any- thing., but they had not.—Patrick Dooley and Thomas Noon corroborated. Inspector Bowen deposed to apprehending the prisoner in the fair ground and to his pretending to be drunk. They found on him 6s. 6d. in silver and 6d. in copper. He spat in Inspector Spinks's face at the police station. He had had drink, but wasn't drunk.—P.C. 7 said he saw the prisoner come out of the boxing show, and sound the pockets of some young women.—lnspector Spinks produced an imitation of a bank note, a tradesman's advertisment, found by him upon the prisoner.—The prisoner denied that his name was Hughes; that was his wife's naine.—His wife was called and said his name was Hughes, and they came from Liverpool.—The prisoner said he had been in the habit of going under the name of Thomas Hughes, but his proper name was Thomas Brown.—The prisoner's wife said she had been insulted by Inspector Spinks, which he denied.—The prisoner was sentenced to a month's hard labour in jail.—Mr. Hunt said the magis- trates had power to apply the 7s. found on him towards his conveyance to orison.—The magistrates decided to do this.—The Prisoner: You can't do that; I shall ap- peal against that.—Mr. Hunt: It is only by decisions such as these that we keep Warrington free of these char- acters. We used to have from 20 to 30 during the fair week. Now we have hardly half-a-dozen. s THREE RUFFIANS ASSAIL TRH POLICE.

At the Borough Police Court, on Monday morning, Patrick and Owen Woods were charged with being drunk and disorderly in Dolman's-lane, about eleven o'clock on Saturday night, and assaulting P.S. Jones and P.C. Hollinworth, and Patrick Kilduff was charged with assaulting P.C.'s Hollinworth and Wood on the same occasion.—P.S. Jones deposed that he found the prisoners Woods drunk and fighting with a man named Ward. in Dolman's-lane. Witness got hold of Ward, who was bleeding, but let him go, finding he was not to blame. Then he laid hold of Patrick Woods, who struck him, and Owen Woods then came and struck him also, and P.C. Hollinworth took them into custody, and at the corner of Union-st. Kilduff came up and tried to rescue them. The prisoner Owen tripped witness and Hollinworth, and brought them to the ground, and while they were down Hollinworth's " snaps,""which he had put lion Owen Woods broke, and he got away. Patrick Woods struck witness again and knocked him to the ground,but be stuck to him, and blew his whistle, and Inspector Bowen came to his assistance. At the Station Owen Woods would not be searched, and struck Hollinworth, knocking him into the fireplace. 11 —P.C. Hollinworth corroborated. He said when he got hold of Kilduff by the coat he wrenched himself out of it and got into a house. He made a bolt at P.C. Wood and knocked his hat off. The man ran into a house, but P.C. Woods ran after him and managed to get him out. He was very 'violent all the way to the stotion, and when he reached the station, struck him in the Wiest, and knocked him in the fire.— P.C. Woods gave corroborative evidence.—Two young women were called for the defence who denied that Kil- duff struck the police, and glijd the other prisoners only struck Ward in self-defence. cine of the women, Bose M'Allister, Kilduff's sister-in-law said P.C. Woods hit her on the eye and Hollinworth used her mother something scandalous. They were not taking the prisoner.s away quietly but ill-using them. The constab!gs dented these accusations. P.S. Jones said when Kilduff ran into the house he fell over some gentlemen and knocked some crockery over, and the two young women came out and made a bother and P.C. Woods just shoved M'Allister by the shoulder. Her mother was never touched, and never complained that she had been, and if they had minded their own business matters Would not have been so bad. There were over,loo people about, and the police had to fight their way through them, and, if they had not stuck to the prisoners, would have been seriously assaulted. The prisoners were sextenced to pay Z 1 and costs (21 6s. 6d.) each, or go to jail for 14 daYs' hard labour.

div.head: MINOR CASES.
div.p: MINOR CASES.

WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. SATURDAY.—Before Alderman Burgess (in the chair), Messrs. L. Veasey, R. Garnett, and J. Geddes. DESERTION.—George Slack was again brought. up on remand charged with being a deserter from H. M. S. Canada, on the 4th July, 1890.—Constable Berry gave evidence to the effect that he apprehended the prisoner. Slack, however, denied this, and said that- he surren- dered.—Prisoner was remanded to await an escort. WIFE ASSAULT.—John Maddock was charged with un- lawfully assaulting and beating his wife, Jane Maddock, on the 25th November.—Mrs. Maddock said that her husband came home on Wednesday night, and told her that she was drunk. He went to bed and woke about two o'clock in the morning, when he seized hold of her by her hair and commenced to thump her on her head and face. She often had to leave the house all the hours of the night and sleep in a neighbour's house or in an out- house.—Alderman Burgess said that prisoner had been before the Court on a variety of charges since 1872, some of them very serious ones. He was sent to gaol for cne with. The wife was allowed a separation order, and prisoner was ordered to pay kls. 9, week towards her maintenance. FINED FOR BEING DEttlglt AND DISORDERLY.—John Connor. Tuarr.—John Heaton was charged with stealing sd. in copper, and a pipe from Henry Fox, at twenty minutes to twelve o'clock, on Friday night. It appears that the two met in Horsemarket-st., and Heaton said he had 2d., and asked Fox how much he had. Fox replied that he had 5d., which prisoner obtained from hies on the pretence of obtaining lodgings for him with it. On reaching Friar's-green,Heaton ran away with the money, but was caught by a police constable.—As Fox did not appear to prosecute, the magistrates dismissed the case. MONDAY.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Greenall), Alder- men Harrison and Francomb, and Major Pickmere. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—,•George Didsdale, drunk and disorderly in Wilderspool-road; on Saturday night, was fined ss. and costs.—Annie Eliza Scully, charged with a like offence in Horsemarket-St., on Sunday night, was dismissed.—Mary Travis, on Town Hill. on Nov. 22nd, ss. and costs. A FIRED CRIAINEY.—Thos. Smith, for having his chim- ney on fire on Nov. 21st, was fined is. FORSAKING WIFE AND CHILDREN.—John McCarty, lately a sailor and now a Ship Canal labourer,was charged by Mr. B. Shearer, on behalf of the Board of Guardians with absconding from Warrington on the 19th of May, leaving his wife and children chargeable to the Union. —The defendant said he had sent his wife £4.—Mr. Shearer said the wife had not told him this.—The defen- dant only owed 53.6d.and costs. The mac,ristrates,having heard a further statement by the defendant, from which it appeared that he had done all he could in his circum- stances, and had been away at sea, the case was ad- journed for six weeks. TIIESDAV—Before the Mayor (Alderman Greenall) and Mr. R. Garnett.

SCHOOL CASES.—iiii, --foließvin-g-- were prosecuted by Mr. G. Riley, School Attendance Officer, for 'not sending children tcrschool :—Eliza Evans, John 'Mackie, whose son pleaded "toothache and bellyache," as his excuse for not attending, Joseph Thompson, bootmaker, and Wm. Ferney, 2s. 6d.—James Travis, labourer, ss.

WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. John Fairclough (chairman), and Alderman Wright. FIGHTING.—John Alalony was charged on a warrant with fighting in Dial-st., on the 31st of August, also with assaulting his sister. Mary Stuart, the same night. P.C. Amson and the prisoner's sister proved the charge. She said he had come to her father's house drunk and applied for lodgings, but they would not accommodate him, and put him out. He smashed 12 panes in the window and assaulted her, causing her to bleed pro- fusely. In answer to the prisoner she denied hitting him, but said her mother hit him because he was chok- ing her father.—The prisoner was sent to jail for one month's hard labour. DRUNK AND DisoanEnrx.—Alice Thomas, drunk and disorderly at 12.10 a.m. on Tuesday, in Battersby-lane, was fined 10s, and costs. FRlDAY.—Before Aldermen Harrison, (chairman), and Wright and Dr. Gornall. Diorrx AND DISORDERLY.—Henry Thompson, drunk and disorderly in Horsemarket-street, on Thursday night he having been pretending to have fits in the street, and exciting compassion in consequence, was dismissed. John Thompson, a cripple, in Horsemarket-st., the same night, dismissed. ARMY DESERTION.—Robert Burns, charged with • absenting himself, from the training for 1891, at Bury of the 20th regiment of Fusiliers, was remanded till Monday. MORE WOMEN'S QUARRELS.—ALLEGED WOUNDING WITH A KNIFE.—Mary Eden White, employed at Wilkinson's fustian cutting shop,and living at 120,Longford-st., was charged with assaulting Jane Cook, also employed at Wilkinson's, while engaged at her work on the Ist inst., and Jane Cook was charged, by cross-summons, with assaulting White on the same date. Mr. P. Davies ap- peared for White. It was alleged that Cook was vio- lently assaulted by White, and struck her with a knife wounding her in the head and necessitating her removal to the Infirmly, and that White taking advantage of Cook being there had taken out a summons before Cook could.—For the defence it was stated that Cook had

div.head: THE. FA MAN ER, SATURDAY, DECEMBER 5, 1891.
div.p: THE. FA MAN ER, SATURDAY, DECEMBER 5, 1891.

aggravated White by abusibg li6rit and her mother, and that Cook was accidentally wounded by the knife which White was grinding when the assault was committed. The first case was dismissed and in the second the de- fendant was bound over in the sum of £5 to keep the peace for six months and mulcted in costs.

WARRINGTON COUNTY SESSIONS. WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. Peter Stubs and Major Pickmere. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—John Knockton, drunk and disorderly on the 22nd of November, at Southworth- with-Croft, who had to be carried home by four men, ss. and costs.—Wm. Knowles, at the same place, on the 16th of November, ss. and costs —James Stevenson, drunk and disorderly at Sankey Bridges, on the 14th of November, and John Conroy, disorderly on the same oc- casion, were fined ss, and Costs each. , ASLEEP ON HIS CART.—Thomas Jones, asleep on his cart, at Penketh ,on the 24th of November. He had been out all the previous night travelling with a furniture van.—He was ordered to pay the costs. TRESPASSING ON LAND.—John Green was charged with trespassing in pursuit of game, on the 19th of Novem- ber, on land in the occupation of James Warburton. Mr. White appeared for the prosecution, on behalf of the Hon. Mr. Powis, owner of the land. A gamekeeper de- posed that the defendant fired a gun on the land, and on being pursued threw it down. The defendant said he was shooting sparrows.—He was fined ss. and costs.
RUNCORicr PETTY SESSIONS.
Mol4l3AY.—Before Mr. Henry Reynolds and Mr. James

_ Hindley. DRUNEHNNESS.—The following were each fined for be- ng drunk and disorderly :—Wm. Malkin, John Edward Jones. Kate Carroll, John Moors, "James Harris,John Jas. Connell, Mary Ellen Doyle, and Thos. Murray. COAL DEALERS FlNED.—lsa,ac: Broadhurst, Railway Arches, Brindley-st., Henry Cawley, Vine-st., and Jos. Jones, Shaw-st., retail coal dealers, were each sum- moned by Mr. W. D. Laird, chief Inspector of Weights and Measures for the county, for not having registered their places of business as required by the bye-laws. As this was the first case, the Bench imoosed the small fine of Is. ,and costs, Bs. 6d. ,Broadhurst did not appear(being represented by theßev. C. Finch), and in his case the costs amounted to 10s. 6d. PROFANE LANGUAGE.—Ann Bufton was fined ss. and costs for using obscene and profane language in Copper- street. BEGGING.—Wm. McDonald pleaded guilty to begging at Sutton, on Sunday, and was sentenced to seven days' hard labour. AN UNLAWFUL PURPOSE.—Henry Cook, a young man, pleaded guilty to having on the morning of the 29th of November, at Runcorn, been found on premises in the occupation of Robert Bazlev, shoemaker, Egerton-st.— Alfred Rawlinson, of 11, Suffolk-st., chemical labourer, deposed to findinc, the prisoner secreted on the premises. 1 He was sentenced to seven days' hard labour.

div.head: MORE REVOLTS IN CHINA.
div.p: MORE REVOLTS IN CHINA.
300 CHRISTIANS MASSACRED,

PRIEM SIINDAT.—Two serious revolts have broken out on the northern side of the Great Wall of China. The origin of these risings is involved in obscurity. In one case a large insurgent band has occupied a small town to the north-east of Kinchow, and against these rebels the troops forming the garrison of Sha,nhai-kivan has been despatahed. The other rising, which has broken out in the district of Takou, due north of Kaiping, is much more serious. The local mandarins, after temparising, came to an arrangement with the insurgent leaders whereby the latter undertook to spare the inhabitants as a whole on condition that they should have free license to sack and pillage in respect of the Christians alone. As a consequence, the European missions and the houses of native Christians were handed over as a prey to the ferocity of the rebels. The most frightful atrocities were perpetrated on the unhappy people, who, after being subjected to every form of torture, were massacred to the number of 300. Of the Europeans and natives not a single soul is believed to have escaped. The Imperial Government is thoroughly alarmed at the state of affairs and Li Hung Chang is acting with great energy. He hag despatched several thousand imperial troops to the front to hold the chief points where the rebels might pass through the Great Wall. In order to si2cure greater expedition, the Viceroy has given orders to the Chinese commander to avail himself of the railway, by the use of which three days will be saved. Protestant missionaries bave abandoned Tsun Hoa, near the Great Wall, to the north-east of Pekin, the local authorities having , declared themselves unable to afford them any protec- tion. A " Daily Chronicle" telegram. dated Tientsin via Shanghai, November 28, says—Official depatches have reached here with full details of the massacre of Chris- tians at Takou. Previous advices gave but a faint idea of the atrocities practised. They are almost without parallel,even in China. The members of the little Belgian mission had, no opportunity of escaping. The slaughter commenced with the native converts. Many were put to death with fiendiah cruelty. Children of tender years were seized by the savages, hacked with knives, and then roasted in a huge fire. Worse still befel the nuns attached to the mission. They were subject to the I grossest indignities, and brutally outraged by the fiends, who afterwards brained them with massive clubs. The Belgian priests were crugy tortured, but met their fate with extreme resignation. In one case heart and tongue were torn from the body and burned by the savages in their murderous frenzy. The most astounding statement is that after the miscreants had been satiated with out- rage and slaughter they were feasted and feted by a lead- ing Chinese mandarin in the district. The foreign dip- lomatic body at Pekin are simply furious. The whole European colony is boiling over with indignation. The news from Mongolia is increasingly serious. The rebel forces are reported to be growing larger,and their forward march has continued so far uninterrup'edly. The Im- perial troops have not yet got into touch with the rebels. Further detachments of troops have been ordered for- ward. The rebels in their southward march have occupied towns without resistance. and requisitioned supplies from the inhabitants. It is reported that they have captured the large town of Leno-Yang.

div.head: "••••.1......i11i.• CHARGE OF WIFE ASSAULT.
div.p: "••••.1......i11i.• CHARGE OF WIFE ASSAULT.
ALTERCATION BETWEEN A SOLICITOR AND
aDiliiliit- HARRISON.

At the Warrington Borough Magistrates Court, yesterday, George Ball, of Winwick-st., was charged with assaulting on the 21st ult., at the King's Arms, Catherine Ball, his wife, from whom he is separated and to whom he allows 7s. per week.—The com- plainant having deposed to being knocked down by the defendant, Mr. Jenkins cross-examined her with a view to showing that the assault was due to her conduct with two navvies, when the Chairman (Alderman Harrison) remarked that this appeared to him quite irrelevant.—Mr. Jenkins said it showed the necessity of a change there when such a re- mark was made. His course of procedure was a perfectly sensible one for an advocate to pursue. The Chairman's interruption was a very serious one, endangering the issue head to lay before him. Re was entitled to show that this woman's behaviour justified the assault.—Alderman Harrison said Mr. Jenkins could not possibly justify in that way an assault upon any human being. The husband had another remedy.—Mr. Jenkins said it was with extreme regret and pain that he heard that proposition seriously advanced from a gentleman presiding on the bench. It was one of the most illogical he ever heard in his life. He never heard a proposition come from the bench so ill-advised, so inappropriately made.—Alderman Harri- son said he would not sit there to be insulted, and he would not allow Mr. Jenkins to go on in that way. Nothing could justify the man in committing such an assult, that was but common-sense.—Mr. Jenkins said if such was the Chairman's opinion it was useless for his client to come there. Alderman Harris on maintained that the line of cross-examination was a perfect waste of time.—Mr. Jenkins here proposed to the defend- ant that he (Mr. Jenkins) should withdraw from the case, remarking that when a gentleman sitting on the bench gave expression to such views it was impossible to get justice there. The complainant's cross-examination was, however, pro- ceeded with, and Mr. Jenkins remarked that the defend- ant was separated from his wife, and contributed 7s.per week for her maintenance, and observing her conduct with the navvies had crossed the street, and given her a gentle push, causing her to fall.—Alderman Harrison said that was a very different thing. She had sworn that he had knocked her down.—Mr. Jenkins: Will you lis- ten to the whole case? lam an advocate.—Alderman Harrison: lam very sorry to have an altercation.— Mr. Jenkins: I won't altercate. I have no altercation. As an advocate I am conducting my case to the of my ability, and in my own way, and won't be coerced by you or any other man.—Alderman Harri- son (warmly) : I won't coerce you, and don't want to do so, but I repeat that this man is not justified in com- mitting an assault on his wife. He is charged with as- saulting her, and to that you have to confine yourself. If you go on like this,we shall be here all day.—Mr.Jenkins : Have you finished now P—The Chairman : I have finished at present.—Mr. Jenkins then proceeded with his case, and several witnesses,including two constables, having proved the complainant's objectionable conduct with the navvies, the Bench dismissed the case.

div.p: RUGBY.

ST. HELENS A v. FRODSHAM.—This match was played at St. Helens on Saturday. Thc Saints ran out the win- ners by two tries (four points) to Frodsham nil. RUNCORN RECREATION V. ST. ANNE'S PARISH CHURCH. —Played at Runcorn, on Saturday. A high wind pre- vailed, but both sides played a good game. St Anne's scored their try in the first half, while the Recreation scored in the second, the kick at goal failing in each case. Final result.—Runcorn Recreation 1 try, 1 minor; St. Anne's 1 try. _ . _

_ WIDNES V. RUNCORN "A " TEAMS .—This fixture was played at Widnes on Saturday. Mullinger kicked off for Widnes, the ball going to touch in the visiters' 25. The advantage was soon lost and Runcorn became at once dangerous. Farmer, by a well-played kick into touch, prevented what appeared to be a sure try. Several scrimmages in front of the home goal only resulted in a dead ball. Further scrimmages in front of the goal re- sulted in a free kick for Runcorn, which was ineffectual. Runcorn again pressed, but relief was obtained for the homesters, by a free kick, and play was for some time in midfield. Runcorn playing with the wind in their favour, now gained • a lot of ground from a free kick, and a lot of scrimmages took place in front of the Wid- nes goal, but Runcorn was unable to get over, and was driven back. Final result—Widnes" A " nil. ; Runcorn "A" nil.

LEIGH v. WIDNES. Played at Leigh on Saturday before a fair attendance. Leigh were po,irly represented, Coop being away playing for Lancashire, and Smith, Bent, Winstanley, and Shovelton. Widnes were without Plumpton,Peters, and Holmes. A strong side wind blew across the field. Widnes kicked off, and after M. Masters had returned, the Leigh forwards made a rush,and Evans scored a try, which he also converted. Splendid passing by Leigh was neutralized by the good tackling of Widnes. After a fine dribble by Ewan, Anderton got a try, but no goal resulted. the Widnes forwards played up finely, but could not penetrate the Leigh defence, and then Anderton broke away, and passed all except the full back, who tackled him by the ankle. Half time score : —Leigh, 1 goal. 1 try ; Widnes, nil. Final result—Leigh, 1 goal, 2 tries, 2 minors; Widnes, 2 tries.

RUNCORN v. MOSELEY. This Midland team paid their first visit to Runcorn this season, but were weakly represented, while Run- corn were without Crompton, Abrams, Faulkner, and others. May, of the "A " team, was called up for Crompton's place. Rogers started for the visitors, and May returned. Play at once became very fast, but neither side had any advantage. After some even play in midfield, Runcorn broke away and pressed the visitors, and after some scrambling play, the ball was carried over the line, and one of the visitors failing to save. 0. Hughes scored for Runcorn. but the kick at goal failed. Frona the kick-off Runcorn again pressed, and some very exciting play followed on the line. Here Palethorpe got possession, and, evading his opponents, got clear, and scored after running three-quarters of the field. Rogers took the place kick, whith failed. On re-starting, Run- corn dribbled to the visitors' line, where more scrambling play followed. S. Robinsou eventually scoring for Run- corn. H. May kicked a splendid goal. At half-time the score was—Runcorn, one goal and one try; Moseley,one try. On changing ends Riley started the ball, and Shaw put in a good dribble, which gained considerable ground. Several exciting scrimmages followed on the line, and when the pack broke up, May kicked over the line. For obstruction by Yates, Pendlebury was awarded a try, but the kick at goal failed. The remainder cf the play was very even, and the game ended in a win for Runcorn by one goal and two tries, to Moseley one try.

WARRINGTON V. BARROW. For the first time since the above clubs have arranged fixtures, Barrow on Saturday claimed a victory over Warrington in their annual engagement at Wilderspool. This was brought about by an exceptionally weak team doing duty for the locals, for when it is taken into con- sideration that the losers were minus the services of such players as James and John Bate, Fair Turner, W, Nevins and Webster, it will be agreed that the team did very well to make such a capital fight as the result proves— Barrow, a dropped goal and a try, to Warrington a try. Barrow were fresh from a victory over Oldham, a,ud had a capital fifteen. The wes,ther was anything but agree- able, and the" gate "suffered to a considerable extent. Barrow kicked off, and the Warrington goal was almost secured in the first minute, Boscow having his kick charged, and the leather was rushed, but Evans was handy, and the oval was sent dead. This early attack roused Warrington for, on the drop-out, Thornley, Jolley, Berry, and Ashton wereprominent in a forward display, and the Barrow 25 was reached, Bowker effect- ing a save. Judicious kicking on the part of Evans and Heesom maintained the pressure, and an apparent over- anxiety of Warrington afforded the necessary relief. A.ntrobus cleared his lines well, and when almost free from opposition threw across to Potts, the latter tactic being defective. It was Barrow's turn to give an ex- hibition, and a pretty display between Haney, Chapman, Boaden, and Dickenson, found Boscow defending. Bow- ker eventually got away, and punting past Boscow, the latter was lacking in speed, and T. Dickenson scored a well deserved try. Although the task was easy, the place failed. Barrow were again on the aggressive soon after the re-start, but this time their efforts were nulli- fied by Potts tackling well, and Lawless being conspi- cuous with a short run and kick. Barnes, Molyneux, Donohue, and Hampson dribbled down at a fast rate, but again their failing in being too anxious proved fatal to the chance, and the effort had a futile ending. Evans kicked exceedingly well, and a permanent attack was set up by Warrington. Airley was faulty on several occasions, but he received valuable assistance from his three-quarters, and Bowker kicking finely took play near the half way. A glaring breach of the rules by Haney saw Ashton having a shot at goal, and although the kick was a good one, the shot went wide of its mark. Bowker ran the oval out, but play was generally confined to the visitors' quarters. Another penalty kick fell to Warrington for wilful obstruction, and although the Icick was in a more favourable position Barrow charged it down, but the outcome of it all was Barnes and Holmes, leading up Warrington to the line, and a minor was notched. This point did not satisfy the homesters, for the drop-out saw them putting their best energies foremost, and Ashton, Holmes, and Dono- hue each obliged with short dribbles. Dickenson and Haney, effected a short relief, but Boscow soon had them back on the defence Heesom was applauded for a fine kick, which took play under the Barrow posts. Boscow was again called upon. and, needless to say, was not found wanting. Play hovered at neutral ground for a short period, but eventually Lawless and Antrobus passed splendidly across the scrimmage, and the move- ment being seconded by smart work by Jolley,Raddles, and Berry, Airley saved his side by kicking to Boscow, who again found touch near the half-way. Lawless tackled Chapman accurately, but the surprise of the day was in store the next minute. From some short passing the oval fell into the hands ot Thorniley, and this player, feigning to pass in his progress. foiled the efforts of the Barrovians, and Heesom at last taking his pass in true style, a clinking score was the result. Evans took the easy place, but failed to augment. Jolley showed up again on the drop out, and although Potts got clear he failed to pass Bowker, and half-time arrived with the scores equal, a try and a minor each. The light was becoming bad, and it was evident the latter portion of the game would be played in darkness. The re-start was opened by Ashton and Boscow responding to Dickenson's reply, the homesters having a look-in in the first minute. Chapman foiled his opposing half, and only the sure tackling of the home backs prevented the Warrington goal being lowered. Antrobus got clear from a scrimmage, and a run of thirty yards found Barrow on the defence again. Some grand fielding of the oval by Heesom and Evans, coupled with some fine kicking, were loudly applauded. and the home centre was again cheered for a brilliant run from a pass,by Randles, having the ill-luck to knock on when but a couple of yards from the posts. In like manner were Warrington pulled up several times, and by degrees the oval was worked out of danger, and eventually an excursion was paid to the Warrington goal, and T. Dickenson receiving possession, dropped a fine goal. Warrington never recovered themselves after this, and the play,which could not be properly discerned, owing to darkness, was apparently of a give-and-take nature, and when the whistle sounded " no side," Barrow retired victors of a pleasant game by a dropped goal and a try to a try—six points to four. Teams—Warrington : Boscow, back ; Evans, Heesom, and Potts, three-quarters; Antrobus and Lawless, half backs; Ashton, Jolley, Bandies, Berry, Donohue, Hamp- son, Thorniley, Barnes, and Molyneaux forwards. Barrow : Airley, back ; T. Bowker. T. Dickenson, and Boaden, three-quarters; Haney and Chapinan,half backs; Trewick, Weatherall, Leake, Greaves, Bleazard, Halsall, J. Bowker, E. Dickenson, and Parkinson, forwards. Referee, Mr. J. H. Smith, Widnes.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
FOOTBALL.

The battle of the Roses is over once more and York- shire have again had the proud satisfaction of beating their most powerful rivals. When we come to look into matters, however, Lancashire have no need to be ashamed, as in point of wins alone they have just as good a record as their neighbours, whilst in the total number of goals and tries they have a long pull. If points had always been counted according to the modern sys- tem, the balance of successes would have been largely in favour of last season's champions, who can look on the past with much satisfaction.

It was unfortunate that the elements were not favour- able to the game ea Saturday, as the light Lancashire forwards would undoubtedly have shown up better on a dry turf. As it was, although they were on the average a stone lighter than their bulky antagonists, they were every whit as good; they not only held their own in the pack, but were very smart in the open. A good deal has been said about the speed of the Yorkshire scrimmagers, but the visitors were quite their equals in this or any other department. Indeed the two teams were well watched in every way, and it was a piece of ill-luck that Lancashire should by a penalty kick merely lose their chance of again carrying off the championship. This proved a costly mistake on the part of Coop. Both the last two victories of Yorkshire were obtained by means of penalty goals, and as they have only scored one try in the last three years, they have not shown much of their boasted superiority ever their most dangerous opponents.

The saturated ground was against individual brilli- ance, as fast runs or dashing spurts were almost out of the question. Coop has been seen to better advantage. Occasionally he did some smart things, but now and again he did not get rid of the ball with his customary readiness. Marsh was quite at his best, particularly in defence, and M'Cutcheon could hardly have been im- proved upon. His tackling was often useful. Valentine was too well watched to be dangerous, Lockwood paying him special attention. Berry and Cross found them- selves opposed to two half-backs who knew how to play the game, Briggs being a decided success. Berry's passes were often spoiled by the agile Bradford player. Summersgill justified his selection as the centre three- quarter for Yorkshire, but Dyson performed very mode- rately. Goldthorpe was always reliable at full back. There was little to choose among the forwards, Paisley, Jowett, Nichol!, and Bedford shining on the one side, as did the two Wilsons, Pyke, Kent, and Bollough on the other. The arrangements for the match, we should say, were a distinct credit to the Huddersfield officials, every one of the twenty thousand spectators having a splen- did view of the game.

The. seven League games that were down for decision on Saturday were all contested un terribly heavy grounds, and form was upset in more instances than one. In six out of the seven the home team were victorious. The solitary exception was Sunderland, who won at Stoke by three goals to one. The goal-keeping of Rowley and the back play of Clare and Underwood were alike very fine, but the splendid Sunderland forwards were well-nigh irresistible. The Wearsiders are now strongly fancied for the championship, for which Aston Villa have the best record. The Midland cracks were at Everton dn Saturday, where they found the state of the ground all against them. They had no chance in the second half, when they lost five goals. The Bolton Wanderers, who have still the greatest number of wins, were completely routed at Deepdale. The visitors did all the pressing up to the interval, but they could not get a goal. Afterwards the North End were almost constantly on the aggressive, and ran out victors by four to none. The first game between the clubs was won by the Wanderers by three to none.

Blackburn Rovers were performing in' the " Black Country," and a sorry time they had of it. The Wolver- hampton Wanderers' field was a veritable quagmire, and the cup.-4olders could not shape at all. They were van- quishud by six to one. The Rovers' defence was very feeble aud uncertain, Arthur's goal-keeping being nothing like so steady as that of Rose at the other end. Accring- ton were completely overwhelmned at Nottingham. When the clubs met a week ago the" Reds" were successful, but now they had not a look in, and were beaten by no fewer than nine goals. Oswald reappeared for the win- ners, and made a wonderful difference. Burnley owed , their victory over West Bromwich Albion to a penalty I goal. The new-fangled punishment gives the goal-keeper no chance whatever. Darwen reversed the result of their fixture with Derby County. Defeat by seven to none they turned into a win of two to nothing. The Barley Bank encloN49 Wa.4 41 4 fearful state, and made football a farce.

The doings of the Alliance clubs were doubly interest- ing owing to the failure of Notts Forest at Sheffield, and the pronounced success of Newton Heath at Walsall. The Forest were beaten for the first time, and the Heathens have now practically as flattering a record. The excellent form of the Newton Heath team is very gratifying, and it is to be hoped they will keep it up. They have only lost one out of nine Alliance engagements and it now makes little difference to them whether they play at home or away. In the Lancashire League Blackpool have won five out of six fixtures, the other being drawn, and they have the excellent goal average of 22 to five.
A MELANCHOLY CASE.
SUICIDE OF A WIREDRAWER.

Another case of suicide has occurred in Warring- ton during the week. The individual whose life has thus been unhappily ended is Thomas Wigley, wire- drawer, who resided at 32, Catherine-st. The de- ceased was subject to fits, and last June, while in a fit, he sustained an accident to his right arm at the Whitecross Works, where he was employed, which necessitated his being confined to the Infirmary for some time, and unfortunately incapacitated him permanently for work. As a consequence, the de- ceased became very despondent, and on Saturday morning declined to partake of any breakfast, and at night, about ten o'clock, he came home under the influence of drink, and was in a quarrelsome humour, his wife, to avoid unpleasantness, having to leave the house. She did not return till seven o'clock on Sunday morning, when she found the house locked up. She came back again on Monday afternoon, and still finding the door locked, she had Use door opened by a man named Holleys. She was horrified to discover her husband lying on his bed with his head immersed in a pool of blood, and his throat cut, a large bread knife stained with blood lying beside him. A next door neighbour, named Mary Narroway. stated that on Sunday night she heard a sound as of gurgling proceeding from the deceased's bedroom. An inquest was held, by Mr. S. Brighouse, coroner, at the Three Pigeons Inn, Tanners-lane, on Tuesday afternoon. Elizabeth Wigley, the deceased's widow, said he had been subject to fits for 20 years. He had done no work for several months owing to the accident at Whitecross works. The deceased had been much troubled by being thrown out of work. He had recently paid a visit to Whitecross works is search of employment, but was un- successful. Witness referred to his conduct on Saturday and Sunday, and to the discovery of the suicide on Monday. She had heard him say "he wished he was out of the road as everyone frowned on him." The Coroner said it would be dangerous to have had a man like Wigley about the works' as he might have fallen into lithe machinery. Ann Elizabeth Wigley, a married daughter of the deceased, said she had been residing with her father and mother. The deceased had charge of her baby on Sunday and would not give it up to her. It was 12 months old. She became frightened, and when she asked for the child he "punched and kicked her." There were other little children in the house with the infant. She got possession of her child on Sunday afternoon.—Geo. Honeys, puddler,deposed to finding de- ceased in bed with his throat cut. He had used a large breadknife for the purpose. The deceased had been very strange in his manner of late. The jury returned a ver- dict that the deceased had committed, suicide while tem- porarily insane.

div.head: LIGHTING OF WILDERSPOOL.
div.p: THE LIGHTING OF WILDERSPOOL.

For some time now an agitation has been going on in Wilderspool and Stockton Heath for the pub- lic lighting of certain roads, and the following petition has been prepared and signed by many of the inhabitants for transmission to the Local Gov- ernment Board.—" To the Local Government Board. The township of Appleton in the county of Chester, forms part of the district of the Runcorn Union Rural Sanitary Authority. The township has a populat'on of persons of a total rateable value of £14,711 14s. id. The persons whose signatures are hereto appended are rated to the relief of the poor in the said township and the assessment of the hereditaiments belonging to them, amounts, at least to one tenth of the net rateable value of such township. Certain streets and roads therein are,in consequence of the want of lighting, dangerous and unsafe for the use of foot passengers, particularly Wilderspool Causeway and North wich-road, which are main thoroughfares,and the only means of com- munication between the county of Lancashire and the county of Chester for a very large district in the year 1890. The number of passengers, vehicles, and cattle using Wilderspool Causeway from the sth to the 13th May was counted, and it was ascertained that 10,469 pedestrians, 6,488 vehicles, and 350 cattle, used the said road. Since these particulars were taken the traffic of all kinds has materially increased. The lighting of the said roads in question will beof great benefit and convenience to the inhabitants of the district. We therefcre respectfully apply to your Board for an order declaring the provisions of the Public Health Act, 1875, with respect to the light- ing of streets, &c., put in force in the township of Appleton, and that the Runcorn Union Rural Sani- tary Authority may be invested with the necessary powers, rights, capacities, liabilities,and obligations, of an urban authority under that Act for the pur- poses aforesaid.

div.head: -INQIIIIZY OFFICERS
div.p: -INQIIIIZY OFFICERS

The Clerk read a letter from the Local Government Board with reference to the proposal of the Guardians to dispense with the services of the inquiry officers. The Board asked how the Guardians proposed to deal with cases in which applications might be made by parents who select schools for the attendance of their children at which a fee was charged. —The Relieving Officer (Mr. Ward) said no fees had been paid since September.—The subject was adjourned until next meeting. MR. H. G. LINAKER'S REMUNERATION._

Mr. H. C-1-.--Linaier, of Frodsham,wrote as follows : Referring to the previous correspondence respecting my remuneration for work done since the death of the late Clerk, I beg to say I have taken the opportunity of con- sulting a very eminent authority on Poor Law upon the matter in dispute,and he advises that my request to have paid to me such a sum as the late Clerk would have re- ceived had he been living and such further sum as may be agreed upon for services rendered in connection with the accounts and the audit is not at all unreasonable. It is extremely unpleasant to myself, and I am sure to many members of the Board, that my own,and I may add my family's, connection with the Union should terminate in a dispute of this kind, and in order to meet the evident wish of many Guarlians I respectfully ask you to pay me the sum of £3O by way of compromise. I think if you will consider this matter carefully you will come to the conclusion that I am not asking anything unfair raid I have no wish for us to part unpleasantly.—Mr. Hey- wood gave notice that at the next meeting he would move that £3O be paid to Mr. Linaker for past services. Mr. Heywood moved the adoption of the Finance Com- mittee minutes, recommending the payment of accounts amounting to £133. The balance in the treasurer's hands was £11,152 ss. 6d.

The Medical Officer reported a case of typhoid fever, and two cases of scarlet fever at Norley. He had issued the customary preventible orders.

_ SIIIP CANAL SEWERS. Mr. Lionel B. Wells, engineer, reported re Ship Canal, -tisttt he had visited the Twenty Step Bridge on the 20th inst. and found that work on the subway had been resumed, the North shaft having been built 25 feet and the South shaft 20 feet above the arch of the subway. He found the remainder of the sewers between Twenty Step Bridge and Runcorn, in the same condition as before

Tall POLLUTION OF KBCKWICK BROOK. Mr. W. R. Earp, of Preston Brook, wrote with refer- ence to some remarks made at the last meeting of the authority, relative to an Aston farmer carting °tannery refuse on to his farm for which some members would seem to blame him. It was every evident to any tanner that there was not a single member of the Board who knew anything at all about tanning, unless indeed Mr. Chanies Reynolds happened to join them,and Mr. Aaron's constantly harping of the sulphuretted hydrogen of which by the way he seemed to be very fond—(laughter) —seemed only to lead them astray. He thought,therefore that he would explain the nature of the refuse from tan- neries so as to justify farmers in using it, and especially the one alluded to, and also to enable the memners to form a more correct idea as to its pollutable matter. In the first place the actualta.nning was always done by an infusion of vegetable matter—in his case of bark, the acorn cup,and a berry known as mvrabolain. Atter this material had had all the goodness brewed out of it it was ehrown away as refuse and was either burnt or cartel away by farmers. They would see from this that such refuse consisted merely of spent vegetable matter such as decayed leaves would make. There was no chemical matter about it any more than there was about spent leaves. Knowing so much it must be evident that the Aston farmer .would be doing a good thing both for I himself and his landlord in taking the trouble to cart the matter on his farm, and he referred them to the good effects of such material on a farm of 40 acres at Mere. He hoped this information would throw a little more light on tannery refuse.—Mr. Heywood said this letter did not touch the point. Mr. Earp said nothing about the depillary process, which was entirely chemical in Mr. Earp's case.—Mr. Aaron suggested that the Clerk should ask Mr. Earp what chemicals he did use, as there was sulphuretted hydrogen in the brook. He had an idea what Mr. Earp used besides bark.—Mr. Wilkinson said the bark and the pit had nothilg to do with the matter at all. If the brook was polluted why did not they take proceedings.—Mr. Farrington, the nuisance inspector, was called in and asked if he had a copy of the analyst's report. He replied no and the dis- cussion was adjourned for its production at the next meeting

THE SEWERAGE OF STOCKTON HEATH. A letter was read from Mr. Clifford Smith, of Bridge- water Offices, Walkden, enclosing a memorial from the tenants of houses in the new road recently made by the Ship Canal Company and running froin St. Thomas's Church, Stockton Heath, to Chester-road, pointing out the necessity of a permanent sewer in the road. The absegice of this sewer was hindering the further erection of property in this locality. The present cesspools were objectionable and a danger to the health of the inhabit- ants.—The Inspector said this matter required immedi- ate attention, and a Committee consisting: of the Guar- dians of the township and a number of local gentlemen were appointed to deal with it. THE SEWERAGE OF TIELSBY. _ _

•./a4.• The Committeeppointed to consider the alleged in- sufficiency of the se\werage at Helsby reported that, they had made an inspection of the sewer outfall,&c., and the private drain to Mr. F. Thornley's premises was found the most offensive of those inspected,and the Committee would like to know by whose authority and permission it had been constructed. Several attempts had been made by previous committees to improve the sewer up- on Mr. Thornley's property, but that gentleman stoutly and'strongly 6bjected to anything being done,though the Committee were glad to understand that he had since withdrawn his objections. The • Committee were of opinion that the drainage of Helsby would compare favourably with other places situate within the same sanitary district in which extensive sewerage schemes had bean carried out, but at the same time they were unanimous in opinion that if the sewer in Mr.Thornley's property was diverted from its present course it would be a great improvement to the said property, but to do this Mr. Thornley would have to be consulted and arrangements made with the joint railway companies, and it was resolved that Inspector Farrington confer with these parties—Mr. G. C. Taylor added a postcript that he could not agree that the sanitary system of Helsby was satisfactory but experience in other parts of the Rural Sanitary Authority showed that it was no use doing anything with drains unless a water sapply for the parish was carried out at the same time to keep the drains clear and flushed.—The report was adopted.

WHY DOES A WOMAN LOOK OLD BEFORE HER HUSBAND?

Every _woman who has her own housework to do knows that washing-day is the chief cause of the careworn look, broken health, and premature old age, notice.able in so many of her sex. Many a woman has to bend over a steaming wash-tub full of soiled clothes—to boil all the forenoon, and rub all the afternoon—arid while still warm and perspiring from the hot, filthy steam, run out into the cold—bare- headed and bare-armed—to hang up the clothes on a freezing line. This is done, not once, but week after week, and the wonder is how any woman lives through it—many don't! The sudden change from the hot, perspiring labour and wet steaming room inside to the cold air outside produces the natural result: a cold,. followed quickly by pneumonia or diphtheria, or some kindred disease, ending in the death of the poor victim. Friends call it a dispensation of Providence. What the woman actually died of was poor soap, hard labour, and exposure.
