letters to the Vittor.
THE BISHOP OF CHESTER'S CHURCHMAN- SHIP.

• Sir,—lt appears that Bishop Jayne, of Chester,had an invitation this month from the Rev. J. C. Sowerbutts, of Stockport (Wesleyan), to preside over a missionary meeting of an undenominational character. His lord- ship in a most intolerant, un-Christlike letter declines to preside over a mixed assembly, on a public platform, on which would be found Churchmen and Nonconformists, met together with a single eye to advance the Redeemer's Kingdom. Such an act of uncharitableness bespeaks bigotry of the narrowest sort. Of course it may be ex- pected from men who teach "Apostolic succession," "The power ef conferring the Holy Ghost in confirma- tion," &c., but it is certainly not the teaching of Him who never placed one Apostle to be superior to another, but said "Call no man father (spiritual adviser) ye are all brethren." It passes comprehension how any clergy- man, even though a bishop, cam go within the chancel rails and say " Let your light so shine before men that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven," and yet decline to asstrible with other Christians. They were first called " Christians" at Antioch. Bishop Jayne in effect says Churchmen only can be saved. Article nineteen says something different, and it is in the true spirit of this rule we can find Bishops Ryle, Carpenter, Hill, and numerous others are only too pleased to co-operate with others to further a good cause. Tomline, Bishop of Lincoln in article 23. says : " But though, I flatter myself that I have proved Episcopacy to be an Apostolic institution, yet I readily acknowledge that there is no precept in the New Testament which commands that every church should be governed by. bishops." Archbishop Tennison said—" He thought the narrow notions of churches had been their ruin, and that he believed the Church of Scotland to be as true a Protestant Church as the Church of England, though he could not say it was so perfect." Had this divine been living now he might have added—" See what the Free Church of Scotland is doing for her clergy; not one of them with less salary than two hundred rounds a year, with residence in most, if not in WI parishes; each con- gregation the power of selecting their pastor." • After the revocation of the Edict of Nantes a crowd of • Hugnenots poured into this country. A French Church with its own form of worship and Presbyterian ministry was established in the Crypt of Canterbury Cathedral, where it continues to this day, and Archbishop Grindal was the superintendent of this Presbyterian Church. Archbishop Whitgift said—" No form of church govern- ment is by the Scriptures prescribed to or commanded the Church of God," and Dr. Cosin, his Chancellor said— "All churches have not the same form of discipline, neither is it necessary that they should, seeing it cannot be proved that any certain particular form of church government is commanded to us by the Word of God." Nympkas all had churches in their own house. Will any Ritualist point out to us whether a priest, bishop, or deacon officiated ? Where two or three are gathered together in the name and spirit of Christ there exists a true church.—Yours, &c.. ROBERT FOULKES. Frodsham, November 30th, 1891.
SCIENCE AND THE IMMORTALITY OF THE SOUL

Sir,—ln bidding a final adieu to my indomitable critic, , it May be as well to remind him that I am far from being insensible to the humorous side of the discussion. His pompous proclamation of the birth of a bantling, the linked concatenation of nature's laws ; his wild and reckless baptism of the offspring, pitiless in its relentless comparison to a " red herring trailed across the scent," thereby conflicting with every paternal emotion, and putting to rout nature's immutable laws of heredity, a result as marvellous as any miracle; his precipitate retreat into the mazes of metaphysics, notwithstanding his boasted insinuation of an education "higher than that of a conventicle ;" his remarkable and puzzling statement, on a former occasion, that he "liked the flavour of dignity, honesty, and earnestness" in an opponent's letter, his ebullitions of temper in which he hurls his thunderbolts of wrath with indiscriminate recklessness on to the heads of opponents : all these incidents afford unprecedented scope for fun, frolic, and merriment. Considering the importance of the theme, and the varied interests depending upon it, I prefer to turn to a crucial point in the discussion. There is a wide-spread sentiment that science mono- polizes the whole field of human knowledge. The existence of such an opinion is not wonderful, consider- ing the recent progress of science in every department. So extraordinary hasteen this progress, and so extensive are its triumphs, that it is no marvel if the scientist, elated with success, should seek to render science co- extensive with human knowledge ; and fling into the limbo of nonentity whatever subject should fail to com- ply with the methods of scientific investigation. Such a course, however, would prove an egregious error. If true, it would sweep from the domain of knowledge such subjects as God, the soul of man, &c. It would even strike out as superfluous the study of human nature as described in the works of Spenser's "Fairy Queen," Shakespeare, Milton, and others. These authors were not scientists ; nor had they opportunities of studying science. Nevertheless their works are immortal, and contain the most precious contributions our literature possesses. These are subjects of human knowledge accordingly outside the domain of physical science. These comprise the soul of man as a rational and responsible being, and also God ; and our knowledge of these is due to consciousness and reflection. Indeed, when science becomes speculative it is extraordinary to what extent it depends on metaphysical arguments. What is the atomtic theory so much vaunted in our day, but a meta- physical theory? No man has ever seen an atom, and, with our present powers, it may be truly be said no man shall ever see one. Nevertheless, this theory is a highly probable one. Science, moreover, proposes to regard the atom as indestructible, and therefore immortal, in ac- cordance with the great principle of the indestructibility of matter and energy. If so, why should it be regarded as absurd to maintain the immortality of the soul? Moreover, our knowledge of the soul is far more certain than our knowledge of the existence of an' immortal atom. The theory of the Ether too which fills all space, and which is regarded as the medium ef light-vibrations, &c., is purely metaphysical; it is entirely beyond the evidence of the senses : and for its establishment one has to fall back on reasoning or reflection. One of the strongest arguments for the existence of the soul as a distinct and independent agent arises from the establishment of the law of the conservation of energy. Accordinc, to this law one form of energy is capable of transmutation into another. Work can be transformed into heat, heat into electricity, &c. Now if the soul is material it must be capable of transformation into heat or electricity. Such an absurdity no one supposes, and actordingly the soul must be viewed as an agent dis- tinct from matter and energy. It.is self-poised, and acts from within. The soul of man therefore is a distinct and independent agent. In possessing conscience and freewill, man is responsible to his Creator and must ren- der to Him an account of his talents.—Yours, &c. GNOSTIC.

In the first place he treats the "soul" as though it I coUlirhe d dciâted 'frith' the ••-mi nd and tells us -the former is the gift of God and is that which distinguishes man from "the lower order of animals." Ilere,we have a. quite new mammalian classification. Herein I find my education to have been very defective, inaemuch as I have always regarded mail as being an animal and dis- tinguished from his congeners of the animal world by his higher structural—mental and physical—develop- ment. But new it appears that it is to be done by some intangible and unlocateable attribute! If this is to be a sample of "soul improvement" I think a course of "mental improvement" might be substituted with mani- fest advantage to the members of the association: if they could stand it. To see the need of this; mark what treatment this most important subject of evolu- tion gets at their hands. Had this been a question of law, of physic or some such branch of special siudy, the members of the association might, and probably would, have kit the need of the advice of some specialist in that study, and would have hesitated to express crude and offhand opinions upon a subject they had neither studied nor understood. But not so in a subject like that of evo- lution, requiring, as it does, an intimate 'knowledge of a vast number of facts in biology and palceontology, close reasoning and accurate generalization from these facts! On a subject of such complexity and involving much special study for its comprehension, these young Friars- green philosophers undertake to make pronouncement after half-an-hour's discussion and less study! It will be news to the world of science that "the theory of evo- lution fall to the groupd because it fails to provide us (the Y.M.C.A., I presume) with the missing link between instinct and reason " ! Now, not insisting upon the fact that there is no such missing link and never was, in- stinct being merely a species of lower inherited reason, how would this one "failure to provide" overturn and destroy the great array of facts and the" logical inferences from facts upon which the hypothesis of evolution is founded? How is this new test of the validity of evolution to be applied in the case of, fossil animals? I have not yet i come across a fossil instinct—a fossil reason, orany connecting link between them. 1 oan't say the same of fossil reasonings ; these are as plenty as blackberries. But what would Mr. J. Horton have? Surely he is not Quixotic enough to wish to resurrect the obsolete fable of special creation ? This has indeed fallen to the around, and that not through the failure of one fact alone, but, in consequence of the vast majority of physi- cal facts and phenomena being entirely adverse to such an explanationof how things came toi be as we see them. In one thing, however, I do admire the essayist. He is consistent. I have known people who profess a belief in systematic Christianity, at the same time avow entire concurrence in the central facts of evolution. In this at least Mr. J. Horton is more logical than they. He has what Herbert Spencer calls !‘ the inarticulate fear." of science as the destroyer of sacridotalism and religious formula's. He is quite logical in this. Certain it is that the ideas of evolution and any creed involving a belief in special creation cannot find rational lodgment in the same head at the same time. These two ideas are entirely and completely incompatible and are mutually destruc- tive. They cannot be entertained simultaneously with- out intellectual suicide. But this incompatibility is no argument against evolution for the substantialtruth of which we have abundant and ever-increasing evidence; but rather against the antagonistic theory, which is without either evidence or probability. And here I wish to be understood. The great mistake people make, is in thinking that true science and true religion are necessarily and naturally antagonistic. No greater mistake could be made. On the contrary Religion and Science are complementary; both being necessary factors in 'the complete man: Science always has been—is now—and I hope always will be destructive solely of the outside dry husks—the man-made externals of religion. Is there a living man bold enough to maintain that the religion ef to-day is not the better for having thus passed through the purifying fire of .scientifie criticism ? Finally there is one fact Which alone should have'pre:, vented the essayist from draWing lame couclusions from halting premises. It is this—At one, period of his pre- natal existence he—like the rest of mankind—had a well-developed tail—and in every other respect was indistinguishable from a puppy of like age. Take this and the occurence of the fossil reptile-bird--or feathered lizard—Archeoptrix, and let our friend give us a rational explanation of them in the light of specific creation. I firmly believe that all these artificial tremours for the truth would vanish as an ugly dream could these people but see the ability of the Groat First Cause to preserve His own truth. Want of faith is their disturbing element.—l am, &c., Penketh, November 29th, 1891.
JOHN PEERS.

- - - - - - Sir,—lt was with mixed feelings that I read in last issue the report of a discussion on a paper read by Mr. J. Horton on "Soul Improvement." Regret and amuse- ment were the two uppermost sentiments in my mind when reading this report. Take the regret first. I have been led to understand that the Y.M.C.A. is doing good work among the young men of Warrington by encou- raging the principles and practise of good citzenship. Well, sir, lam sorry to find the Y.M.C.A. leaving these well-beated tracks to enter upon the discussion of a sub- ject requiring more of self-preparation than they appear to have given to it; sorry that so laudible an object should be imperiled by the introduction of matter which, ,if not irrelevant, is apparently above their capacity for its adequate treatment. Now it is in this treatment of the subject I find amusement; albeit amusement not un- blended with sorrow that the young men of the Christian Association have not bet:er mental pabulum provided for them than what is here reported. lam not acquainted with Mr. J. Horton, but think had he been a shoemaker discoursing on "Sole Improvement " the subject would at least have been free from its present vagueness, been more practical, and been less likely to lead the essayist into making statements for which he can assign neither reason nor probability.

PARISH CHI7RCH TEMPERANCE SOCIETY.—Two entertain- ments were given in the Drill Hall, one. on Friday, and the other on Saturday evening, in aid of the funds of the Parish Church Temperance Society. The programme consisted of tableaux, illuminated with the oxycalcium light, descriptive of well-known songs and pictures. WESLEYAN MUTUAL ,IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY.—A meeting in connection with the Wesleyan Mutual Improvement Society was held in the schoolroom on Monday evening, Mr. E. Winston being in tho chair. A paper on "The Atonement" was read by Mr. F. Moston. A discussion followed, in which Messrs. E. Moston, Brown, Brereton, and Briggs took part. PRIMITIVE METHODIST BAND OF HOPE.—An entertain- ment in connection with the Band of Hope was given in the chapel, on Tuesday evening, Mr. Joseph Thorpe in the chair. Mr. H. Beale, of Manchester, delivered an address, and Mrs. Beale sang at intervals during the evening. Songs, recitations, &c., were also given by the members. The collection was in aid of the Band of Hope funds.

div.p: LYMM.
CADISHEAD.

MISSION HALL.—On Monday evening a series of ori- ginal views, illustrating the mode of construction of the Manchester Ship Canal, were exhibited in the above hall by Mr. C. R. Sayer. Among the series were views of the bridges and locks in different stages of completion. There was a fair attendance. Mr. Moorson presided. ENTERTAINNENT.-4 public entertainment was given in the schoolroom, on Saturday evening. Mr. C. Martin presided. Mr. J. Wood, of Cadishead, addressed .the audience, taking as his subject "What can we do to stem. the evil of intemperance?" and showed that it touched us in our trade, our homes, our churches, our schools, and our personalty. His address was heartily applauded. Miss S. Whitfield rendered a solo. The entertainment was well attended, and a collection was made to meet expenses. WESLEYAN CHAPEL.—Sunday being the day set apart by the Wesleyan Conference as Temperance Sunday, the preacher, Mr. John Bennett, of Didsbury College, gave a sermon in the morning upon total abstinence. In the evening he preached an evangelistic sermon, in which he denounced hypocrisy, and spoke severely against long- faced Christians. The choir sang "Peace be still !" There was a very fair congregation. In the Sunday school temperance addresses were delivered by the superintendents and teachers.

SHA.KESPEA.II33 AND RELIGION.

In connection with the Mutual Improvement Association an essay entitled "Shakespeare and Religion" was read by Mr. J. T. Budden. Mr. T. Gandy (the president) occupied the chair. There was a good attendance. Mr. Budden said he could not altogether agree with the way in which Shakes- pear's plays and their author were held up in the pulpit and other places as models for the public to copy from. Shakespeare lived a life very.much at variance with the opinions advanced in his works. Ile had also obtained the matter for some of his compositions from sources other than his own. .At the close of the essay a discussion followed,in which Messrs. Packer, White, Peers, Gandy, and Mrs. R. Garnett took part. Mr. Budden replied, and the meeting closed.

div.head: TEMPERANCE SUNDAY,
div.p: TEMPERANCE SUNDAY,

Sunday was the day appointed by the Wesleyan Conference for the special consideration of the temperance qudetion. In connection with the Wes- leyan Chapel at Penketh, the pulpit was occupied morning and evening by the Rev. Mr. Armstrong, of Diclsbury College. In the morning Mr. Armstrong preached an excellent sermon on the benefit of total abstinence, both as regards the moral and physical phases of the quWion, and showed in an able and lucid manner the dire and ill effects of intempe- rance. The sermon was attentively 'listened to. There was a good congregation. In the afternoon Mr. Armstrong delivered a temperance- address in the Sunday school to the 'Schdlar.3. It was very interesting, and much appreciated by all present. Other teachers also spoke on the question.

div.head: DROWNING ACCIDENT AT WIDNES.
div.p: DROWNING ACCIDENT AT WIDNES.

Yesterday, Mr. W.T. Husbanct. deputy coroner, held an inquest at Widnes, on the body of Frank Whitfield, of 12, New-st., who was drowned in the St. Helens canal on Wednesday afternoon. The evidence showed that deceased was master of the flat Henry, belonging to the United Alkali Company, used for the purpose of carrying acid. On Wednesday, he berthed the boat near Hutchison's works, and with the intention of going ashore he made a jump to a fiat lying near by, but he dropped into the water between the two. He seized a rope .but before the boy on board could aid him he released his hold and fell in the water and was drowned. A verdict of accidental death was recorded.

TilE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, DECEMBER 5 1891. BRIMSTOOAN AN' TRAYCLE. THE REV. C. GARRETT AT -TsuxED.) - - WARRINGTON. On Wednesday a meeting in connection with the Wesleyan Band of Hope was held in Bold-street Schoolroom, Warrington, and was addressed by the Rev. C. Garrett. Mr. R. Garnett, J.P., presided, and amongst those on the platform were the Revs. J. Gunnell, A. Freeman, T. Ross, F. K. Freestou, and J. WPrnock, Mr. S. B. Stringer, &c. The CHAIRMAN said it was always a pleasure to come and hear Mr. Garrett, and he was just thinking as he came along what should they do if Mr. Garrett was not here ; he had done so much,and not only in Liverpool, but also in other parts of the country, to spread the truth on that great question. Whatever their opinion might be as to total abstin- ence in adults there could be no question about the 'benefit to be derived from it in the training of young people. (Hear, hear.) They had throughout the ' country a large number of Bands of Hope,and he was not without hope that the million members which had been sought for would be obtained during the present year. Bands of hope had been doing glorious work for some years,and it was very grati- fying to know that the religion of the present dal, combined with it something more than in his memory it used to do. (Hear, hear.) The great question that was put before their good Methodist people years and years ago was how to get their souls saved, a very important thing, but their bodies were very often a secondary question. He was very glad to say that, to-day, the servants of God were labouring ardently and earnestly with right principles with reference to that great and importaut question. He did not think there was anything that could, be considered more important to-day than that their children should be trained With right views and right principles. Early training made all the difference in life. What they wanted to do was, if possible, to put a barrier betwixt the unpolluted lip of the child and the intoxicating cup. (Hear, hear and applause.) They were sometimes successful in reclalin- nig some besotted drunkard and helping him to a better and nobler life, ,but in the case of children it was very much better if they never learned the taste, and had not the bitter lessen of having to give it up. (Ap- plause.) Mr. PERKINS then gave a report as to the financial con- dition of the Band of Hope. The Rev. C. GARRETT, who was received with loud applause, referred to the wonderful change. that had taken place in regard to the temperance movement in his time. At one time everything wad against them, but novv all was changed. Temperance had become part of their Methodist organisation,and it would be just as easy to eliminate their Sunday school agency or their mission- ary agency as their temperance agency. It had become apart of their organisation and a part of immense im- portance, and yet they were only at the beginning of what would have to be carried on and completed by the boys of to-day. He had been told if they did not touch the drink it would not touch them, but it touched them on every side. It affected their trade, in regard te which there were competitors springing up on every side. A gentleman who had been in America had told him that when he looked at that country, at what was going on there, the agencies at work and the temperance that pre- vailed, he felt sure that unless they waked un very early in England they would have to take a back seat., As bearing upon this part of the question he alluded to losses which were *unstained by manufacturers owing to workmen not coining to their work at the proper hours at the early part of the week, and he quoted an instance in which one large firm was said to have lost £30,000 a year from this cause alone. He was of opinion that if publicans got the money out of a man by making him drunk they.ought to be made to take their finished work home. (Hear, hear and laughter.) They had twelve million of British children in this land, and the greatest enemy to those children was drink. He asked all the boys and girls present to remember Ihree reasons for not taking.drink—because it was dear, de- ceitful and destructive.' (Hearrhear and loud applause.) Mr. S. B. STlNoiliz, in moving a vote of thanks to Mr. Garrett and the Chairman,said he was that night inspired with more hope for Bold-at, than ever before when he saw so many young people, and he'trusted that would be the beginning of a grand and glorious work in connection with their church and throughout the whole town. (Ap- plause.) The Rev. F. K. Freeston seconded the vote of thanks, and referred to the long and noble stand Mr. Garrett had taken on that sacred question. It was sonietimes said that Warrington was a town about as bad as they "make 'em "in regard to the temperance qpestion, but in the early days of the temperance movement there were 'men in Warrington who did very good work. He had recently been reading that interesting book, Mr. Winskill's history of the temperance question. The book was very beautifully illustrated and amongst the illustrations they would see one young man in the bloom of health, looking as though teetotalism were not a dreary thing at all, and underdeath that picture were the words" Robert Garnett of Warrington." (Applause.) rhe vote of thanks was then put to the meeting and carried with acclamation.

• -Mr. Joseph Harrison, who has for 14 years occupied the post of Station Master, at Latchford, has been promoted to the responsible position of night stationmaster at Lime-st. Liverpool. The post is a new one, and will necessitate Mr. Harrison being on duty from five o'clock in the evening until two in the morning, Between these hours about 70 passenger trains are received and 50 despatched from this important centre. The new duties will be commenced on Monday week. Mr. Harrison will be much missed at Latchford. He is an active worker in connection with both the Wesleyan Mis- sion and the Good Templars. He is one of the trustees of the Latchford Temperance Hall, and is society steward for the Wesleyans and treasurer of the Sunday School. He is highly esteemed as Stationmaster, being courteous and obliging to all classes, whilst watchful of the interests of the Railway Company. Mr. Harrison's successor at Latchford will be Mr. Potts, who is at present sta- tionmaster at Middlewich. Other charges ensue, Mr. Scraggs of Fiddlers Ferry going to Standon Bridge near Stafford, while his post is. taken by Mr..llavid Ellison of Latchford. Mr. Ellison is at present clerk to Mr. Ash urst at 'Bank Quay Station and is to be congratulated, like Mr. Harrison, upon deserved promotion.
MA.RRIA.GE AT THE FRIENDS MEETING HOUSE.

A, most interesting ceremony took at the above place of worship on Thutsday last week, when the marriage olltobert Nightingale, of Lymm (son of Johu,and Elizabeth Nightingale), and Edith Raw- linson, I, Academy Place, Warrington, only 'daugh- ter of James and Jane Rawlinson, was solemnized in the presence of a large kattpiring of friends, who heartily joined in wishing happiness and prosperity to the bride and bridegroom. From the fact that a long 'interval had elapsed since a like ceremony was witnessed, viz., in 1868, and also as the bride and her parents were well known in connection with the welfare of the school, and the liouse,eyery effort was made to show the esteem and respact felt towards them. The ceremony was a(most impressive one, and not soon to be forgotten. Prayer and ex- hortation were offered with earnestness for divine guidance, by Mr. Walker, of EccleF a ministPr of the Friends. Alderman and Mrs. Holmes, along with many esteemed Friends,were also present. At the close a photo was taken of the party by Mr. Lud- wig, of Bridge-st. Kindly expressions were offered to the newly married people at the two meetings held in the Mission Room, during the afternoon and evening. The bride was attired in a dress of shot silk trimmed with white swan's down. Miss Dickinson, of Wigan, was the bridesmaid, and U. L. Nightingale,of Lymm,brother of the bridegroom, best man. The presents were very .numerous, and were much admired by all.

"Thine were size ov a shillin', an' mine were ten times as big, becose they were as big as hofe-a-sovran!" Aw hooap nobody'll spoil this bi tellin' me aw should said twenty times as big as a shillinrfor they were th' size ov a sovran * * This week, like Macbeth, we "have supp'd full with horrors "—wod wi' morthers, suicides' acci- dents, fires, explosions, an' one thing an' another. Aw were on th', spot two minutes after th'explo- sion i Blegburn, an' ow meet as weal try to fly as try to tell heaw aw felt when aw fost clapt mi' eeu on ti' gap o' fifteen yards or moore, med i' one o' th' principal streets i' less nor a miunte's time; aw've ne'er heeard o' owt Elie id sin' aw were horn. Well, it's a good job id dudn'd happen ov a merkut day, or th' loss o' life wod ha' bin summat awful. Some o' th' wonderful escapes are r'aly marvellous, for leeavin' eawt o' th' question th' landlord missin' bein' smoor'd, brunt to deeath, an' dreawned, aw'm towd as a woman were gooin' into th' bazaar wi' a -child o' four or five ; th' child run away fro' her— as childer will—an' till hoo wei.e fotchin' id back th' explosion took place. Then, another woman were gooin' into th' bazaar but hoo dudn'd ayther on ackeawut o' th' strong smell of gas, or some other cause: onyway, hoo hedn'd bin gooan moore ncr hafe a minute afoore th' blow up. This terrible affair teyches us a lesson, an' thad is nod to let onybody meddle wi' owt they dorn'd understand, an' nod to do sooa us-sels ; i' this ease th' cost is five lives, an' no end o' trouble for five families. Aw darsay some fooak 'll mak a strong, arg yment fro' id i' favour o"lectric leet for heaw see an streets, and everything considered aw'm i' favour on't mysel'. Wod a scandalous affair this Russell case is! Iv he nobbut dud hafe o' wod he's said to ha' done he owt to ha' th' "cat," an' be tarred an' feathered. It's thib trash as sets fooak to thinkin th' aris- tocracy owt to be sweArt off th' earth °together ; they doru'd step and th c, an' see as he'd just ha' acted th' same iv he'd biu a collier or, a weyver, or owt else but a Earl. Th' grand owd name o' noble- mon hes fairly bin dragged through th' clutch, an iv aw mon suggest a new readin' for some on 'em id wod be ignoble mon.
AN OTHER 0 REAT GAS EXPLOSION.
SIX MEN INJURED.

An alarming gas explosion occurred at Anderston Cross Glasgow,on Wednesday,the street being torn up, and six men seriously injured. It appears that the foreman of the work on the underground railway went into a por- tion of the workings with a naphtha lamp,and a tremen- dous explosion immediately occurred. The street sank, and flames shot forth. Of the six men injured, Mc- Govern and McLachlan were removed to the Infirmary. The remaining sufferers are Constables McMillan and Patterson, and Messrs. Lundie and Moulson.

div.head: BURTON CYCLE CO.
div.p: THE BURTON CYCLE CO.

This Company, which has, its .business in War- rington, has been exhibiting a number of machines at the Stanley Cycle Show, at the Crystal Palace. Their excellence and novel features have attracted no small attention. One of them was illustrated in the" Daily Graphic" OrMonday, and described as the travel-stained record breaker. "The Examiner and Times" _ _

"The Burton Cycle Company, of Warrington, whose anti-friction soring-framed machine has already made some reputation for its patentee, have introduced a rear driving safety bicycle in which the chain is supertieded by an ingenious arrangement of cog whcels. The effect Is marvellous, a speed of two milea an hour in excess of that of any other machine being guaranteed, whilst for- hill climbing it is clear that a .directly working cog wheel has more purchase than a chain." "sport and Play" follows suit with the following reference:— .

"Burton Cycle Co., Warrington.—ln reviewing the exhibits of this firm at Oa last Stanley Show, we prop- hesied a sucoessful career for the Burton anti-vibration safety, which a,t that tune struck us as being a real good thing, and the development of events has proved the correctness of our anticipations. Some slight alterations of detail have been effected sinae that date, but the principle of construction remains the same. Six mac- hines in all are on view; 'and the chief specialty is a patent anti-friction driving gear safety, in which chain is entirely dispensed with by means of a large interme- diate gear wheel, fitted with a series of bronze rollers working between the cogs and communicating with the driving wheel and the cog wheel on rear hub. The back fork is made in two parts, and the bearing for the large intermediate wheel is: formed at the junction of the fork. We were shown a machine fitted with the Burton anti- vibration atrangement, which has travelled some six thousand miles during the past seasqn without a single mishap, and those_ who liave ridden it speak in _high terms of praise of its easy runaing qualities."

div.head: CONCERT AT PRESTON BROOK.
div.p: CONCERT AT PRESTON BROOK.

A very pleasant and successful concert took place in the Preston Brook Mission Room, on -Wednesday evening. The programme consisted of thirteen items, but, owing to the many encores, reached over twenty before the close. , The first part opened with a pianoforte :duet " Zainpa," and was performed with great skill and power by the Misses Earp and McWbannell. The second part was opened by Miss Whitley,who played Sydney Smith's" Fairy Queen" with brilliancy and taste. Miss Wright, of Halton, sang "Little Guardian and " Commn thro' the Rye,". both of which were encored. Miss Hether- ington, ot Runcorn, sang "Only tired" and The song that reached my heart," and was also twice encored. Mr. Morris, of Runcorn, gave "Love's request "and "Anchored," and also had to treat the 'audience to two more; and Mr. Scott of Runcorn, who supplied the comic part of the entertainment, was twieo recalled. The other performers were members of the Preston Brook choir, who gave two glees in a very charming manner, in addition to which the Misses Jones and Clare and Mr. C. Jones sang a trio" Ye shepherds tell me ;" tin d an encore was called for but not responded to. Mr. C. Jones rendered "Blow high, blciw low" in good form, whilst he and Miss Jones gave the well-known duet "Very swpicious for which they received an encore. The concert finished with the National Anthem. Miss Jessie McWhannell was the able accompanist. Before the close the Rev. T. Clark, who Presided, moved a vote of thanks to Mr. W. R. Earp for his trouble in getting up the entertainment which had been so successful and which he was sure they had all thoroughly enjoyed, and also to the performers—some of whom had come a consider- able distance—for the very good selection of music which they treated them to. This resolution was received with acclamation. Mr. Earp in replying said he was much pleased indeed to note the way in which that resolution was received, and he thanked them more on behalf of the performers than for himself. for he was sure that what little work had devolved on him had been more a pleasure than a trouble. At the same time he wished to point out that,after all,the audience deserved the most thanks, for no matter how much trouble were taken nor what talent presented itself it was in the audience where the great success lay. He was sure he could thank every one of that audience very heartily 'on account of the performers, both-for the very appre- ciative way in which they bad received them on the stage and also for the very hearty vote of thanks . that had been passed.'

On Thursday evening a large attended meeting was held at the Co-operative Hall, .•!,ankey-street, on the occasion of a meeting in connection with the above-named society. Mr. George Wallington, in the absence of Mr. Thomas Morris, through a press- ing engagement, presided, and there were also present Mr. Curran, surveyor to the society; and Messrs. Dell, Taylor, Horrocks, and Hayward, .Directors.—The Chairman read a letter from Mr. Morris explaining that he could not be present. A lime-light entertainment illustrative of Stanley's experience in Africa and of" Happy homes of the people "and "What Perfect Thrift Building Societies ! can do for the people," was then given by Mr. Wm. I Horsley, of Harrogate. Subsequently the Chairman I made some remarks, after which Mr. Horsley daily- I erect a lecture on " How to live rent free." I The society, he said, had three distinct objects. It ! was a purely Co-operative Building Society.; it could be used as a savings bank, and it gave pro- tection in case of death, by a free ballot at death I Ass Building Society it consisted of 399 members,* ! called ballot members, who paid • subscriptions of 6d., Is., is. 6d.. and 23. per week. Each GI. repre- sented a share of the value of £lOO, and members were entitled according to subscriptions to receive an appropriation of from .111100 to £4OO, and to use this money in the purchase of a house, houses, or land, repaying the same at rate of £6 per hundred per year, for 16 years and eight months, without inteYest. Having obtained the house for say £2oo,he took the rent for it and paid that to the society in yearly.monthly,or quarterly instalments and in 16 years and eight months had paid for tfie house. The society would be used as a savings bank, thus.: If he did not wish to use his appropria- iott_h_e, ceuld sell it to anyone or to the society, and the societfs-pricp. wa, £lO, with all subscriptions returned. This was better than a five per dentrhan. vestment. Again if a member did not wish to wait , for his ballot, he could purchase £lOO to £4OO from , the society at a deferred payment of £75 for £2O0— that was an annual payment of £l6 10s. For £2OO he could purchase a house that would produce at least £l2 a year rent, by paying only an additional sum of £4 10s. a year, extended over the 16 years and eight months. In addition to these advantages the society gave a free ballot in case of death to the deceased's representatives. Subscriptions on notice being given ceased to be payable, in case of sickness or being out of employment,and sick members took; part in ballots. Several questions were asked by Mr; W.Diggle and others, and answered; and a vote of I thanks to the Chairman closed the proceedings.

div.head: DR STEVENSON'S HOMES.
div.p: DR STEVENSON'S HOMES.

MUSICAL 'MEETING IN THE PUBLIC HALL. On Thursday evening, the Public Hall was well filled with an alipreciative audience, to hear a musical entertainment provided by one of Dr. Stevenson's choirs, on behalf of the above homes. The choir, which numbered about 30:boys and girls, was under the conductorship of Mr. F. A. Mann: After the choir had sung "Angels of Jesus," the Rev. A. Freeman engaged in prayer, after which the Rev. J. Gunnell addressed a few words of wel- come to the children and friends, and then called upon Mr. Charles Parker, of Penketh, to preside. Mr. Parker, who was received with applause, said it appeated to him that a special obligation rested ' upon the people of Warrington to support institu- tions like the Children's Home. All efforts to del with social Wreckage had a right to claim from this town practical help. Warrington was somewhat celebrated for its leather manufacture, for its large. iron and wire Works, but its chief claim for distinc- tion sprang from the quantity and quality of its ales. Who has not heard of " Warrington ales"? Who had not seen something of the misery,squalor, and wretchedness which sprang from and gathered round the well-known signs in neighbouring towns? In the abser,ce of representative men he would in the name of the good friends there, in the name of the people of Warrington, and in, the name how- ever unworthy he might be to say it, in the name of the great liquor trade, he would bid Sister DOI% and the children welcome. (Applause). The chileren then went through their Programme consisting of solos, duets, choruses, which were very much appreciated by the audience. During the interval Sister Dora apologised for the children being un- able to give encores, owing to the length of the programme, and also apologised for the absence of her father (Dr. Stevenson) he being engaged on im- portant business in connection with Wesleyan Methodism. She then gave a short account of the method of conducting their work in the homes. They have at the present time nearly 900 ceildren distributed in the several homes, one of which is in Edgworth, Lancashire, their ages ranging from as early as three weeks, to fourteen or fifteen years. Since the commencement, over 3,000 had passed through their homes which children had hailed from different parts of the country so that, they felt justified in calling for help from the general public. The children were taken into the e'homes irrespective of the creed of their parents, or of any inequality, and without reference to their age. The girls are taught domestic work, whilst the boys follow different handicrafts. Sister Dora stated that by means of their own skill, in their indus- tries, such as printing, &c., they were able to swell the funds by 000. (Applause.) At the close of the programme, Sister Dora pro- posed a vote of thanks to Mr. Parker for presiding, after which the meeting terminated by the singing of the National Anthem. SAD DEATH OF AN OSTLER. Shortly after three o'clock on Friday afternoon, Benjamin Sweeney, formerly an ostler employed at the Legh Arms Hotel, Golborne,who was admitted a few days previoUsly into the Leigh Workhouse, died from the kick of a horse. On Tuesday morn- ing, Mr. J. W. Barlow, deputy coroner, held an inquest on the body at the Leigh Workhouse. The horse, which was a young one, kicked him in the abdomen. The jury returned a verdict that the deceased met his death in an accidental nianner.

On Wednesday afternoon a Sale of Work was opened in St. James' Schoolroom, Latchford; by Mrs. T. H. Lyon, of Appleton Hall. There was a good attendance, amongst those present being the Mayoress (Mrs. E. Greenall), Mrs. Beamont, Mrs. Willis, Mrs. Parr, Rev. B. C. E. and Mrs. Carleton, Mrs. Lister Kaye, Mr. and Mrs. C. S. Burgess, Mr. and Mrs. H. N. Houghton, Mr. Tauranac, Mrs. M. EdleSten, Mrs. Chandley, Mrs. John White, Mrs. Melville, Mrs. Harrison, Dr. White, &c. The stalls were presided over by the following :—Fancy stall, Mrs, Slater, Mrs. H. N. Houghton, Mrs. Picton, Mrs. G. Venn, Mrs. Marsh, Miss White ; plain work stall. Mrs. Warburton, Mrs. Hall, Miss Parry, and Miss E. Taylor ; china stall, Mrs. .J. H. Warburton, Miss Hedgecock, and Miss Middlewood ; toy stall, Miss Connibear and Miss Perry Williams; flower and fruit stall, Mrs. Herbert Woods, Misses Taylor, and Miss A. Garnett ; doll stall, Miss 11. Slater, Miss M. Broadbent, Miss M. Blackly, and Miss A. Burgess ; Tpfreshment stall,Mrs. Fairhurst. Mrs. Wignall, Mrs. , • • : d Mrs. Newall. The Rev. F. Slater, in alew intro. atory remarks, eaid that, as St. James' parish Was not a very rich one, they had every year- a sale of work to help their offertory. The needs of the parish were, at the present time,rather 'exten- sive.- In the first place they must have £4O if they 'could get it in order to make expenses balance at Easter. Then they wanted several very necessary re- pairs done,and he supposed if they liad£BotheY would be able to meet the churchwardens' expenses. Their Day School also wanted some help, and they hoped to get some £2O for those schools. They had done extremely well in their examinations this year, and ;.they quite expected they would get the excel- lent merit grant, and if they did that, they should have earned more than they would have given to them, as they would not have had an equal amount from other sources. To avoid that another year they wanted £2O. The whole of these sums would amount to £lOO, and last year they raised £Bo.—Mrs. LYON then, in a few appropriate remarks, opened the sale of work. A vote of thanks was then passed to Mrs. Lyon, on the motion of the Rev. F. SLATER, seconded by Mr. C. S. BURGESS.

div.head: SALE OF WORK AT BURTONWOOD.
div.p: SALE OF WORK AT BURTONWOOD.

In connection with St. Michael's Church, Burton- wood, a two days' sale of work was opened on Thursday afternoon, at two o'clock, in the school- room, by Mrs. Willis, wife of the Rector of Warring- ton, in the unavoidable absence of Mr. James Warburton of Dallam, who could not attend on ac- count of the death of a relative. There was a fair atten- dance, and before the opening ceremony, the Rev. I. Johnson said, of course they were all aware of the object they had in view, which was to clear off the expense in the church, incurred by the new heating apparatus and other repairs which had been cafried out during the last few months. For the comfort of the worshippers, the wardens had expended about £l5O, and it was their de- sire to clear that off before other things were taken in hand. (Applause.) Mrs. Willis then formally, declared the bazaar open,and said she liked bazaars, because they made such a kindly feeling among the parishioners, and drew them together. (Applause.) The sale then proceeded, there being four stalls laden , with useful and fancy articles, and a fairly good business was done. The following ladies had charge of the stalls; Mesdames Wilson, Johnson, Mouncey, Jno. Fairclough, T. Hewitt, Ganthorpe ; Misses Rimmer, Fairclough. Nor- cott. Warburton, N. Webster, Sharpies, E. W. Webster. —The refreshment stall was in charge of Miss Howard and Miss Jackson. In the evening a concert was given by Mrs. Latimer and several friends from Earlestown.

RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.

The monthly meeting of this Authority was held at the Workhouse, Warrington, yesterday morning. The Rev. G. E. Roberts presided, and there were also present- Messrs. Long, Heaton, Aukland Owen, Mather,Kilshaw, W. Houghton, Jolley, J. Houghton, Humphreys, Swinton; S. Sutton (clerk), W. Owen (surveyor), Dr. Sephton (medical officer), and F. Kerfoot (inspector of nuisances.) TeNnetts.—Tenders for the piping of a ditch at Orford, were considered, and that of Mr. F. T. Bennie was ac- cepted. PLANS.—The following plans were submitted and ap- proved : Mr. Newton, house at Grappenhall ; Mr. Bing- ' ham, six houses at Sankey; Monks, Hall, and Co., exten- sion of mills. THS DEATH RATE.—The Medical Officer reported that during the past month the number of births had been 28 and the number of deaths 16. The death rate, was 15 per 1,000, as compared with 18.7 during the last three months, and 73 in the corresponding month last year. COMPENSA.TION.—The Clerk reported that the Corpora- tion- of Warrington had paid over to the Authority the sum of £1,062 which was agreed upon as their propor- kion of the loan in reference tothe sewers in the Winwick i•oad district which had now been taken over by the Corporation. • THE LIGHTING QUESTION.—The Surveyor reported that the Street Improvement Committee had considered the letter from Mr. Haddock, the manager of Warrington Gas Works, estimating the cost per 'tamp, both in Pad- gate and Penketh to be £3 per annum, but subject at the end of a year to a change of conditions and after a time, if the Corporation required it, the lamps to be purchased by the Authority and the amount of gas con- sumed paid for. The Committee decided that under no circumstances would they agree to purchase the lamps and pay for the gas, but that they would offer for the lighting of Padgate 14.3. per lamp per annum, and for the lighting of Penketh £3 per lamp, in consequence of the greater distance for the lamp-lighters to travel. Afterwards, the Committee attended at the gas offices and met the Gas Committee. The Clerk laid the case before the Gas Committee, and in the case of Padgate the Gas Committee accepted the terms of £2 14.5. per lamp per annum for eight lamps,and in the case of the 10 lamps at Penketh promised to sent he Clerk, a reply in time for the meeting that morning. The Gas Committee pro- mised that the lamps in Latchford should all be fixed before the 4th of December, and they were now fixed. —-A letter wasTead from MI.. Taylor, secretary of the Gas Committee, stating that the Committee were pre- pared to carry out the scheme of lighting Penketh on the following conditions : Ist The Rural Sanitary Authority to find a responsible person to light the lamps ,the said person to be engaged by the Gas Department at 7s. per week. 2nd, the lamps to be lighted at dusk and put out at midnight during a period of 40 weeks each year. 3rd, the Gas Department to be paid £2 18s. 9d. per annum, for each of ten lamps. 4th, the lamps to De fixed and maintained at the cost of the Gas Departmont. If the number of lamps be increased to 14. the price per lamp to be reduced to £2 103. 9d., and if there he a further argumentation of the- number a further decrease of the charge would be made.—This offer of the Gas Depart- ment was accepted.

LATEST NEWS.

SERIOUS ILLNESS OF THE DUKE OF DEVON- SHIRE. Lord Hartington, who was to have addressed the Unionist workers at Bacup, was suddenly summoned to Holkar Hall last evening owing to sudden illness of his father, the Duke of Devonshire. VERDICT IN THE RUSSELL CASE. Yesterday the Jury in the Russell matrimonial caSe retired at 18 minutes past five, and returned into court at 11 minutes past six with a verdict for the res- pondent, Earl Russell. The petition was accordingly dismissed. Lady Russell was not in court at the time, but Earl Russell waited for the verdict. He was re- ceived outside the court with mingled cheers and groans by a.large crowd. FATAL BOILER EXPLOSION. NEW YORK, FIZIDAY.—Number seventy-one Broadway was partly wrecked this morning by a boiler explosion. Several persons were killed,and among the injured is Mr. Rusiell Sage, the inillionaire financier. THE CHINESE REBELLION. Contradictory telegrams one to hand as to the rising in China. It is stated on the one hand that the rebellion is a comparatively small matter ; and on the other that a conflict has resulted in 600 rebels being killed.

SUSPECTED MURDER. -- Thomas Peter Griffiths, a collier, living Ttt Pentra Broughton, near Wrexham, 'is in custody charged with causing the death of a colliery fireman named William Jones. After a visit to Wrexham with Griffiths, on Mon- day, 23rd ult., Jones was found lying dead at the side of a railway, and inquiries by the police led to the issuing against Griffiths of a warrant, which was put in force on Wednesday. 410` DEATH OF LORD COMBERMERE. Lord Combercnere, of Combermere Abbey, Whit- • - church, who a few weeks since was run over by a cab in London, and broke his leg, died somewhat suddenly in London, on Tuesday night, at the resi- dence of his son, Richard Cotton, of the Coldstream Guards. Deceased was 71 years of age. He was popular with all classes, and was a well-known figure in the hunting field in Cheshire and Shrop- shire. There were few better judges of horses, and he frequently officiated at agricultural shows. His lordship's son, Robert Stapleton Cotton, comes to - the estate. The late lord, second Viscount Combermere, and a baronet, was born November 24, 1818. He sat as M.P. for Carrickfergus from 1847 to 1857. He was a D.L., and a J.P. for Cheshire, and a J.P. for Shrop- shire. In 1844 he married Susan Alice. daughter of Sir George Sitwell, and who died in 1869. His lord- ship had two sons and two daughters, the latter married, one to Lieutenant-Colonel Cecil Lennox - Peel, and the other to-Lord A. V. Paget, son of the second Marquis of Angelesey. Lady A. V, Paget's residence is at Tarporley, where also her father re- - sided. Captain Cotton-Joddrell, M.P. for the Wirral • Division of Cheshire, belongs to a collateral branch of the Combermere family. At Swansea, Swansea, on Thursday, a sailor named William - Smith, was remanded,charged with shooting a man at a, public-house last evening. The injured man's deposi- tions have been taken. Mr. Rowland Rogers, who has been organist of Bangor Cathedral for over twenty years, has resigned the ap- pointment, the Dean of Bangor having objected to his taking part in musical performances in Dissenting chapels.
